THE PARISH CHURCH DAY SCHOOLS.- 1_ The general circumstances attending the management of our Day Schools are now pretty well known, but the Managers wish to again remind parishioners that voluntary contributions towards the cost of maintaining, adding to and Improving the school buildings are of the greatest importance There is also the other point, that two of the Foundation Managers of each school will in future be appointed by its financial supporters, namely : —by Donors of £5 at any one time, and Subscribers of half-a-crown or more per annum for the three years immediately preceding the election. The next election will take place in March, 1907, and therefore votes can only he secured under the latter head by a sub- scription of is. ed, per annum to the three schools, or of 2sBd at least to one of our three schools before the end of Decem- ber. No response has yet been made to our appeal of last Spring, but the matter is one of such importance, we again urgently appeal so our many friends and well wishers in the parish, and trust that all will help towards safeguarding our Church schools by Contributing. Subscriptions of any amount sent through the Clergy, the Treasurers or any other of the School Managers. will be gratefully acknowledged. F. W. WILLIS, Chairman of Managers. The Rectory, Warrington, November, 1904.

THE PARISH clines DAY SCHOOLS.— Referring to the above circular t ) which we ask your kind and favourable reply, we give below some further facts and figures from which it will be clearly seen how greatly it is to the interests of Ratepayers that our schools should be kept in operation and efficient; but this cannot be done un. less the managers receive from voluntary sources an Annual Income varying in accordance with the requirements of each school. Recently, exhaustive inspection has been made of schools in Lancashire and Cheshire provided by the Education Authorities out of funds raised by rates and such schools are found to have cost from £l2 to £2l per bead of average attendance for buildings only. If therefore, our schools are taken at the lowest estimate say £l2 per bead, the value as per table appended works out to the large sum of £33,430. From these figures it will be seen at once that, apart from the question of religious teaching which is a vital one and must weigh with all good Churchmen, the closing of our Schools would necessitate the provision by the Educat:on Authority of other School Buildings at probably a greater cost than given below. This would mean a very heavy increase in the Education Bate which would be still further increased by the remission of school pence which now go to reduce the establishment expenses of the Education Committee, May I therefore press upon yon the importance of liberally contributing to the three Schools and ask you to kindly fill up the annexed form, giving the amount you are willing to subinribe and stating to which of these Schools you desire the amount to be appropriated, and forward it to me before the last day of this month. The above circular explains the privileges such Annual Subscriptions confer upon the donor. F. W. WILLIS, Chairman of Managers. The Rectory, Warrington, December 16th, 1904. more than ever convinced that the' man must have fallen asleep in his pantry end have dreamt it. But we were not done with her yet. A week or so afterwards, and when we were quite settled in, one of the maids who had been down to the village declared that on a path that led trough the shrubbery to a side gate she had met a lady who seemed in great distress. According to the girl's story she was wringing her hands. It was too dark for the maid to see her face. _

"You are quite sure of what you are saying?" I asked, when Simpson brought the girl into my presence. • "I am quite sure sir," was her reply. "I held the gate open for her to pass through. "Did she speak to you 1 " "Not a word, sir!. She just went by me as if she did not see me."

"This i; really one of the strangest things I ever heard," I said to my wife, when we were alone together. "I wonder who the woman is, and by what right she trespasses on my grounds? If I meet her, I shall put the question to her." Christmas was now drawing near, and we had invited a large house party to spend the festive season with us. Among the number was a young fellow named Desborough, who had just got his troop in a Lancer regiment. We had placed him in a room in the bachelors' wing, which was the oldest portion of the house. He and I were the two. first to reach the drawing - room before dinner.
"I say, old man," he began, "how many people have you got in the house?"
I t,Old gim.

"Yes, but who is the other one—the lady with the sorrowful countenance, and a jolly pretty one at that?" • "There is no one else," I replied. "I have given you the names of all of them." "Well, that's funny! For I'll swear she was no housemaid, and I've seen your wife's maid. Are you sure you are not rotting me ? " "Perfectly sure! Describe this mysterious individual to me." "Well, I'm not much of a hand at that sort of work,but I know that she was jolly good-looking, with what looked like a lace mantilla on her head, and she seemed to be in rare trouble. She was• wringing her hands and looked so sorrowfully at me. that for a moment I was almost tempted to ask her what was the matter." "Wait here a moment," I said. "I'll run upstairs and see if I can discover who this person can be."

I did so muttering as went that I was getting a hale tired of the lady's visits to my house. But though I searched the bachelors' wing and such other rooms as I could enter no trace of her coul4k I discover. I returned to the drawing-room and informed Desborough of my ill success.

"Well, you can say what you like," 'he answered. "I saw her as plainly as I can see you now." Thus the matter dropped for the time being. My wife was the next to be faveured with a glimpse of her. It was Christmas Eve, and the ladies had been down to the church to decorate the edifice for next day. It was almost dark when they started to return. My wife remained behind the party for about ten minutes to discuss artain matters with the Vicar. It was snowing heavily when she left the church, and the country looked indescribably beautiful in the light of the full moon. Her version of the story is that she had just left the shrubbery and was passing along the path that ran at the foot of the Terrace when she looked up and saw a woman, dressed in black, leaning with her hands upon it, looking down at her. She declares to this day that she was too surprised to be frightened, or to say or do anything. Then the woman walked away from her, wringing her hands as if she were in great grief. Three minutes could not have elapsed before I had been told, and was out on the Terrace in pursuit. I looked about, but there was no sign of her, and, stranger still, there was not a footmark other than my own upon the snow. The matter was getting beyond me. I could not make head or tail of it.

Next day, after the morning service, I took the Vicar aside and asked him if he could give me any clue to the mystery. I told him the matter was getting serious. The servants declared that it was a ghost, and, in consequence, were threatening to leave me. "Well, I will not deny," he said, "that some- thing of this sort of thing has been village gossip for a great many years, and more than one person has laid claim to having seen it. Personally I have never done so. The story goes that it is the spirit of a Spanish woman who was once the mistress of the house. If you will come into the church again I will show you a tablet to her memory." I followed him, and discovered the inscription in question. It described her (for reasons already stated I will not give her name) as being the wife of the owner of the house, and also set forth the fact hat she had died in the year 1782. "There's not much to be gained from that," I said. "But the coincidence is, to say the least of it, singular." I then thanked him and rejoined my party. That evening was devoted to the usual amuse- ments associated with the season. lam afraid we were all very juvenile, and must have shocked the grave Simpson. We played Dumb Crambo, acted Charades, and at last came to Thought Reading. In my turn I went out of the „room while an experiment was preparing. The hall was brilliantly lighted, and I give you my word that I had no thought of the 'mysterious lady at that moment. Suddenly I looked up to see her passing along the corridor at the top of the great staircase in the direction of the bachelor's quarter. Seizing a hat and coat' ran up the stairs just in time to see her turning the corr-A3r of the corridor. I set off in pursuit. She was evidently making her way to a little door that led by a flight of steps to the garden below. By the time I reached it she had disappeared. But throwing open the door I saw her passing swiftly along Ulla garden path towards the shrubbery. Donninrmy hat and drawing on the coat, I con- tinued my chase. She passed out of the Wicket gate and turned into the narrow lane that led towards the Tor. It was the night of full moon, and was almost as light as day. Without leaving any track upon the snow she sped on at such a rate that I had great difficulty in keeping her in sight. At last she reached the foot of the Tor and began the ascent. This was more than I had bargained for, for it must be remembered that my feet were in evening dress shoes and that the snow was lying inches deep upon the ground. However, having come so far, I was determined to see what the end of it all would be. Stagger- ing, falling, I began the climb, the black figure speeding on ahead of me, never pausing for a moment. At last it reached the summit and stood, -while perhaps I could have counted twenty, upon the topmost boulder. It made a weird picture, I can assure you. Then she raised her arms above her head and fell through the air to the rocks nearly two hundred feet below. On my honour it was so real that I gave a great cry as I saw it. I scrambled down to see if there was any sign of her, but there was none. The tragedy ended with her death. I went home scarcely able to believe the evidence of my senses. Next day I took Desborough up the Tor with me, and described the scene to him. I believe he thought I had dreamt it all. We stood at the foot and looked up at it. "By Jove! it would be a ghastly place to take a leap from," he said. 'ls that a cave up there ? "
He pointed half way up the face of the cliff. There certainly was a cave there.
"Perhaps that is thp clue to the mystery," I cried. "A man could be lowered to it from the top. As soon as the snow goes I'll have a look at it."

A week later I took several of my men and a strong rope and visited the Tor once more. After having taken every precaution they lowered me over the cliff till I reached the narrOw entrance to the cave. I managed to squeeze myself in, and then lit a candle which I had brought with fne. Three steps took me into a fair-sized cavern and shewed me as strange and terrible a sight as man has' ever looked upon. Stretched out upon the floor was the skeleton of a man; scattered round him were remains of books and what might once have been a blanket. I took up one of the books, and inside the cover found the name of the man whae wife's tablet I had seen in the village church on Christmas Day. Later on I examined it carefully. Inside was written: "I am dying of starvation. They will not let my wife bring me food. I have destroyed the papers. Farewell, my own beloved wife." Thus the mystery as solved. The poor remains were brought down from their long resting-place and decently interred. Since then the Black Lady, as the village folk call her, has not ben, seen. Ido not pretend to account for it. I simply give you the story. ETHI3 END.] ,

Board of Education. There was no desire on the part of the committee to say that the school was not f efficient. It had done splendid work in th,e past and they believed it would do still better work in the future but conditions might alter and the only guarantee which the public had was the Government inspector, and the fact of the school being recognised by the Board of Education which would mean the earning of an annual grant to help the finances. The Committee also asked for a majority of representatives on the govern- ing Board. Some little difficulty had arisen in that matter and there was some opposition to the Com- mittee's proposal. They suggested that there should ,be six representatives from the Warrington Council, one from the Lancashire County Council and one from the Cheshire County Council on the governing body of six- teen—that would give the bodies dealing with education in the immediate neighbourhood a majority. The com- mittee took it by the granting of financial aid they assumed financial responsibilites entirely for the school That would mean that if they gave financial aid at all, they must meet deficits. Under those circumstances they must surely have full control, because thpy would be responsible for the expenditure on the school. The Committee felt that in a town of the size and situation of Warrington, the Grammar School should have, instead of 80 or 100 students, at least 200. That,they considered, would be impossible with the present high fee, and they had advocated that there should be a reduction approxi- mating to about £3 per student per annum. The Committee asked that greater encouragement should be given to boys seeking admission to the ' Grammar School from Elementary and Secondary schools. They believed the Grammar School ought to be and would finally be the top of their 'educational ladder and they wanted to make it accessible to every- body with brains within the borough. By asking that , the appointment, dismissal, and determination of the staff should be rested in the governing body, the cora- -1 mittee were bringing the school into line with all modern tendency in that respect. The members would easily see the reason for the insertion of the clause in regard to the headmaster's remunerations. At present the headmaster was partly paid by the capitation grants and if the- committee expected an increase in scholars some modification should be made in that direction. Alluding to the Secondary school, Mr. Upson said that for some mysterious reason, the Board of Edncation were trying t,‘ tell the committee to increase the fee now paid by the scholars. Why they should do so he had never been able to fathom, but he noticed that other educational authorities were being troubled in exactly the same way. It seemed to the committee that, being responsible for the education of the children of the borough, they ought to make it possible for every child to have a higher and more advanced education than he could get- in the primary school. They believed that if they increased the fee to the extent 0f,.£3 per annpm they would very consider- ably lessen the number of children in the school and narrow the area from which the scholars were drawn. The committee were prepared to resist the Board of Education's request that they should practically double the fee, as long as they could resist anything. The Board had been somewhat reactionary in the second

I done more• satisfactorily by the existing voluntary methods. Personally, he (Alderman Bennett) thought that things of that kind done voluntarily and haphazard were not often done successfully. The only way to ensure that children gut proper instruction on the subjects was to make that instruction systematic, and not to leave it to the will of the individual headmaster. kla believed doctors sometimes had fads—(laughter)— but a recommendation coming from such a weighty body ought not to be ignored. The DIRECTOR read the petition which stated that I the object was to lead children to appreciate at their true value healthful bodily conditions, especially as to pure air, food and drink. Instruction should be given at an early acre on the nature and effects of alcohol. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said that amongst the numerous diseases to which Alderman Bennett refarred as having afflicted the town and neighbourhood for some time ;past, " wind " was a very serious one. If a hygienic course would do anything to romove mental flatulence he would support the amendment, but as he was afraid it would not, he should support the action of the Com- mittee.

Councillor CRAirc did not think Mr. Yonge sheath allude to the subject as though the Committee took it as a doctors' fad. It was not viewed in that light at all. What influenced the members of the Committee was the opinion advanced by two headmasters and the Principal of the Training College, who explained that the subjects were already taught in the public •elemen- tary schools—and probably more efficiently taught than they would be if the instruction was made compulsory. Mr. Ursos said he must protest against Mr.- Yonge putting into his mouth words which he never uttered. did not say the question was a fad, nor did he believe it to be so. What he did say was that he thought it would be a great mistake to put it on the time tables just as it stood. The members of the com- mittee had a great deal of sympathy with the object of the gentlemen who had signed the petition, and he did not think any class in the c otnmunity was so well aware of the evils of intemperance as were the teachers. They came into daily contact with some of the results of intemperance, and they did everything they possibly could to warn, instruct, and guide the children aright. A few months ago he dis- tirbuted in his school seventy-eight certificates stating that the children who received them had a scientific knowledge of alcohol. His scheme of instruction for standards I, 11, and 111 included scientific teaching on I alcohol. The laws of health were taught to all the girls who received instruction in the subject of domestic economy, which dealt with habits of cleanliness, and the need of pure air, water and food. Almost all the girls over eleven in Warrington were taught." cookery. If they were going to make instruction in hygiene and temperance compulsory, they became lessons to be taught in the same way as arithmetic, reading and writing, and the personal relationship between the teacher and the child was destroyed. Teachers were daily engaged in teaching the laws of health and they had before them constantly boys and girls who were violating those laws. In those cases the parents were sent for and the teachers pointed out to them the consequences of a persistence in those

BY GUY BOOTHBY.

I have seen some curious sights, and hare taken part in some equally curious affairs, in the course of my career, but I can safely assert that the story I am going to tcll you now equals, if it does not excel, anythirn•° I have ever known. I had . just come from South America, where I had been ranching for a good number of years, and, having been more successful than the majority of men who go in for that occupation, had returned to the Old Country with the inten- tion of making it my home fcr the remainder of my existence.

If you are prepared to spend the money it would not seem difficult to find a house of the description you require. Yet only those who have tried it know what a serious business it can be. One will be too large and without sufficient land, another too small and with more land than you care to be bothered with. My wife and I visited innumerable places, and at last were beginning to despair of ever finding what we wanted. Then, quite by chance, I happened to hear of the property with which this story is connected. It was necessary for me to visit Plymouth in order to meet a friend who was returning from Australia. The beauty of Devon is proverbial, and never prettier than in the autumn. After my long absence abroad, it had a charm for me that I find it difficult to express in words. The dark red soil, the luxuriant hedgerows, the babbling brooks, and the vast solitude of Dartmoor appealed to me with over- whelming force. This was the county for me' if only I could find the description of place for which I had been, so long and wearily searching. While I was awaiting the arrival of my friend's vessel, I made it my business to call on one of the leading house agents in order to make inquiries. Alas for my hopes! He had nothing on his books that I cared even to consider. I tried another, and yet a third, but with the same result. There were houses in plenty in the town, but they were useless; there were others in the immediate neighbourhood, but each had some drawback. I bade the last agent "Good-after- noon," and returned to my hotel very dis- appointed with my ill success. That evening my friend arrived p,nd, in the pleasure of welcoming him, I forgot for the time being my quest of a residence. I was nearer success, however,, than I imagined.

On descending to the coffee-room next-morn- ing I found a letter upon my plate. It was from the first agent upon whom I had called on the previous day. Quite by chance, he stated, he had happened to hearEof an estate situated in a charming little village on the edge of the moor. The house was an old and picturesque one, and the property consisted of some seventy acres. Some slight repairs would have to be effected, for the reason • that the house had not been inhabited for some considerable time, the owner being abroad and unable to keep it up. In conclusion it was stated that the estate would be either let on lease or sold outright. I carefully studied the particulars enclosed, and, as I did so, began to feel that it really looked as if I had dis- covered what I wanted. When my friend descended I told him the news, and invited him to remain a day longer in order to come out with me and inspect it. Ile consented to do so, and that afternoon we chartered a carriage and drove out.

There are reasons why I suppress the name o the village. They will, I expect, be obvious to you. Give a dog a had name and hang him, may apply as well to a property as to the canine race. The Hall, as the place was called, was on the further Aide of the village, and was on the very edge of the moor. The agent had described it exactly when he had declared it to be a picturesque old building. It stood on high"ground, and immediately behind it rose the steep side of Brin Tor, crowned with enormous boulders that gave it a strangely wild appearance. The house, itself was approached by a lengthy carriage drive, and, as I learnt later, had been built in the days of the early Georges. From the first moment that I saw it I liked it. We drew up at the steps and alighted.

I presented the housekeeper with the order to view, whereupon she examined it as if it were a banknote for a thousand pounds, and she was not quite certain as to whether it was genuine. At last, however, she condescended to admit us, and we entered the large, square hall. It was paved, and I must confess did not present a very inviting appearance. The oak pannelling, how- ever, was handsome, while the grand staircase was massive and finely carved. With no very good grace the old woman threw open the door of the room which I judged to be the dining- room; thence we proceeded on our tour of investigation. The house, with the exception of the kitchen and a bedroom, was quite unfurnished, and certainly stood in need of repair. It possessed, however, great possibilities, and I felt sure that when furnished and put in proper order it would make a charming dwelling. By the time our inspection was finished the afternoon was well advanced and, if we desired to get back to Ply- mouth in time for dinner, it behoved us to start at once.

That evening I wrote a long description of what I had seen to my wife, inviting her to join me in order that I might have her opinion. Next day she arrived. She proved to he as charmed with it as I was, and by the end of the week following matters were in excellent trim for my becoming its owner. As soon as the necessary legal formalities bad been complied with, my wife set off for London on furniture-buying thoughts intent, while I remained behind to hurry on the work that had to be completed before we could come into residence. At last—it was the second week in November, if my memory serves me— the furniture began to arrive. A makeshift bedroom was prepared for me, and I exchanged the hotel in Plymouth for my own abode. For the next few days my life was not altogether a bed of roses. Everything had to be arranged, the servants were new, while the furnisher's men required strict supervision to prevent them spending the greater part of their time at the village inn. However, it was all done at last, and I fclt that when my wife gave it the few finishing touches, which only a woman can do, it would be as nearly perfect as a man could wish to have his home.

It was on the day that my wife arrived that the first curious circumstance occurred which it is the purpose of this story to relate. We had finished dinner and were sitting in our drawing- room discussing affairs in general and wondering when the butler was going to bring in coffee. "I told him we would have it immediately after dinner," said my wife:,
_ I rang the bell and almost immediately he appeared in answer to it. He looked round the room in surprise as if he expected to find a third person present.
"We will have coffee, Simpson," said'my -wife. "Always let us have it as soon after dinner as possible." .
"You will excuse me, madam, but I thought you were engaged with a lady." "I have ET:in no lady."'
He looked'at her in bewilderment. "A lady came up the hall," he said, "just as you left the dining-room, and I thought she came in here." I looked at the man sharply; apparently he was sober.

"You must have dreamt it," I continued. "No, sir, I am quite sure I did not. I saw her quite distinctly, and would know her again any- where. She seemed in great trouble, so that is why I did not disturb you. I am very sorry, sir." He departed to bring in the coffee. When he returned I asked him to describe the person in question more minutely. I gathered that she was tall, and had a beautiful face, but with a very sad expression. She was dressed entirely in black, and had, what he callecl, "a black lace shawl" upon her head. The man was deeply in earnest, but I could make neither head nor tail of it.
"Let us look round," I said. "I am quite-sure that the hall door has not been opened since dinner, and if she is in the house now we shall doubtless and her."

Accompanied by my wife we set off and visited all the rooms on the ground-floor, not omitting the servants' hall. My wife questioned the maids, but one and all asserted that they had not been into the hall since dinner. We next tried all Elie rooms upstairs :with the same result. Simpson's mysterious black lady, if she had existed. was certainly not in the house, INA

div.head: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
THE FUTURE OF THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL
Board of Education and Secondary
School Fees.
THE TEACHING OF HYGIENE AND TEMPERANCE.

Less than an hour sufficed to transact the business before the Warrington Education Committee on Monday evening, but matters of considerable importance were dealt with. Mr. F. Monks presided and there were also present :—Alderman Bennett (vice-chairman), the Mayor, the Revs. John Yonge and Father Wilson, Councillors Wilkinson, Tingion, Craik, Lord, Sankey, Roberts, Ellison, Fulton Smith, Brough, and Burton, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, H. Kingdon, C. H. Unsworth, E. Plinston, R. T. Fairclough, J. Upson, J. 1/ Buckton, W. Bibby, G. Walker, and J. Moore Murray (director of education). a • THE FUTURE OF THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL. _IMPORTANT PROPOSALS. THE SECONDARY SCHOOL FEES.

- At a meeting of the School Management Committee a letter, dated the 19th November, 1904. was submitted from the governors of the Warrington Grammar school intimating that they consider that the committee's pro- posals in regard to the school should be first placed before the Board of Education before the governors express their views upon them. It was thereupon resolved that a reply be sent to the letter, dated the 20th August, 1904, from the Board of Education—which sun' -. gested an amendment of the scheme for the government of the school and a Contribution from the Committee to its funds—embodying the followine, observations :—(1) The Committee are of opinion that Local Authority ought not to grant any financial aid to the Grammar school until the school has been placed under the inspec- tion of and has been duly rocognised by the Board of Education; (2) the committee will be willing to recom- mend the Local Authority to grant such financial aid as may be necessary to make and maintain the" Boteler " Grammar school as an efficient secondary school, on the following conditions (a) that the gov,rning body of the school should be so re-constituted that a majority of its members shall be representatives of the Local Authorities—the County Borough of Warrington, and the Counties of Lancashire and Cheshire; (b) that there should be some reduction in the maximum fees charged, and it is suggested that such maximum fee should be £9, and the minimum £6; f,c) that greater encouragement should be given to boys seeking admission to the school rom the elementary schools at the age of 12. and from

the Secondary school of the Local Authority at the age of 14 years; (d) that the appointment, dismissal, and determination of the staff of the school shall be vested- in the governors ; and (e) that there should be a modifi cation of the terms of the present headmaster's remunera- tions, as, in view of the expected increase of scholars under the improved methods, the existing arrangements, especially inirespect of capitation grants, would be inequitable. A letter dated the 10th November, 1904, was submit- ted from the Board of Education, with reference to the Committee's application for the continued recognition of the Secondary school, and asking that the fee of ninepence per week, 10s. 6d, per term, and 30s. per annum, should be increased to not less than £3 per annum, and that exemption from such fee should be granted to not more than 25 per cent. of the total num- ber of scholars in the school ; and that the Head Mas- ter should be allowed to exercise the power of appoint- ment and dismissal of the assistant teachers in the school subject to the approval of the governors. It was decided that a reply be sent to the effect that, the amount of the fee was fixed after very careful con- sideration of the local circumstances, and that any in- crease therein would result in a considerable reduction in the number of children in the school ; and that the committee are not prepared to grant powers to the Head master of the school which they do not delegate to any othet of their officers, and that the appointment and dismissal of assistant teachers must rest with them. The committee recommended that Mr. Alderman Bennett, Mr. A. J. Jolley, Mr. J. Upson, and the director be appointed to represent the committee at the third annual meeting of the North of England edu- cation conference to be held at Liverpool on the 6th and 7th January, 1905. The committee also recommend that ,the railway fares of not more than 20 assistant teachers, desiring to attend the conference, be paid by the committee.
THE TEACHING OF HYGIENE AND TENIPERANCE.

, A communication, dated the Tith November, 1901 was submitted from Sir Williatn Broadbent. on behalf of the committe of the medical profossion of the United Kingdom constituted to pro- mote the teaching of hygiene and temperance in public elementary schools, asking the committee to sup- port their endeavour, by means of a petition to Parlia- ment, and also by provision being made for the training of the teachers in their schools to qualify them to give such instruction.

The committee felt that the introduction of the com- pulsory teaching of these subjects into the curriculum of their schools would not be as effective as the instruc- tion whiCh is being constantly and spontaneously given, and it was accordingly decided not to take the action suggested in the malter. In the absence of the Rev. Morley Stevenson, who was away from town. Mr. Upson moved the confirmation of the minutes. Dealing with the future of the Grammar School he said the committee were asked in the Board of Education's letter to make a definite grant which would, of course, ultimately come from the rates to meet a growing deficit in the management of the sehool. Before that aid could be given certain condi- tions must be fulfilled. In the first place the com- mittee asked that for the security of the general public the school should be certified to be etlicient by the

request they made, that the headmaster should have the appointment and dismissal of teachers. Masters in the primary schools did not appoint or dismiss, neither did the officials of the Corporation, and the committee did not see any educational advantage that would be secured by the adoption of the Board's suggestion. Alluding to the forthcominc, course of University Extension lectures on "The social questions of the present time" by Mr. S. J. Chapman, M.A., Mr. Upson said the committee anticipated that the subject selected would appeal to a very much larger public than the purely literary subjects hitherto lectured upon. The committee had secured a promise from Vice-Chacnellor Hopkinson, of Manchester, to distribute the prizes and certificates to the students at the School of Art, Secondary School, Pupil Teachers' classes, and the Technical Institute on January 19th. The gathering, which it was hoped would be a great success, would not be purely educational in character as the students of the Secondary School would present musical items.
Couniillor Caanc seconded the adoption of the minutes.

IThe REV. Jowl YONGE moved an amendment that the , committee should support the petition in favour of the compulsory teaching of hygiene and temperance in I , I the schools. He wished to know whether it was the ; , opinion of the committee that a very important , coMmunication from a most influential Source which he thought, commanded the respect if all thinking , people should be passed over in the rather cavalier style in which the sub-committee passed it. He was one if a , minority of two who voted in favour of recommending the acceptance of the suggestion and be would like the , committee to refute the decision. He knew his friend nr. Upson had a very strong opinion that the teaching of hygiene and still more particularly of tern- i ! perance n an elementary school was the introduction of something in the nature Of a fad. He (Mr. Yonge) did not , agree with that view at all. He did not think a body I , I including all the highest men in the medical profession , was given to fads. If the medical gentlemen .saw the I , importance of the instruction being given, it was hardly I for that Committee to look upon it as a mere fad, whim, , or caprice on the part of fanatical teetotalers, but as strong advice given by the most competent body to give i , it in the whole Kingdom. , The CHArttatlN suggested that it would be better if i Mr. Yonge moved that the resolution be referred back. I Alderman BEETT said he voied against the resolution I and he took largely the same view as Mr. Yonge, although he was not by means a fanatical teetotaler in fact he was not a teetoltaler at all. He thought the evils arising from drink were so ' greatand serious that anything which would tend to implant those evils strongly and vividly in the minds of Ithe children could not fail to be of very material benfit , in their after-life. As to hygiene, he thought that in face of the terrible diseases which had ravaged the town during the last few months and the last few years it was important that the children should be taught from the very earliest stages. the laws which tended to promote good health and sanitary and cleanly conditions. Mr. Upson contented that was

habits. The teachers were able to do far more good in that way than if the subjects were on the time table. The object the petitioners aimed at was being attained at the present time. Alderman BENNETT : In your school. Mr. UPSON: I think I may speak for all the schools in Warrington that I.know of. The Rev. JOHN YONGE said he wanted to disabuse Mr. Upson of the idea that he purposely misquoted him. He did not know whether Mr. Upson used the word fad in the discussion, but he used it in talking to him (Mr. Yonge) on the subject afterwards.
A Jo-te was then'taken and the amendment was lost. RAILWAY FARES FOR TEACHERS.

Mr. G. WA.LKFA referred to the decision of the com- mittee to pay the railway fares of twenty teachers at- tending the educational conference at Liverpool. He wished to know whether the committee were establish- ing a precedent. Mr. UPSON said the conference was one of great im- portance and the Chairman of the committee said that as it was meeting almost at their doors it would be a splendid opportunity for some of the teachers to have their minds broadened and illuminated by the great speakers who would address the meeting. It might be a considerable time before the conference was within easy reach of themagain. The Committee thought the money would be exceptionally well spent. Councillor LORD: Are we in order in sendingkhe money?
As Sir. Upson had replied the question was ruled out of order and the minutes were confirmed. THE CLOSING OF SCEIOOLS FOR BAZAARS AND TEA PARTIES. _ _ NEW RULES. _ _

The School Attendance Com—nalt—t-ee had resolved that the managers of the schools be requested to arrange for all bazaars, tea parties, ecc., to take place during the holidays; and that a school must not be closed for these purposes until application has been made to the committee and their sanction obtained.
Councillor ELLtsos moved the adoption of the minutes. Mr. WALKER seconded. _

The Rev. J. Y-0-.V-G-E said the resolution as to bazaars was rather an eye-opener and would land many churches and Sunday schools in a very considerable difficulty. The matter should be looked at very carefully as if the new rules were immediately enforced, arrangements which had already been made would he disturbed. He moved that the resolution be referred back. Councillor TINNION seconded, and contended that some notice at any rate should he given. Some managers had already entered into obligattons for the early part of the year.

The l'talrOrt observed that he saw no objection to the resolution as it stood, as application could be made to the Committee if managers wished to arrange for bazaars, Szc. He was sure the Committee would be generous enough to grant any reasonable request made to them. (Hear,hear.) Mr. PLINSTON said schools had been closed without notice and the consequence was there had been a loss to the town.
Mr. BUCKTON said he believed managers could close a school if they liked, hut they mast inform the committee

and the inspector. He agreei, however, that schools were often closed unnecessarily. The DIRECToW. stated that the Committee gave direc- tions to the managers as to the opeaing and closing of the schools. The holidays were arranged by the com- mittee and not by the managers. Councillor ELLisos said the committee had only one object in view, and that was a better attendance of the scholars which helped the rates considerably. There was nothing in the resolution to prevent a request being made to the committee for permission to hold a bazaar or a tea party at any time. The conarnitiee would seriously oonsider each application. acnendment waslost, and the minutes w ere approved. STREET NOISES AND TEACHING. WOODEN SETTS WANTED.

At a meeting of the Sites and Buildings Committee a letter was submitted from the manages of the Parochial School drawing attention ta the desirability of a wood block roadway being laid opposite the schookin Church street, but the committee regretted that they could not see their way to take any action in the matter. A further letter was submitted from the mangers, of the school, taking exception to the proportion of the cost of the recent painting and decorating of the school charged to there. The committee after consideration, could not] sea their way to make aay concession therein.

The IVaYort moved, ani Councillor Craik seem led, the confirmation of the minutes. Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH said he took exception to the committee declining to take action in the matter of the wood block roadway. The committee seemed to be shirking their work.

The 61AIRNIAS : Have you Only found that out lately? (Laughter). Mr. KußcLouGH,maintained that it was part and parcel of th 3 work of the committee to see that the schools were in such a condition that the teachers could do their work properly. The noise outside the church street school was so great that on Wednesday in parti- cular a child on the far side of a class could not her what the teacher was saying. Mr. WALKER said the inconvenience had been felt for years but the noise had been aggravated since the introduction of the tramways.

The CEIAIRNIAN : Is that -the real reason? Mr. WALKER replied in the arfirmative. He aided that it was almost impossible to hear what was said and hs did not know why the inspector had not drawn atten- tion to the matter.

Councillor TINNION said that if there was one thing he admired about Mr. Fairclough it was the bull-dog tenacity with which he stuck to a thing. (Laughter.) He had brought the matter before him (Councillor Tinnion) as chairman of the Paving and Sewerage Committee years ago. It was unfair to say the noise started with the introduction of the tramway. Mr. WALKER.: It has been aggravated, I said. Councillor TINNIoN said it seemed tb him that the managers had built schools which could only be ventilated by opening the windows and they expected the ratepayers to put their schools in order by putting down wood paving. Mr. FsurtoLouox : T. object to that statement. The schools are in a satisfactory state. They are the healthiest schools in Warrington to-day. Councillor TINNEON : I did not say they were not healthy, but you should put in double windows. The Paving and Sewerage Committee decline to spend money in the interest of any particular school. Alderman BENNETT thought the committee might consider in the case of new streets that required re-paving the desirablility of the wood pavement. That principle had been adopted in regard to places of worship and it was just as important that there should be_no excessive noise outside schools.
Councillor TINNION replied that as a paving and Sewerage Committee they had nothing at all to do with that.

The MAYOR : Mr. Fairclough ought to know that this is the Sites and Buildings Committee and not a Pavini-and Sewerage Committee. We have no funds for the purpose and cannot collect any. We have more trouble and bother from this particular school than from all the rest of the ton put together. It is very unfortunate that managers of schools should be on committes where they can air their own grievances. (Laughter.) The minutes were agreed to. THE NEW SCEIOOI.3.

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee the following report of the spacial sub-committee was con- sidered: Since their last report the sub-committee have met once, on the 9th December. The Afayor (the chairmln of the Sites and Buildings Committee) reported the result Of an interview he had had with H.M. Inspector on the subject of the recognition by the Board of the building to which it is proposed to transfer the St. George's Mission School, and it was resolved that the following resolution ba submitted to the Education Committee for adoption, viz :—'That this committee is prepared to give an undertaking to the Board of Education that the erection of the proposed" Bolton" Council School in Latchford and " Beamont ' Council School in Orford shall be proceede d with forthwith, and that they shall both be ready for occupation not later than August, 1906: Letters were submitted from the trustees of the Silver-street Wesleyan School, intimating that they would be pre- pared to accept the sum of £5,000 for the land and buildings, such sum not including the furniture and fittings, and it .was resolved, that, before proceeding further in the mat ter, the Borough Surveyor be requested to furnish the committee with a valuation of the land and buildings in question. It was also resolved that, subject to the use of the premises in Brick-street for the purpose of providing temporary school accommoda- tion to replace that provided at the St. George's Mission School being approved by the Board of Education, certain articles ~nt present in use at the last mentioned school be purchased at a cost of £25. At a further meeting of the special sub-committee it was decided to enter into an agreement with the trustees of St. George's Mission for a continuance of the tenancy until the last' day of July, 1906." On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. PUNSTON, the minutes were agreed to.

div.head: FATAL ERROR. Old Lady's Mysterious Death at Stockton Heath.
div.p: A FATAL ERROR. Old Lady's Mysterious Death at Stockton Heath.

The singular circumstances attending the death of Elizabe,th.Aspinall (72), a widow who resided at 37, Cawdor-street, Stockton Heath, formed the subject of an inquest which was held by Mr. R. Dobson, district coroner, at the Mulberry Tree Inn, Stockton Heath, on Monday evening. Jane Southern, sister of the deceased, said deceased and her daughter (Mrs, Penny) had been living with her for four months. Deceased was cleaning out the cup- board on Friday afternoon when she came across a tin containing powder, which she thought was liquorice powder, and said she would have a dose the following morning. Deceased and her daughter took some about 10.30 on Saturday morning. .About twelve o'clock deceased complained of being dizzy and rested on the sofa, and witness gave her some tea. Mrs. Penny's son came home from work at 1.15 and took the powder to a chemists, to'see if it was right and was told it way. He afterwards\ went for Dr. Parker.

Miss Dora Penny, grand-da?ghter of the deceased, said she went to Egremont a little over twelve months ago to visit a friend. Before she left her friend gave her, in a casual way, a tin, containing powder, which she said was liquorice powder. When witness reached home she put the tin in the cupboard and the powder had never been used since.

Dr. Parker said he was called to see the deceased on Satnrday at 1.30 and found her suffering from profound stupor and nearly unconscious, with mutterings of delirium. She hada darkly congested face with evident signs of heart failure and widely dilated pupils. He administered an emetic but she only swallowed some of it. He also gave the daughter (who was similarly suffering) an emetic, and was successful in administer- ing it, which made her vomit. Deceased was quite incapable of swallowing anything. Witness then went for a stomach pump and after a few minutes' absence returned, hut while operating with it, she showed evi- dent signs of dying and he desisted. Death occurred during the next half hour. The powder resembled liquorice powder in smell, but was darker, and might have been easily mistaken. On igniting some of the powder he found it burned and gave off an odour as in the case of an asthmatic powder. The symptoms of the deceased showed that the poison- ing was due to an irritant poison to which class asthmatic powders belonged. The Coroner said the circumstances were exceedingly sad and painful, and the evidence seemed clear that a mistake had been made.
The jury ret-111;;;Fii,--Verdict of "Death from misad- venture, by a poisonous powder self-administered in mistake for liquorice powder," and expressed their sympathy with the family.

div.head: PEACE SUNDAY.
div.p: PEACE SUNDAY.
THE REV JOHN YONGE ON SOCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL STRIFE
Unemployed 3iiestion, A Problem far
The Church,

Last Sunday, being observed at many places of worship as "Peace Sunday," the Rev. aohn Yonge preached a special sermon in the morning at Wycliffe Church. He said it was at leash a signiflcent testimony to the growth of the peace idea that the observance of that special Sunday because increasingly prevalent year- by year. Dealing with the true mission of Christianity, preacher said there had been a marvellous and time-long divorce between man as a spiritual being responsible to God and man as a fellow being. responsible to the whole human family. In seeking to make a man right for eternity, it had been forgotten to seek to make him a godly citizen of the world. The consequence had been, and yet remained. that even Christian men lived among their fellows iii spirit and style utterly diverse from those of the Saviour Himself. They ignored their social obligations. They repudiated their true relations with men of other language and nationality. Hence had arisen, and still continued, the inharmonious and unhappy conditions in which class arrayed itself against class and nation against nation, all over even the so-called" Christian"

world. Christ came to procure, proclaim, and promote peace among men. Now, while they saw the urgent necessity of vastly larger recognition of the world-wide mission of Christianity as the promoter of human peace, they must not ignore the fact that the influence of the Christian truth and spirit bad already been doing this. It had penetrated beyond the barriers of prejudice and ignorance hitherto maintained among Christian people. We were now, unhappily, face to face in this twentieth century with terrible spectacles of "...oda' and international strife. Oar own nation was only just shaking off
A TRENIENDOUS ATTACK OF WAR FEVER

through the hallucination of which we did a probably grievous wrong in the belief that we were enforcing an unmistakable right. And we were also in the presenc3 of great social inequities and sufferings which were producing very serious and grievous distresses. More- over, the tjaily press barrowed over hearts by the ghastly records of the murderous coaflict in the Far East. Still, there had been real progress in the direction of human peace. Social conditions have been ameliorated throughout Christendom. Brutal customs between men individually, brutal tyrannies, and brutal glaveries had been extinguished by the influence of Christianity. True religion always made for right human relations as was instanced by the effects of the revival of religion in WA! There should, con- tinned the preacher, be no feuds between Christians. Differences of opinion should not be suffered Ito harden into personal alienations. Another message of Christmas time was "peace between class and class." This must and would come about by means of the establishment of right relations in what created I the present
UNEIA.PPY cos•Drrroxs BETWEEN CLASSES OF SOCIETY

_ in our own land? Whence came the bitterness, the antagonisms, the jealousies, the hatreds, the strikes and lock-outs, the endless controversies between capital and labour? Did they come of righteousness, of truth, of judgment, or of some stern, rentless, inevitable Fate? We knew perfectly well that such was not their They came of unequal and inequitable relations, of !the unhappy working of nnjust laws, of selfish and often' cruel disregard of the needs and rights of men, of ignoble and un-Christian greed of gain, of every mark fightingghting for his own hand regardless of the claims and necessities of his fellows. Was wealth in the right, when it took advantage of the helplessness of poverty to exact labour at even less than the barest living wage? Could there ever be social peace while all the prosperity was on one side, and all the adversity on the other, of the social scale? Was that social condition Christian which permitted some to be full while others were hungry? Was that the fulfilment of the law of Christ which enjoined men to "love their neighbour as them- selves?" Take the tremendous problem that now con- fronted us every day

div.head: PROBLEM OF THE UNEMPLOYED;
div.p: THE PROBLEM OF THE UNEMPLOYED;

True it was that there were, and ever would be con- siderable who were the parasites of society—the loafers, the ne'er-do-well. the people who would not work, ard who were nor in the least ashamed to beg. Beyond those, there NV:18 a hugh host of both men and women who would work, but could not get work, and multi- tudesiof whom, in expressive Lancashire phrase. were more or lass being " clammed " to death. He did not hesitate to say that the problem directly and supremely belonged to thefihurch of Christ. Boards of Guardians warp wf)rthy bocges of people, but they were far too afraid of the votes of ratepa,yeis to he intensely de- voted to the necessities of the poor. Political parties were ervillly impotent for the self-same reason—they were afra;cl ef the polling booths. It was not a. political question in the ordinary sense. It was a humanitarian and therefore Christian question. He was very much inclined to believe that it was coming to be a question ABSOLUTELY VITAL FOR ALL CHRISTIAN CHURCHES what they sometimes—with perhaps just a trifle of superciliousness—called " the world" was not likely much longer to retain any respect or confidence for the- church. if' it continued supine and indifferent to the vital qu%stiou of the needs and livelihoods of the people. It was the spirit of Jesus that was everywhere needed in all the varied sections of the church which bore His name truly as individuals, learn wisdom fre- quently in the difficult and trying school of experience. , The British peopleall over the world had learned con- siderably how

THE BITTER EXPERIENCE OF THE SOUTH AFRICAN WAR. We were still enduring the evil consequences of that war in hampered trade and increased taxation, to say nothing of the sacrifice of life and desolation of families that was suffered among all classes. Experience had thus re-awakened the sentiment of peace, and Provi deuce had placed upon the British throne a statesman as well as a Sovereign, who astutely discerned that the- greatest interest of the world, was peace. The President just re-elected to office by the over- whelming majority of the Americsn people had been pronounced in his sympathy with the promotion of peace among the nations, and the American people themselves, by their extra display of interest at the Peace Congress were evidently in full sympathy. These facts were strong evidences of brightening hope for the peace of the world. But meanwhile, every daily paper was being made sad and ghastly by the details of the war betwaen Russia and Japan. After quoting Tolstoy's protest against war, the preacher said it was the spirit of Tolstoy and of the lovers of peace and of the believers in Jesus, and the Spirit of Jesus Himself that would eventually prevail. Should not the aim of the churches be to promote that Spirit? Should not their aim be to restrain the poli- ticians who would gain their ends by the force of arms rather than by the slower methods of peace ? Christian people were called to stand by peace principles,to assert them, to defend them, and to propagate them. They must refuse to disgrace their pulpits, their platforms,. their social programmes, their votes, municipal or political, by any acceptance of might over right,of force over weakness, of war over methods of peace.

A stiiking and most delightful display of useful and reliable novelties for Christmas gifts may be seen at Messrs. Beresford's of 77, Church-street, Liverpool Anyone wanting gifts at reasonable prices would do. well to superb variety in their two windows. In the one,purses, dressing-bags, card, letter, cigar and cigarette- cases and handsomely fitted dressing-cases are to be seen in so delightful a profusion that it would make one hesitate over choice in so excellent a variety. The other window is most tastefully filled with ivory, silver, ebony, and satinsvood toilet-brushes. They are making a speciality of ladies' brushes in handsome plush cases. These make a most delightful present, while the - gentlemen's cases of military brushes are equally serviceable. Altogether one would do well to visit Messrs. Beresford's at 77, Church-street, Liverpool before finally deciding on Christmas and New Year gifts. fbeir motto seems to be reasonable prices for- reliable quality.
THE WORKING OF THE EDUCATION ACT.- NATIONAL CONFERENCE IN L ONDON.

The reports from all parts of the country as to the way in which the Education Acts 1902-3 are being administered to the detriment of the children and the promotion of priestly dimination have determined the National Council of Evangelical Free Churches to hold a Great National Conference in London. Free Church School Managers and educationalists from all parts of the cotaitry will be invited. Invitations will also be given to Free Church members of and candidates for Parliament. The place of meeting has not jet been fixed but the date will be the first week iu February. Rev. Thomas Law, general secretary, is carrying out the arrangements.

div.head: YEAR'S THRIFT.
div.p: A YEAR'S THRIFT.
3ATISFACTORY REPORT AT THE SAVINGS BANK MEETING.
Workingmen and Football.
A WORD MUT THE TRADING AGITATION.

Significant details of the savings which are annually accumulated by the thriftiness of the working classes were afforded at the annual meeting of the trusteas and managers of the Warrington Savings Bank which was held at the Bank, Buttermarket-street, on Tuesday. Mr. William Long presided,and the attendance iucluaed the Revs. Canon Willis, J, Yonge, W. Bracecamp,and J.H.G. Hollinc;worth, Councillor Craik, and Messrs. J. Geddes (vice-chairman), H. Roberts, C. White, W. Tinsley, G. "Thompson, J. Longland, C. D. Parkinson, C. Jackson Holmes, John Dexchurst and W. A. Proud (actuary.) THE YEAR'S TRANSACTIONS.

In presenting the eighty-seventh annual report the Committee of Management gave the following summary ,of the business transacted during the year :—Eight hundred and thirty accounts have been opened or renewed and 529 closed, leaving 13,937 open accounts; -an increase for the year of 301. There have been 18,925 ,dep mits, and 10,232 payments, making altogether 29,207 transactions (an average of 95 daily), an increase of 939. £2,310 2s. 9d. has been invested for depositors in consolidated stock. The amount now due to depositors is £347,388 19s. 11d. •, the amount of stock held by deposi- tors is £18,032 Os. 2d. ;making a total of £366,420 Os. id. The assets of the bank are as follows, viz. :—lnvested with commissioners on general account, L 346,981 14s 7d; invested with commissioners on surplus fund accounts, £4,100; Government stock. £18,032 03. 2d. ; balance in treasurer's hands, £3,280 15s. 9d. ; freehold premises and furniture, £1,300 ; total, 373,394 10s. 6d; deduct amount due to depositors, £366,420 Os. Id., leaving a surplus after paying depositors in full of £6.974 10s. sd. The surplus has been increased by £424 Os. 11d. In addition to the stock held for depositors .£18,032 Os. 2d., the National Debt Commissioners have in their hands £350,781 14s. 7c1., which is considerably in excess of the total liabilities. The continued steady increase in the, number of accounts and number of transactions is a most gratifying feature of the work of the bank. The greater proportion of the transactions are of small amounts which shows that the bank is pro- viding a ready and safe investment for the class of depositors for whose benefit the institution was estab- lished. Premises have been s m cured in Queen-street, Earlestown for a branch bank, a ad the committee hope to open it early in the New Yea r. The committee regret having to record the death o f Mr. James Tinsley, a trustee and supporter of the bank for many years; of Mr. John Harrison, a manager and for ten years a member of the Management. Committee, also of Mr. Thomas Tnnstall, the late actuary, a highly esteemed .official for over 30 years. The actuary read the detailed balance sheets. THE CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH. WORKINGMEN AND FOOTBALL.

The CEIXIItNIA.N moved the adoption of the balaace sheet which ha said was very satisfactory. Reviewing the events of t4e year he, slid they all jotaei with the officials in lamenting the loss the bulk had sustained by the death of Mr. T. Tunstall, the late actuary, who at- tended those meetings for so many years. He could not say enough to express how high a place Mr. Tunstall held in his estimation, and they all knew what spirit he put into his work for the bank. They greatly regretted Ida loss.(llear, hear).Death had'been busy amongst them, and they missed several old faces,Mr.John Harrison,who was devoted very sincerely to the work of the bank, and Mr. James Tinsley having passed away. Alluding to the business transactions, Mr. Long said the Savings Bank Act which had been passed since their last meet- ing. gave much more extended powers to saving banks and would tend to make them more'useful in their work. Competition was as keen in banking as in every other department of life, and while they on their part wished to carry on and extend their workings, they must at the s ame time do it with care. The annual report showed that they were now preparing the premises for a branch bank at Earlestown, which would be opened two or three evenings in the week. They had other places in contemplation where they could still further extend. He hoped that as Warring- ton itself grew the work of the bank would grow in like proportion. The longer he lived the more he saw the immense benefit which came from the exercise of thrift, but unfortunately the amount of money spent in nn - known ways, particularly by the working classes, was very great. Money was spent in things which did posi- tive harm, and not only that but money was frittered away on so called amusements such as football meetings For his own part he could not understand how people could spend money in such ways. If it was for the physical improvement of the men by playing a good game, then hecould understand it, but to go Saturday after- noon after Saturday afternoon spending their time watching other people play he could not understand, because they got no physical help from it. • One of the facts which showed that the 'bank was doing a good work was that the increase of transactions during the year numbered nearly a thousand. He thought good had resulted from the opening of the bank daily instead ':three or four times a week, and everything was in a sound condition. He noticed the fact that the person who ought to be the highest authority on thrift—the Chancellor of the Exchequer—had, in a speech to his constituents, referred to their report spread to the effect that because consols were low, savings banks were not as safe as they ought to be. He rightly pointed out that the savings banks had the credit of the British Empire behind them. (Hear, hear.) At all events the Government was at their backs. It had, if be might so put it, taken res- ponsibility from them and given security to the public. Nothing more was needed to show the people that their money was safe in the banks and would be available for a rainy day. Mr. J. GEDDES seconded and the balance sheet was adopted.
MR.. H. ROBERTS SUGGESTS LOCAL BRANCH
BANKS.

Mr. H. ROBERTS moved that the report of the Com- mittee of Management be adopted, that the valuable services rendered to the institution by the gentlemen acting on the committee be acknowledged, and that the best thanks of the meeting be tendered to them. He remarked that he had been roughly comparing the bank in the various departments during the last .ten -years, and he thought the results were very interesting. buring that time the number of accounts opened had increased by 27A per cent.; the balance due to deposi- tors by 17:4 per cent.; the number of deposits by 521 per cent. ; and the amount of deposits by 271 per cent. The number of accounts closed was 18 less than ten years ago, which he thought was extremely satisfactory ; the number of payments had increased 471, per cent.; and the total number of transactions carried through had increased by 55 per cent. (Hear, hear.) Those figures showed clearly the increased sphere sof useful- ness which the bank now occupied. With reference to branch banks, whilq he was not going to say a word in deprecation of the opening of the branch at Earles- town he thought there were several districts in Warringon where they might, as an experiment, -open places for the receipt of deposits, 8:c. The town had grown very rapidly indeed, and while
.SI=MSNI

that bank, as the head, was in a fairly central position there were people to whom it was somewhat of a labour to come there. Therefore, when they remembered that they were in competition with the Post afice Savings Bank which atall the braaches was capable of receiving and paying out money, he thought they might consider the advisability of opening receiving houses, as it were, at say Stocktou Heath. Latchford, Sankey and Winwick. In the Sankey and Winwick ends of the town there was a fairly dense population of the very poor people to whom the bank should be of inestimable service, and if they could do anything to train them into habits of thrift they would tie doing them a very substantial service. He thought the result would 1:45 financially successful, and of extreme usefulness to the residents in the districts. The recent Savings Bank Act had opened up another field for investment. Reference was made to the amount of money invested in consols for depositors. In regard to what the highly esteemed present financial genius of our country had said about savings banks, he was perfectly right as to their being fully equal to their liabilities because the Government was behind them, but the drop in consols raised an important question. Taey had a number of depositors who had purchased for ,them through the bank, consols for permanent invest- ment. If through force of circumstances any of those people should be compelled to realise, they certainly stood the risk of loss of capital. If, on the other hand, there was any anpreciation in value, they would benefit accordingly. There was a certain element of specula- tive risk in regard to the purchase of consols. The Act recently passed opened up investment in municipal funds which not only bore a rather larger rate of interest to the depositor but were always realis- able at their face value—that was the Corporation itself undertook to repay the full value of that debt. He mentioned that as a matter which might be carefully considered by the Committee of Management, because investments of funds under Corporation security were free from liability of depreciation. On the other hand, however, the value was not capable of appreciation, as n the case of consols. Canon WILLis seconded the resolution.

A WORD ABOUT THE TRADING AGITATION. The CHAIRMAN said that with rcierence to Mr. Robert's suggestive speech he might say they were encouraged by such suggestions thrown out by prac- tical men of business, and the points he had raised would receive attention. In fact some of them had already been considered and it was for the convenience of a large number of depositors in Earlestown and Newton that the first branch bank was being opened. With reference to the investment of deposits he thought there was a good deal to be said in favour of local in- vestments so long as they considered them perfectly safe. Wm rington, he hoped, was settling down to hard work again after that unfortunate agitation—and he still held his own strong opinion upon it. It was an ill-timed and badly managed agitation and one which had certainly not redounded to the credit of Warring- ton. Now that it was over he would only say tha things of that sort depreciated the position, in the financial world, of Corporation securities as securities for investing in. It set people wondering whether Cor- porations, if they were guilty of such charges as were brought against them, would be a safe and proper in- vestment for the savings of depositors. He was not saying that he thought that was the case here for a moment, because he thought Warrin4ton could take a position as good as any Corporation in the country. (Hear, hear.) Savings banks, he was of opinion, should have a desire to help forward work in their own particu- lar towns rather than have only the one investment in Government securities. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was then approved. THE CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN RE -E LECTE D.

Mr. HOLMES proposed there-election of Mr. Long and Mr. Geddes as chairman and vice-chairman respectively and testified to the ability an.. courtesy which they had brought to bear the discharge of their duties. Mr. DEWHIIRST seconded. He said they all knew how prosperous the bank had been during the past year It seemed to have been a very loadstone to the people, and much of its success was due to its excellent manage- ment the influence of the Cl-tirman and Vice- , Chairman, and the trust the people had in them. (Hear, ' hear). The motion having been carried, Mr. Long and Mr. Geddes returned thanks. Mr. WILLIAM RICIIA.RDSON was elected a trustee in place of the late Mr. James Tinsley. The following gentlemen were added to the list of managers :—The Revs. T. W. Barber, H. B. Firth, G. C. Brigs T. A. J. Ridpath, Captain G. R. Crosfield,Messrs. J, L. 'Smith, James Richardson, and J. H. Smethurst, The Committee of Management consists of the trustees and several managers. Some discussion took place with regard to the attend- ances of members of the committc 3, Councillor Craik remarking that he did not consider the figures altogether satisfactory. The CHAIRMAN said the business of the bank was well attended to by the committee as a whole. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: WHEN'S GM.
div.p: WHEN'S GM.

Christmas Traditions.—There are many ancient aphorisms concerning the weather of Cnristmas Day, most of which favour the conditions a§ they are invari- ably portrayed in the Caristmas annuals. Some however rather contradict one another. Thus we are told "A clear and bright sun on Christmas Day foretelleth a peaceable year and plenty." Another proverb says, "If it snows on Christmas night, the crops will do well." But one would scarcely expact the two conditions of weather on the same day, or that they would portend the like result. There is more unanimity among those proverbs which condemn a warm and wet Christmas as meaning generally, an empty granary, empty barrels, a fat churchyard, a cold Easter, and other evils. The wind may be tolerated for "If windy on Christmas Day the trees will bear much fruit." There is, of course, little in all such sayings, which are just about as unreli- able as that the weather on Christmas Day will accord with tradition. Father Christmas, like the family ghost, does not always appear at the proper time and season, though we still like to think of Yuletide as it is pictured in the Christmas numbers, with its skating parties' its snowball fights, the old gentleman falling on the treacherous slide, and the lady all snow-flaked, and half hidden in wraps and furs, hurrying from her carriage to enter the hostess's house. Royal Visits.—The King and Queen have paid an un usually large number of country house visits this year,- as have also the Prince and Princess of Wales. It has been seldom that eitherathe King or the Prince, has not been on a visit to one or other of the great houses, and directly after the Christmas holidays their Majesties will once more go on a visit to the Duke and Duchess of Devonshire at Chatsworth. The few days which the King and Queen spent in London before proceeding to Sandringham for Christmas, were devoted to seeing many of the Royal warrant holders, at Buckingham Palace, and purchasing Caristmas presents. The house party at Sandringham will include a num.)er of guests for shooting iduring the holidays, and on Monday January 2nd, their alijesties will leave for Caltswerth, the visit to the Duke and Dachess of Devonshire ex ' - tendin<, over four or five days. The One Amusement.—After-dinner card-playing has displaced most of the old-fashioned Christmas amuse- ments. Perhaps a few evenings are spared for dances and theatricals, but really all that is now expected of one is to be able to play Bridge well and talk about motors. Those who are well up in these accomplish- ments are sure of many invitations to the houses of their friends and many who have no particular liking for card-playing been forced to acquire more than a passing acquaintance with Bridge rather than be shut out, among the ranks of the unsociable. This is regretted by many who look upon the mania for Bridge as one of the signs of the wickedness of modern life. The Dean of Norwich even goes so far as to say that the gambling fever, like other vices, will sooner 'or later become depicted in the countenance. There is no question that Bridge is played in many of the best houses for high stakes, but as a rule people limitlthe points according to their means. The King and higefriends usually play shilling 'points; in the London clubs, women's as well as men's, the rule is ten shillings a hundred, but in the majority of middle-class houses, it is not often more than a shilling or half-a-crown, and in many not more than threepence or sixpence a hundred points. Noted Bridge Players.—There are, of course, many houses in which card playing for money is not per- mitted. This is the case at Welbeck, the Duchess of Portland having long since taken a decided stand on this point. The Duke is also of the same way of think- ing, as, though he is a racing man, sport is in his case entirely free from betting and gambling. In the same way when Bridge is not open to objection on the score of gambling, there is nothing to be said against it. On the other hand it teaches one to think,. and a good card player is invariably a capable person. When pretty I nearly everyone in society plays Bridge it would take long to name all the noted players, but among them would certainly rank Lady Angela Forbes, Lady Wolverton, Lady Burton, Mrs. Leopold de Rothschild. Mrs. Wombwell, and Miss Jane Thornewill, who is said to be the best exponent of the game among women players. The Parisian Model.—The Lord Chamberlain's announcement regarding the forthcoming Courts is the herald of busy times In the fashion world. For the present the fashionable throng has drifted to the Riviera, and to Cairo, where the latest styles in dresses are to be seen, but already the great Parisians are pre- paring their models for the spring. Many of our lead- ing modistes visit Paris early in the year, and the majority of the toilettes worn at the Nuns are the embodiments of Parisian models and designs. It is true that of late years London houses have acquired a greater reputation for originality, but the Parisian model undoubtedly retains its leading place in the world of fashion.

Evening Fashions.—Evening gowns and wraps promise to be a great feature of the forthcoming January sales, the most desirable bargains in the latter being probable. Heavy white cloth, lined with thick satin, cut kimono fashion, and simply trimmed with thick silver cords, are among the most fascinating yet inexpensive evening wraps! while cashmere coats or capes, in white, cream, or pale shades, lined with satin,and trimmed with white fur rank next perhaps. Shot taffeta is a very favourite material for more costly evening wraps, ana these are usually richly trimmed with lace and fur. Black for evening toilettes is more than ever worn by women who have the reputation for dressing well. For dancing, accordion-pleated chiffon, voile, muslin, and crepe-de- chine, worn over separate slips of silk or satin, are all delightfully light and pretty, the black bodice to match being relieved with just a tucker of cream lace tied up with black velvet ribbon. Flowers of course enter into the scheme, most wOmen preferring to mix the real and artificial blooms. Only the best artifical specimens should be indulged in, when the deception is invariably successful. All dancing frocks are built to just sweep the ground, and no More, a mode which both the wearers and their partners appreciate. Favorite Christmas Gifts.—Earrings, so say the jewellers,have proved a very popular gift this Christmas tide, some preferring the solitaire, or bouton variety, others the three" drop "or " pear " shapes, while the favorite has unquestionably been the Creole hoop,either in plain gold, or, more fascinating still, in tiny diamonds with an invisibly setting. The very high dog collar in pearls and diamonds, has proved another much sought after gift—young girls—alas for thecontour of their throats—having " cast a favorable eye " upon this particular ornament. Jewelled " juliet " caps have also been much in request, and jewelled muff chains are as much desired as ever. Purses, and "vanity bags," the latter fitted with a tiny mirror and powder puff,and built of plain rich leathers, have been largely ch•-men by feminine" present seekers," so also have the electric pocket lamps and clocks, which are so useful and con- venient, saving us from the hateful groping after mys- teriously vanished matches, and the all too frequent resulting loss of our temper. Concerning Sponges.—To cleanse a sponge that has become sticky, and clogged with soap, soak it for a few hours in warm water, to which has been added some liquid ammonia—a tablespoonful of the latter to a pint of the former being the correct proportions. Squeeze and douse the sponge well, then rinse it thoroughly first in warm and after that in cold waters. It should, last of all, be set in a draught to dry. Sponges should never be laid upon the washstand,a current of air should be able to pass through them, and to attain this end the netted sponge baskets which can be fixed on to the washstand, or the window ledges, are desirable items. New sponges should first be beaten, and then laid in cold water for twenty-four hours, the water being changed and the sponge squeezed occasaionlly, MADGE.

div.head: CHRISTMAS FEASTING AND BILE
div.p: CHRISTMAS FEASTING AND BILE
BEANS.

Christmas feasting often throws more work upon the digestive system than it can do. Hence headache, indi- gestion, biliousness, heartburn, bad taste in the mouth, flatulence, etc., are commonly experienced, and spoil pleasure. Just as the Post office staff needs to be increased to deal with Christmas correspondence, so the digestive apparatus needs help to deal with its extra Christmas work. Bile Bsans give the necessary help. They pro- mote digestion,and the secretion of the digestive juices. Everybody says so who has tried them. "Science Siftings "—that well-known scientific journal—says "Bile Beans increase secretion in the whole of the digestive tract, cure constipation without causing after constipation, and are an excellent family medicine."
