div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.
STOCKTON HEATH v. SALE.

This match was played at Grappenhall-road, Stockton Heath. Sale were first to attack, but off-side spoilt a good opening. After this the home forwards took up the attack and thanks to sterling play by the Stockton Heath halves the visitors never became dangerous. Be- fore half-time R. Pierpoint scored a pass from the left wing. Just before the interval, Eric Fairclough, the some centre half, was injured and for the rest of the game was practically a passenger. Half- time score :---Stockton Heath, one goal; Sale, none. In the second half Sale played the long passing game, thus taking advantage of a weakened half-back line and ran out warners by three goals to ofie. STOCKTON HEATH 2sto v. SALE 2ND.
This match was played at Sale. The visitors had only ten men, and before the finish two men were injured, and left the field. Score :—Sale, four goals; Stockton Heath, one.

div.head: , . _et"
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 24, 1904. FASHIONS OF TO-DAT.

Christmas time is with us and the shop: are vieing with each other in displaying ar sorts of fascinating goods whose beaut 3 and inexpensiveness alike are calculated tc prove an almost irresistible inducPment tc hesitating shoppers. Each sucCeeding festive season seems to bring a greater perfection ir the pretty articles which prove such welcome and useful gifts to both old and young, and one cannot but. marvel at the ingenuity evinced in the manufacture of the beautiful and inexpensive trifles which abound. These are selected to suit every taste, and to come within the reach of all, so that there should be no difficulty in fixing upon something which is not only lovely in itself but is also likely to be of use to the recipient, and is suited to the environments of her everyday life. •So many people thoughtlessly select something because it is pretty without pausing to think whether

div.head: FUR SCARF.
div.p: A FUR SCARF.

or no it will prove of real use to the receiver or whether it will jar with the surroundings and general atmosphere of its new home. To give an elaborate chiffon-trimmed blouse of very pronounced fashion to a girl who rarely goes to social festivities and only to those of a simple and homely description is almost in as bad taste as to present something pronouncedly utilitarian to the frivolous minded maiden whose daily life is one round of gaieties. Therefore, it is a sensible plat before setting forth on a round of Christmas shopping, such as is the delight of all woman- kind, to make a list of those whom we intend to rejoice by seasgnable gifts, and place op- posite each name one or two articles which we feel sure would be welcome, also making a note of just how much money we can afford to expend on the purchase of each individual present. A great deal of unnecessary worry and trouble both to ourselves, our friends and the shop assistants will be avoided in this manner.

My first sketch depicts a fur scarf which is made so that—it can be twisted round the throat or even loosely tied in front. There are groups of tails at intervals which make the wrap look_ handsomer and more up-to-date. In this instance it is perhaps a longer scarf than usual, but that though it adds to the cost thereof also adds to its attractiveness. The muff which matches it is 01 the fashionable shape, namely, ,large and fiat and of the

div.head: PRETTY BLOUSE
div.p: A PRETTY BLOUSE

d granny order L some seasons muffs have been increasing in size, and they now form quite one of the most important features of the outdoor toilette. For those who cannot afford to lay cat much money and yet have plenty of spare time should snggest the purchase of a suitable ,lei-igth of one or pther of the new imitation fund which are [sold by. the yard. These can be cut into the required length and neatly joined together so as to form a long tie; in the case of the caracule little balls connected by cords should be substituted to give a finish in place of the tails.

lAnother useful gift forms the subject of my second illustration, and consists af a pretty blouse designed for evening wear. The foundation of the blouse is soft cream silk, [but there is little of the silk to be seen as the bodice is trimmed round the decolletage by a frill of deep lace headed by a narrow ruche of tulle of the same shade, as the lace. A deep lace flounce also falls ovei the arm, and a soft fall is arranged in graceful folds which reach from the corsage to the knees. The other features of the toilette are a deep-fitting band of black satin fastened by bijlliant buckles and a bright red rose of the cabbage order arranged at the point „where the fall of lace depends. Most girls would find such a gift more than useful just now when there are so many family and other social es on the

div.head: CHARMING HAT.
div.p: A CHARMING HAT.

tapis. A pretty bodice ,such as this can be worn and will evade criticism even when worn with an old skirt which has been smartened ap a little so as to harmonize with existing modes. It is wonderful what results can be 30 brought about at a-very small outlay, and, I therefore can conscientiously recommend a dainty blouse for a suitable • gift from all wealthy individuals to their pretty and per- haps very impecunious relatives. There • are so many. little extra occasions just now when a visit •to . a restaurant, theatre, or concert makes serious inroads on the two or three items ot millinery we can lay claim to and one courts criticism by appearing in the same society of recurrent occasion, in the same hat. My sketch, however, shows what charming results can be brought about by the aid of a lace veil or, perchance, a long lace flounce inherited from some kindly pre- decessor. These, whether they be crearr "old lace," or black, when carelessly twisted round the curving' brim of a hat which foi preference should exactly harmonise with tilt tone .of the lace, make the most fascinating pieces of headgear that any woman cola desire. An old hat can often be thut disguised and made lb re-appear in an alto- gether rejuvenated con:Mien by the aid of dainty lace veil scarf or flounce, and a numbei of pretty ornamental headed pins which car be purchased at most of the. cheaper shops for a few perce
COQUETTE.

div.head: EVENTS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: EVENTS OF THE WEEK.
BLOOMSBURY SHOP EXPLOSION.

Considerable sensation was caused in the Bloomsbury district of London last week by a gas explosion, which blew up a draper's shop and did several thousand pounds' worth of damage. The shop in question belonged to Mr. F. W. Barber, a well-known draper, who occupies the ground floor of a big block of buildings at the corner of Southampton Row and Cosmo Place. Above the shop is Cran- ston's Waverley Hotel, which was crowded with visitors. During the morning a plumber with an assistant had been at work making repairs to the gas main; and at lunch time a strong smell of gas was noticed. Upon ex- amination the man fonnd that the gas was escaping very fast from a plug hole, and sent his kpy to fetch a new plug, placing his hand over the hole to stop the escape as far as possible. Suddenly, however, in some way the gas became ignited and a tremendous

div.head: SCENE 01 THE EXPLOSION.
div.p: SCENE 01 THE EXPLOSION.

report was heard as, far as a quarter of a mile away, followed by a succession of crashes and, screams. The windows of the shop and many. in the immediate neighbourhood were flashed to fragments, and half the shop and its contents were blown into the street. .The Pavemmt outside was torn up, and the lower part of the premises were entirely de- vastate& The policeman on point duty was hurled many yares; the coachman of a brougham, waiting outside, was blown off his seat; a cab on the neighbouring rank was over- turned; and tae flagstaff of the hotel was thrown into the street. Several passers-by were injured, and the only marvellous thing is that no one was killed. About a dozen people were more or less seriously hurt. The roliceman in question had a 'leg broken and sustained other severe injuries: and another policeman was also seriously hurt. Two of the attendants at the Waverly Hotel were in- jured, but fortunately none are in a serious condition. But it was a'most alarming affair.

div.head: NEW PROFESSORSHIP OF MUSIC,
div.p: THE NEW PROFESSORSHIP OF MUSIC,

It looks as though before long this country would have the reproach which has rested upon its music for so long removed from its as of late years scholarships and endowments have been arriving thick and fast from practical patrons of the great art. The latest of these is the liberal gift of Mr. Richard Peyton, to Birm- ingham Univer- sity, which Mr. Chamberlain in his capacity of Chancellor an- nounced at the meeting of the Council last week. Mr. Pey- ton has pre- sentedthe young University of the Midlands with ten thou-

sand guineas to endow a professorial chair of music, and Sir John Holder added the gift of a thousand_ pounds to provide supplementary teaching. Both offers were cordially accepted by the Council, and it was resolved to call the pro- fessorship the "Richard Peyton Chair of Music." To his gift Mr. Peyton attached only one condition, that Sir Edward Elgar should be offered and should accept the chair in question—a stipulation which found an echo in the heart of all music-lovers. Sir Edward Elgar has accepted the invitation of the University of 'Birmingham, and the ap- pointment has now been officially announced. This foundation will make Birmingham a' great musical centre, as there is no question that Sir Edward Elgar is our greatess living musician, and he has already done much to restore English music to a place of honour in the .world. The son of an organist, Jae was born in Worcestershire and first went into a solicitor's office. However, a year later he began to study the violin under Pollitzer Then he settled down near Worcester as a professor and orchestral leader and took up the post of organist to St. George's Catholic Church. Later on he went to live at Malvern as a teacher and began .to compose. Amongst his publications are "The Black Knight" (1592), " Lux Christi" for the Worcester Festival a year later, " King Olaf" for the North Staffordshire Festival in the same year, "The Iniperial March" in Diamond Jubilee year, and other cantatas and festival music, culminating in 1900 in "The Dream of Gerontius " for the Birming- ham Festival. Since then Sir Edward Elgar, who was knighted this year, has composed "The Apostles" and the "Pomp and Circumstance" March, which have set the seal on his fame.
; ISIR EDWARD ELGAR.

div.head: TWO MILITARY APPOINTMENTS,
div.p: TWO MILITARY APPOINTMENTS,

Two military appointments of considerable interest have just been announced. The one is that of Sir George White, who is at present commanding at Gibraltar, to the Governorship of Chelsea Hospital, which has been vacant since the death of Sir Henry Norman. This post is usually given to a Field-Marshal who has filled all the usual

SIR GEORGE WHITE AND SIR lAN HAMILTON. commands and is not a man of great private means. The post itself, however, is not a very valuable one as th. salary is only 560 per annum, but it carries with it a fine house and only nominal duties. In addition, it. keeps the holder on the • active list and full pay, which in the ase of a Field-Marshal is „1,1,300 a year. By common consent Sir George AN'hite, the hero of Ladysmith, had the first claim to the post, and it is an appointment which is very pleasing to the public. The other is the announcement that Sir lan Hamilton who has been representing Great Britain in Japan during ,the war, will succetd sir Evelyn Wood in his command when his time is up. Sir lan Hamilton is one cf the young Hchener Edina and gained great distinetien in South Africa not only in Ladysmith, but later .on as Chief-of- the-Staff to Lord Kitchener. The command to -which he will , succeed has ceased to be an Army Corps, and is now the Western District. Sir • lan Hamilton has, during the past., few days, exploded a bomb in' military

circles. Tliee are his words touching the Russo-Japanese War: "This war has burnt into my mind in a way nothing else could have done that the condition of our Army constitutes a terrible danger to the existence of our Empire. I have learnt here at nothing but the very best will do, and we too often have the worst." Grave words, indeed, but not out of season, and they are already bearing fruit. The Army is to be completely re-armed as regards artillery and field guns, to put it upon a level with the other great powers. The facts of the case are astounding, and a meeting of the Com- mittee of Defence was held on Saturday to consider the subject. -

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

GAOL-BREAKING AT RUNCORN. On Saturday by permission of Colonel Hamersley,the chief constable of Cheshire, " Henco," the gaol-breaker, gave an exhibition of his marvellous powers. Hand- cuffed and burdened with leg irons by Superintendent Ennion, he was placed in a cell with a steel door. He escaped, and also opened an iron gate and unlocked every door in the establishment. The exhibition caused great astonishment among the police officers and others assembled.

div.head: TRANSPORTER _BRIDGE FATALITY.
div.p: TRANSPORTER _BRIDGE FATALITY.

At noon ow Monday, whilst engaged in painting the approach works of the new Widnes transporter bridge, William Nield, aged about thirty-five, living in Irwell- street, Widnes, fell head first into the Mersey and dis- appeared. Two other workmen named Bott and Walker attempted to get a boat, but got into the water, and had very narrow escapes from drowning during their work of rescue. Nield did not fall from the top but from underneath the scaffolding. This is the second fatality of a similar .kind that has happened during the last six weeks. Unfortunately at the time of the accident the local grappling corps were away at a drowning case at Walton. Mr. Byfield, the captain of the corps were also out of town engaged in hooking for the missing men of the Percy. Blanch and Wild Rose. In future however, it has been arranged that a set of grappling irons will be permanently left at the Runcorn Police Station so that a set will always be at hand in the event of coincident fatalities.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

BAND OP HOPE MEETING.—The fourth public meeting ()Utile Hill Cliffe and Stockton Heath United Band of Hope Society was held in Hill Cliffe schoolroom on Monday evening. There was a good attendance, over which the Rev. J. S. Hughes presided. An address was delivered by Mr. R. Pierce Williams, and a capital pro- gramme was given consisting of recitations bs E. Martin, C. Cain. Emily Hamblett, Edith Hamblett, B. Blakeman, A. Cliffe, A. Lonsdale, George Hughes and Clarence Bailey, and songs by Dolly West, Elsie Whit- field, Marian Ilegg and May Vernon. Miss May Isher- wood sang very sweetly "Home, sweet home "and Miss Jones and Herbert Hughes contributed a duet which was much enjoyed. The dialogue "A visit from Father Christmas" was well given by Mary Earle, Joseph Whitfield, Harold Jones, T. Pearse, M. Richmond E. Whitfield, Mabel Cain, May Isherwood and Elsie Whit- field. Other dialogues were "A band of temperance girls" by E. Hughes, E. Bailey, G. Cliffe, G. Bairsto, A. Forsyth, E. Carter, and M. Glassey, and "Two Christmas Visitors," by Messrs. J. Wormll, W. Wilde. J. Whitfield and Miss Worrall. Master Arthur Whit- field and Miss Moreton acted as sccompanists.

div.head: LAND OF KING FSOLOMON'S GOLD.
div.p: THE LAND OF KING FSOLOMON'S GOLD.

Mr. R, N. Hall, F.R.G,S. gives a vivid account of his explorations of the famous Zimbabwe ruins in the January number of the " Pall Mall Magazine" the first of the new issue at sixpence. The investigations made by him at Great Zimbabwe were the natural comple- ment of previous work he conducted during a period of five years amongst other ancient monumental ruins which are scattered so profusely over the whole country lying between the Zambesi and Limpopo rivers. " This region," he says "teems with suggestions of deepest mystery and awe,which hover over some ancient people who, as it it is now believed, toiled extensively for gold some three thousand years ago. The webs of romance woven by Mr. Rider Haggard in "King Solomon's Mines " and ' She' find in Rhodesia their location in certain well-recognised districts, and to I suet' an extent is this the case that it is acommon saying in Rhodesia that' King Solomon's Mines' walk in the country. ",Rhodesia undoubtedly possesses the ancient gold mines, but it also can show the buried ancient city and the lighter-skinned native race with Jewish char- acteristics outlined in She.' Great Zimbabwe is the buried city, and the Makalanga (the people of the sun) are the lighter-skinned native race, and these possess distinctly Jewish traits. The Acropolis ruins with their caves and cliff-passages on Zimbabwe provide the scenes of the last period of existence of She who must be obeyed.' This conclusion passes current throughout South Africa, where Mr. Rider Haggard himself resided for a considerable number of years. Warrington Harriers.

them and, fter correspondence, relations became strained, and Sir William Grantham decided to proceed with his building, having in the meantime submitted his plans to the Local Government Board. The Council, however, would not sit by and see their bye-laws set at defiance, so they took out a summons against the judge, who appeared before the Lewes magistrates last week to answer it. He was represented by Mr. Gill, K.C., with his son, Mr. W. W. Grantham, aq junior; and the Chailey Dis- trict Council briefed Mr. Macmorran, K.C., on their behalf. Thik proceedings were pro- tracted, lasting thre7 days, and at one point Sir William Grantham, who feels the whole affair very keenly, broke down and wept in court. However, the case was not without its lighter side, and Mr. Gill created a good deal of laughter in court from time to time. In giving evidence, Sir William Grantham admittedo;that he had ..spent considerably over £40,000 in building in his time. He also added that .during his career at the bar and on the bench olis had been brought into pro- fessional contact with the, greatest surveyors and architects of the day, cold mentioned that he always carried an ivory measure for use on the bench. • The magistrates reserved their decision in the case• until Thursday in this week, and it is being awaited with no small interest.
T lIREE NEW BISHOPS,

It is not often that three new bishop's are appointed at one time, but last week His Majesty filled up the new See of Birmingham, the vacant See of Carlisle, and the vacancy created by the translation, of the Bishop of Worcester. It was mainly through the instrumentality of the last-named that the new See of Birmingham was created, and it is only fitting that he should be chosen to Ail it. Dr. Gore, who became famous as the /editor of " Lux Mulidi," is a man of great ' encrgv and a born misFioner ; and a town like Birmingham will be far more congenial to him than a Bishopric like Worcester. He is only fifty-one years of age, and was a Canon of Westminster from 1894 until his appointment to Worcester two years ago. Previously he had been librarian of the Pusey Library at Oxford, and Yice-President of Cuthiesdon College. Dr. Yeat man-Biggs,

DR. YE ATMAN-BIGGS GORE. who succeeds him in the See of Worcester, has been Suffragan-Bishop of Southwark since 18,91 and is one of the ' muscular Christians" of the day. He has been examining chaplain to the Bishops of Salisbury and Winchester, Proctor for Convocation at Rochester and clerical secretary to the Diocesan Synod. He is just under 'sixty years of age and a large landowner in Wilts and Dorset. The new Bishop of Carlisle is the Venerable J. W. Diggle; Archdeacon of Birmingham, and rector .of St. Martin's Church 'id that city. He is in his fifty-eighth year, and was a Canon of Carlisle and Archdeacon of West- moreland from 1896 to 1901. He became rector of Birmingham in 1902 and has since then been 'the leading prelate in the great Midland town Until the appointment of Dr. Gore, so his promotion is particularly happy. It was rumoured at one time that he him- self was to be the first Bishop of Birming- ham. He used to be examining chaplain to the late Dr. Bardsley, whom he now suc- ceeds. The 'venerable Ernald Lane, Arch- deacon of Stoke-on-Trent, has been appointed Dean of Rochester in place of the late Dean Hole.

div.head: END OF THE HOOLEY CASE
div.p: THE END OF THE HOOLEY CASE

On Saturday last the trial of Mr. Ernest Terah Hooley and Mr. Henry Lawson at the Old Bailey came to an end, having lasted twenty-one days and prolonged the November session of the Central Criminal Court into the middle of the December session. The result was that the jury acquitted Mr. Hooley and found Mr. Lawson guilty on the count of having published a 'false statement. Mr. Justice Lawrence sentenced the latter to twelve months' hard labour, but allowed him out on bail pending the decision of the Court of Crown Cases Reserved on a point of law as to whether he, was manager of the Con- struction Company within the meaning of the Act or not. The principali count against both prisoners was the charge of having defrauded Mr. Paine,. but it became evident towards the end of Mr. Rufus Isaacs' cross-examination of the chief witness that the prosecution on this
;e were

LAWSON. HOOLEY. enormous, Mr. Isaacs alone having his brief marked at five hundred guineas with a daily refresher of three hundred, but Mr. Hoolev will be the first to acknowledge that he more than earned it. Mr. Lawson defended himself with extraordinary skill, but he has briefed Mr. Isaacs to appear on his behalf before the High Court. Despite its length and the figures involved the case never flagged in interest, and from first to last it was a great battle of legal wits. Mr. justice Lawrence's summing-up, clear, con- cise, and dispassionate, was not the least masterly feature of the trial. Throughout the long days of suspense Mr. Hooky pre- served his ever cheerful and debonnair manner, though he [appeared anxious during the deliberation& tof the jury, Which lasted close on three hours 4

The Day School.—The distribution of prizes took place on Thursday afternoon when the school broke up for the Christmas holidays. Silver medals, with gold centres, were given to the !following scholars who had not missed an Lttendance for two years: Ann J.Simpson, Florence Taylor, Ada Wheeler, Ada Richardson, Tom Parr, Charles Fairhurst, William Garnett, and Robert Reymore while Sarah Booth, Frederick Mainwaring, Edith Ellison, Abel Ellison, Alice Carey,Sarah Fairhurst and James Courtney having made every attendanca possible during the past twelvemonths, received a silver medal. In addition to these, Mrs. Frost of Grappen- hall Hall, who takes groat interest in the school and who distributed the prizes, gave work- boxes, boxes of paints, writing cases S:c„ to the girls for darning and the boys for drawing. Winners :—Standard VII., Emily Wheeler: Standard VI., Violet Brown; Standard V., 1, Ada Wheeler; 2 Dorothy Evans; Standard IV., Catherine McClean; Standard 111., 1, Constance Robbins; 2, Dorothy Eaton; Standard 11., 1, Sarah Fairhurst; 2, Alice Carey; Stan- dard 1., 1, Bertha Fairhurst; 2, Dorothy 'Robbins. Infants: Margaret Tickle, Louisa Courtney, Annie Stubbs; Standard VII.. Walter Shakeshaft ; Standard VI., Albany Hill; Standard V., 1, William Garnett; 2, Arthur J. Evans; Standard IV., 1, Alfred Sarjeant ; 2, Robert Shakeshaft ; Standard 111., 1, Harold Lewis; 2, Richard Marshall; Standard 11., Alan E. Evans; 2; Abel Ellison; Standard I„ 1, Francis Woodcock; 2, Charles Hough. Infants: 1, William Fairhurst; 2, Frank Daniels, Gerald Pearson; 2, Charles Ravenscroft. Another friend of the school, Miss Appleton, offered prizes for good conduct. The children voted for the one whom they considered to be best behaved both in and out of school. The result was as follows :—Upper part of school, Ada Wheeler (girls), Sydney Boughton (boys). Lower division, Mollie Poulson and Richard Marshall. At the conclusion of the prize-giving both the Rector, the Rev. R. Greenall and the Headmaster, Mr. A. Evans, thanked Mrs. Frost and Miss Appleton for their kindness to the children and the interest shown by them towards the school, and after hearty cheers for both ladies, the Rector and teachers, the school closed for a fortnight's holiday.

Assurance Agents' Social. The annual tea and social of the Warrington branch of the National Union of Life Assurance Agents was held last week, 70 agents, their wives and friends sat down to a good meat tea at the Winmarleigh Cafe, Warrington. After the substantial repast Mr. Edwin Plinston, branch president, occupied the chair, and in his opening remarks spoke of the utility of trade unions, pointing out what the National Union had done in Warrington, and closing with some sound advice to the ladies present. Mr. J. M. Whitehead, president of . the Union, followed with a most able address, stating what the Union could and would do forall honest agents, and urging its members to pay strict attention to their calling and master all its details, and in this way add to their income; also to band together as a common brotherhood and uphold the Union motto, " Defence not Defiance." Mr. D. Sheard, general secretary, pointed out the peculiar conditions under which agents worked in various offices, and urged combination as the only way to remedy grievances. By keeping aloof from each other they simply played into the hand of the officials. Let the agents cease to remain isolated: on the con- trary, let them get to know and understand each other, and a mutual compact would come into being, leading them to help and protect each other. The address was much applauded, and at the close Mr. Sheard was thanked for the substantial help he had given, all agree- ing that he had made them better trade unionists. Mr. P. J. Kelly, Liverpool, roused the meeting with a. most able speech on combination. He touched humor- ously on WarringtOn's industries—soap,pins,and beer— his ready wit being much appreciated. He was cordi- ally thanked (as was also 4r. G. D. Moore, Liverpool. and a hope expressed by all present that be would live long to uphold the cause he has so much at heart, A splendid musical programme, under the direction of Mr. J. T. Barton, was submitted,the artistes including Miss Blairs, Miss Fairhurst, Miss Woodland, Mr. E Sanders, Mr. P. George, and the Lyric Prize Quart
WIDNES LIBERAL CLUB DANCING LICENCE REFUSED.

--At Widnes, on Thursday, Mr. Knowles applied for a dancing licence for the Widnes Liberal Club. Mr. Knowles, in making the application, went into details as to the size and safety of the room. 111 r. Andrew Sinclair, architect, said he made an examination of the property. and it was quite safe. Mr. D. J. Brook, who opposed the licence, said his shop was situated immediately under the room. After cross-examining the last witness upon the stability of the building, witness said that dancing had been carried on for weeks, and the vibration had damaged the ceiling of the shop, brought soot down the chimney, and broken the mantles. He had seen the floor give to the extent of a couple of inches during a heavy dance. The bench retired for ten minutes? and upon returning said they were unanimously of opinion that the room was not safe, and the licence would not be granted.

The available statistics do not permit the applica- tion of really scientific tests, although Mr. CHAMBERLAIN never hesitates to assure us that the German workman is much better off than the British workman. But the figures. of pauperism enable the Board of Trade to print a table which shows that in the fifteen years from 1885 to 1900 "the fall iu the average number of paupers relieved in tin United Kingdom has been 14.4 points (or 1-2 i per cent.), while in certain German districts the decline has been 14 point, or about 1?-; per cent." This test, of course, is not comprilensive, as the statistics of pauperism for the whole of Germany are not procurable. But there is a sufficient indication that the tendency of poor relief to decline is more marked here than it is there. In three States of the American Union, which alone are available for the purposes of comparison, the tendency is the other way, but the advantage over us in this respect is very slight. The broad con- clusion is that there is no warrant in our social and industrial condition for the experiment Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is urging, on the plea that after sixty years Free Trade has reduced us to "stagna- tion," which has in it the seed of disaster.

The Progressive Labour League held its first public meeting on Monday evening and it has every reason to be satisfied with the success which attended the gathering. There were no M.P.'s or political" big guns" present to give the League a send-off, and none were required. The League is essentially a workingman's organisation, and the speechmaking was very properly left to men actively connected with the League and closely identified with the cause of Labour. Each speaker made it absolutely clear that the Government's policy with regard to the fiscal question, Chinese Labour, and Trades Union rights called for hearty, condemnation by the knights of labour. The meet- ing was unanimous in its conviction that " the whole of the legislative tendency of the present Government is absolutely opposed to the interests of the working-classes of the country " and passed a resolution to that effect, combined with an ex- pressed determination to secure the return at the next election of Mr. A. H. Crosfield, the Progres sive candidate.

Mr. It. A. Naylor will have to be christened The Incurable Egotist. Every public appearance he makes confirms his right to the title. One of his latest achievements is bsing interviewed by the "Church Family Newspaper," wherein he tells a wondering world how he came to oppose Mr. Lloy- d in Carnarvon Boroughs. Perpend ! "It was this way. A gentleman in Thelwall, who is very much interested in the Carnarvon Boroughs —a Welshman of the old school, a true-hearted patriot, with a burning desire to see the land of his fathers lifted out of the mire and clay of religious and political disaster—came to me at one of my Sunday evening meetings and asked me to rescue Csrnarvon Boroughs from Mr.Lloyd-George. He said, 'You are the only man who could win the seat for the Unionists and for the party of law and order.'" Oh, those Thelwall meetings and those original hymns! What have they not been res- ponsible for? Here we have it on Mr. Naylor's own authority that they so prevailed upon the "true-hearted patriot "—whoever this gentleman may be—that he became convinced at -once that Mr. Naylor and no one else was destined to be the saviour of Oarnarvon Boroughs and the slayer of the Welsh Apollyon, Mr. Lloyd George. The seed thus patriotically sown took root and spread in Mr. Naylor's fertile brain, with the result that he is now the Unionist Candidate foi Carnarvon Boroughs and fully confident of victory—at least so he says. Mr. Naylor has challenged his opponent to resign and contest a Welsh Constit- uency with him at once. Why? Because Mr. Naylor would have everything to gain and Mr. Lloyd George everything to lose. Such challenges are cheap, and provotce nothing worse than a derisive smile. Mr. Naylor need not worry. He will probably get all the fighting he wants at the general election. There was a meeting at Bangor on Wednesday evening alleged to be in support of Mr. Naylor, but the audience persisted in cheering Sir H.Campbell Bannerman and Mr. Lloyd George, while at the end there were hardly enough people left to "pass "the resolution in the approved fashion. Clearly,all the electors are not prepare d to take Mr. Naylor at his own estimate.

Coroner Brighouse is one of the most able and humane coroners in Lancashire. The mere per- formance of duty does not satisfy him, and his efforts to better the condition of the many poor people he comes in contact with are increasing, but it is possible for such a man even as Mr. Brighouse to let his zeal outrun his discretion. The large number of child-burning fatalities is a theme on which the coroner holds very strong opinions. In his view the provision of fireguards by parents should be made compulsory by the legislature, and he yesterday passed some very severe strictures on the supineness of the authori ties and the culpability of parents. One poo- woman who gave evidence as to a burning fatality came beneath the lash of the Coroner's tongue,and in our opinion he treated her with undue harsh- ness. There are thousands of poor people—especi- ally in these times of stress—to whom the provision of fire-guards is an utter impossibility. With them the provision of the bare necessaries of life is a difficult matter and we are sure than Mr. Brighouse, in his calm moments, would not insist on fire-guards before food.

We are not convinced, either, that the resp sibility of providing fire guardi should be placed by the legislature on the parents. A moment's reflection convinces one of the hardships such a law would inflict. Rather the landlord—burdened as he is by increasing rates—than the parent! Why should not the building bye-laws include fireguards within their sphere of action? or, to make the res- ponsibility less a personal one, why not insist on the municipal and County Councils supplying the required safeguard against burning fatalities? The question is a much wider one than the worthy Coroner's remarks would indicate and deserves deeper consideration. We disagree entirely with his suggestion that the provision of fireguards should be made compulsory on the parents, if the expense is to fall upon them individually. The legislature, if it deals with the question at all —and a total of SOO deaths from burning per year is not one to be ignored—must consider the circum- stances of the parents as well as the safety of the children.

The only subject which provoked anything approaching a long discussion at Monday even- ing's meeting of the Education committee was whether or not the authority should support the movement initiated by the leading members of the medical profession to secure the compulsory teaching of hygiene and temperance in the ele mentary schools. The School Management Corn - mittee felt that compulsory teaching would not be as satisfactory as the instruction which is being constantly and spontaneously given and this view was upheld by the full committee with fe v dissentients. It would appear from the explanation given by Mr. :T. Upson that the object of the petition which it is proposed to pre- sent to Parliament is already in a great measure being attained, and the sub-committee had no intention of treating the matter lightly and as a fad. The teaching in these important subjects is systematic, and it will certainly not lose in force by beina the outcome of voluntary effort. The fact that numerous certificates for scientific know- ledge of the evils of alcohol are gained by the scholars is proof that temperance as a part of Klucationis not being neglected. Were a hard and fast rule laid down by the Government, it might possibly result in dimmished attention being paid to the three "

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
DECEMBER 24th, 1904.
We once more, and very heartily, wish all our readers" A Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year."
THE new Board of Trade Blue THE COST OF book, as the " Times " says, LIVING. "offers food for reflection of

various kinds." We believe that, on the whole, this reflection will provide small comfort for the advocates of Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN'S proposals. Even our contemporary is com- pelled to admit that the statistics indicate a very material advantage to the working classes from the economic system which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN desires to abolish. He is fond of assuring us that .this foreign competition is narrowing the area of employment so rapidly that the working man is confronted with the prospect of having no wages to buy his cheat) loaf. But the Blue - book proves - incontestably that the area of employment is steadily maintained and shows no symptom of shrinkage. But what has manifestly declined is the cost of living. To this fact the" Times " itself testifies with com- mendable frankness. "It is satisfactory to find that, taking topther the cost of food, rent, cloth- ing, fuel, and light, the position has been very materially improved during the twenty years from 1880 to 1900. What it cost 120 shillings to provide in 1880 Could be procured for rather under 100 shillings in 1900. That is to say five pounds in 1890 purchased for the workman and his family as much material comfort as six pounds procured in 1880. If we consider some other changes which do not enter into the family budget, we shall see that this does not wholly cover the amelioration of the workman's lot. His food has fallen from 139.7 to 101.8, his clothing Is cheaper by 10 per cent., his fuel and light show nearly as much decrease in cost; while, on the other hand, his rent has risen from 86.6 to 100. . . . He gains by a fall of about 38 per cent cost of food, and' about 18 per cent. in cost of clothing and fuel, while he pays about 14 per ceht. more in rent."

We are content to let this admirable summary speak for itself. It throws upon the Tariff Reformers the onus of proving that some magical inflation of wages must follow the abandonment of free imports in order to compensate the work- man for the inevitable increase in the cost of living. What would be the effect on his family budget of a rise in prices which would follow the imposition of protective duties? All the items we have enumerated would swell considerably. This is certain. On the other hand, a correspond- ing rise of wages is wholly problematical, especially such a rise as would leave the work- 'man not merely as well oft as he is now, but much better off. For if he is not to be materially the gainer by the proposed change, what is the advantage of making it? Thu Board of Trade tells us that it is impossible to establish through comparisons between the industrial condi- tions of this country and those of other countries.

and especially when one considers the spells of industrial depression, it is extremely gratifiying to learn that durihg the past year there has been a steady increase in the number of accounts, which are 301 in excess of the total twelve months ago. As the greater proportion of the transactions are of small amounts, it is evi- dent that the bank is qmte fulfilling its object. The surplus, which stands at £6,974 103. -sd. has been increased by £424. Although the bank has already proved a great convenience to a large section of the community, we should like to see its usefulness extended. There is understood to be a likelihood of at least one branch being opened in another part of the town, and such a develop- ment would doubtless be welcomed.

The much-abused income tax payer is now labouring under another grievance. Hitherto he has responded to increasing demand notes with more or less cheerfulnes and promptitude, but the latest turn of events gives him further cause to feel one of the most harassed contributors to the national exchequer. The tax on profits of trades professions,etc., for "the year commencing the 6th April, 1904," is now being applied for in a demand note, whih states it to be payable on or before the Ist January, 1905, and the majority of the collec- tors have suddenly been called upon to obtain, and if necessary enforce payment by the end of February—at least two months earlier than the usual limit. This appears to us to be an undue hardship, especially in view of the present depression and the fact that the tax is 50 per cent. higher than it was before the war. The change will be the most seriously felt by the struggling shopkeepers who are one of the principal sources of revenue. It has been suggested that as a kind of sweetening of the pill some discount might be allowed for prompt payment!

There has been much muttering and spluttering over the British exhibits at St. Louis. The news- paper correspondents have with practical unanimity made the worst of our display; and they were probably right in doing so, for it is important that our commercial chiefs should know in what respects they are behind. But it would have been unfortunate if the official view had been through such dark glasses; and it is pleasant to notice that Sir Mortimer Durand has a different tale. He writes that he thinks that his Majesty's Government has reason to be satis- fied with the display made by Great Britain. The British exhibits were well housed, and attracted much attention. He admits that in many parti- culars they cannot be regarded as representative of the country; but in some respects they I are very good. Some features undoubtedly astonished the natives. The Yankees did not expect to see our educational system nearly so good, and it is well they should know we are not so backward as we are reported to be. The British art section was supreme. A bustling people generally suffer in art, and though Sargent, who is perhaps the greatest portrait painter of our time, and several other of the very first rank men, have been born Americans, they have become naturalised Europeans. The pavilions of the British Colonies and possessions could not fail of admiration. This was a world exposition; and though the States have such ample resourses, it does no harm to let them recognise the width of our own by object lessons of this sort.

At a meeting of the General Parp)ses Committee on Monday it was decided at the request of the Museum Committee, to purchase a coloured drawing of the old Warrington market place by the late Mr. George Sheffield. Tbe picture will be hung in the art gallery at the Museum.

Railway Man's Narrow Escape. Arthur Booth (26), of 43, Haydock-street, had an extremely narrow escape from being killed on Monday morning. He was following his usual employment on the railway at Sankey when he was knocked down by the 11.25 Southport to Manchester express. He was picked up and inameliately taken to the Warring- ton Infirmary, where it was found he was suffering from bruises on the head and severe injury to the bac*: -

UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS.—Advt. Postponed Through the Fog. A. meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Com- mittee was called for six o'clock on Thursday night, and prompt to time the majority of tl-;e members of the committee put in an appearance at the National Schools, the meeting place of the authority. The Clerk t 9 the committee was not in attendance and the men.ibei4s present settled down to a wait of half an hour, when they come to the conclusion that he had been delayed by the disorganized train service con- sequent upon the fog and the meeting was adjourned for a week. Gipsy Children's Visit.

The annual return visit of Mr. John H. Tomkinson with his world renowned troupe of Gipsy Children is announced and the Company will appear at the Parr Hall, Warrington, next week, commencing with a matinee on Boxing Day at 2.30. The event will no doubt be greeted by the amusement lovers of the dis_ trict with enthusiasm, as it is an entertain_ : ment seldom met with in provincal towns. We have been favoured with an advance proof of the programme for 1901 and have no hesitation in pro- nouncing the company stronger than ever. Among a few of the old favoritei are the Lizzette troupe of lady acrobats,who created such a sensation with their clever and daring performance on their last visit. The new corners are the pick of the variety stage and in- clude the Florida troupe of cake walkers. The musical Keiths, and a host of first class performers too numer- ous to mention individually. Taking the company all round it is without a doubt the most complete com- bination of its kind ever attempted.
LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—.Advt.
Presentation to a Signalman.

Mr. R. Such, a Warrington railway signalman who has been transferred to Winsford, was given evidence on Monday evening of the esteem of his fellow work- men. This was afforded at a gathering which was held at the Railway Tavern.—Mr. Robertson, who presided over the gathering, remarked that they were very sorry indeed to have to part company with Mr. Such as they had always found him amiable and ready to help them. On behalf of the signalmen in the Warrington section, he had pleasure in asking his acceptance of a testimonial and a purse of gold.—Mr. Sankey also expressed his regret that they were part- ing with one who had been respected for the past dozen years.—Mr. Such, in accepting the gifts, said it had always been his aim to live happily and peace- fully with those with whom he worked, and assist them as far as it lay in his power. And knowing his efforts had been directed thus, he was quite satisfied. Ho should entertain pleasant recollections of his stay in Warrington, and particularly of the men with whom it had been his privilege and pleasure to work.
ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLAS, MINERAL WATERS.—Advt. Presentation to Mr. and Mrs. Corney.

On Thursday last an interesting presentation took place at Wycliffe British Schools. That day was the Silver Wedding" day of Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Corney the former of whom has this year completed a period of twenty-one years' service as Headmaster of these schools. The present and past members of the staff (Mixed and Infants' Department) took the opportunity of marking the occasion by the presentation of a pair of handsome silver flower vases. Mr. S. W. Jeffery who made the presentation said that the staff desired to shew their appreciation 'of the cordial relations that had always existed between Mr. Carney and themselves. They hoped that many additional years of happiness were before Mr. and Mrs. Corney.—ln acknowledging the gift, Mr. Corney said how complete was the nature of the surprise to him, and how highly he appreciated this expression of good feeling from the staff. He trusted that there would always be a continuance of those harmonious relations,—Mrs. Corney also expressed the pleasure she experienced in being associated with Mr. Corney in this presentation. Priory School Concert.

An excellent concert was given in the Canservatiire Club Assembly Room on Monday evening by the pupils ' of Miss Williams, the Priory school. At the concert the prizes won by the successful scholars were dis- tributed by Mr. J. R. Young. Miss Williams who ; was received with applause, said she was pleased to say that out of six senior Oxford certificates won at the girls' centre here, two came to that school. Of course many girls did the work and yet did not sit for examination, but she did think that a town as large as Warrington should be able to find sufficient candidates to maintain a girls' centre. She would like especially to thank Mr. Hall for kindly giving the music prize, and Mr. Rymer Young for presenting the prizes and certificate. (Applause.) Mr. J. Rymer Young said he particularly wished to congra+ulate Miss William; on the attainment of the B.A. degree of the London University. Mr. Young then presented the prizes, urging the children to make the best possible use of their opportunities, for upon the experience of their younger days would depend very largely their success and prosperity in later ltfe. The following were the ' prize winners :—Sixth class prize and senior Oxford certificate: Edith Cole, French prize and senior Oxford certificate: Dorothy Smith. Upper fifth class prize and music prize: Ada Isherwood. Music prize, attendance prize, conduct prize: Constance Hall. Intermediate honours certificate, Trinity College London, lower fifth class prize: Mabel Crampton. Examination prize and preliminary Oxford certificate: Dorothy Hall. Preliminary Oxford certificate: Dora Roberts. Certificate for pianoforte playing, Trinity College, London: Bessie Lee, and Doris Williams. Fourth class prize: Agatha Jones. Attendance prize: Ethel Crampton. Third class prize: Emily Stubbs. Second class prize : Keith Young. Upper first class prize: Dorothy Crampton. Lower first class prize : Millie Truslove. The concert was then proceeded with, all the items being well received, Pianoforte duets were given by the Misses Lee and the Misses Hall and pianoforte solos by the Misses Bessie Whitlow, Dorothy Smith, Dorothy Truslove, Vanda Pierpoint, Doris Williams; Connie Hall, and Clarence Newall.l A song was ren- dered by Miss Lucy Percival and a\ vocal duet by the Misses Roberts and Williams, Miss Roberts contri- buted a recitative I:aria, and an action song was well given by the Misses Ferguson, Gregory, Johnson Matthews, Neil, Thomas, and Truslove. The second part of the programme was an operette entitled The enchanted glen," 'in which a large number of scholars took part, showing careful training through- out.

Personal. We have pleasure in announcing that L. G. Corney of the Warrington Grammar School has won in open competition an exhibition of £3O for classics at St John's College, Cambridge. Mr. T. J. Down. We regret to state that Mr. T. J. Down, of Wilders- q)ool, is lying in a very critical condition in a Manchester hospital, where he has undergone an operation. The gravest issue was feared at a late hour last night. The Stockton Heath Trams. Stockton Heath residents will not be pleased to hear of the outcome of Tuesday's meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Committee held under the presidency of 'Alderman Smethurst. The subject of the fares to be charged on the tramways when the extended ser- vice to Stockton Heath is inaugurated came up for consideration. It was decided that from Rylands- street to Stafford-road the fare should remain ld, and that an additional id should be charged from Stafford- road to Victoria Square. The charge of children will be id. fDr the whole distance.

Drowned Through the Fog. On• November 28th, a night upon which a dense fog prevailed, a resident of Grappenhall, Samuel Carter (62) proceeded by car from Warrington to Latchford. After: leaving the car all trace- of him disappeared and nothing further was seen or heard of him until Monday, when his body was recovered from the Bridgewater canal at Grappenhall by Mr. S. J. Woodcock. It is surmised that the deceased missed his way in the fog and walked into the canal. At the inquest which was held on Wednesday by Mr. Yates, at the Dog and Dart Inn, a verdict of Accidentally drowned" was returned. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING TONICS.-63, S..ANKEY. STREET, Warrington—Advt. Society of Friends. A pubic address given in the Friends' Meeting House, Buttermarket-street, on Sunday evening by Mr. William Hobson, of Birmingham, on " George Fox: His time and his mission. Mr. Hobson gave a very interesting sketch of the life of the originator of the Society of Friends. Fox he said, was essenti- ally a man of peace. He preached the doctrine of peace and of the right of conscience, and he was opposed to the taking of the oath. Incidents in the life of Fox were described:and a great deal of valuable and interesting information was given. Fire at the Conservative Club. The promptitute of the kVarrington Fire Brigade on Saturday checked what must otherwise havebeen a very serious fire which broke out at the Conservative Club, Sankey-street. At about six o'clock some em- ployes at the Post Office noticed smoke issuing from the windows of the club and at once gave the alarm. Information was conveyed to the fire station by Mr. A. Swan and the brigade turned out with great prompti- tude with the fire engine " Captain." The fire, which had broken out in the bar, was quickly extinguished, though not before damage had been done to the extent of about £2OO. The fire is snpposed to have been caused by a defective flue. The damage is covered by insurance. XMAS PRESENTS—Try J. S. GARLAND'S, 51 to 55, Bridge-street,Warrington.Splendid selection.—Advt., County Council Scholarships. The Lancashire Education Cournittae offers for competition a number of scholarships, exhibitions, and studentships for elementary and secondary school subjects, art, music, agriculture and cotton technology ' as well as for candidates intending to become pupil teachers. Evening studentships in science, art, ' technological, and commercial subjects are also offered. Full particulars may be obtained from Mr. H. Lloyd- Snape, D.Sc., Ph.D., direction of education, County Offices, Preston. BEST BOOTS FOR ALL.—UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. A New Year Attraction. Warrington will have a special new year attraction on Monday, January 2nd, in the shape of the third annual Eisteddfod which will be held in the Parr Hall. Every effort is being put forth to make the event a big success, and the programme is one of exceptional interest. In the afternoon the principal item will be a local band contest while the evening meeting will witness the chief choral competition. Seven of the best known choirs in the north of England have expressed their intention of competing, and the entry for all the competitions establishes a record. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING of TONICS. I 63. SANKBY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. The Rants' ord and Warrington Light Railway. A special meeting of the Thelwall Parish Council was held on Monday evening to consider the plans for the proposed Kuutsford and Warrington Light Rail- way.—Mr. Halton, who presided, thought the Council were scarcely in a position to oppose the scheme see- ing that the proposed railwily only touched the borders of the township. They ought however, to see that the promoters of the new railway were com- pelled to provide for the safety of pedestrians at Cliff- lane bridge. After considerable discussion the follow- ing resolution was proposed by Mr. Dutton, seconded by Mr. Hewitt, and carried unanimously :—" Mat' Cliff-lane bridge, which, although not in the township of Thelwall, is largely used by Thelwall people resid ing in Waste-lane should be widened before Railway No: 1 is sanctioned, and that provisions should be made to light the roadway under such bridge. That the promoters should be required to provide a wait- ng-room for passengers at the junction of the four roads near the Dog and Dart Inn, which would be the most convenient place for the Thelwall people though not actually in the township of Thelwal. And that, subject to the foregoing conditions being complied with, this Connell do not oppose the Knutsford and Warrington Light Railway.' ASIC for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WATERS.—Advt. Action Against Councillor Madinn. In the Chancery of Manchester, on Monday, before Vice-Chancellor Sir Samuel Hall, K.C., Mr. Cunliffe moved, on behalf of Nathan Yates, chartered account- ant, of Bolton, for an injunction to restrain the defen- dant, John Magian, auctioneer, of Warrington, from representing by posters or other advertisements that a sale by auction carried on by the defendant at Bolton, was under a deed of assignment, of which the plaintiff was trustee, or that the plaintiff authorized such sale. Mr. Grant appeared .for the defendant.— Plaintiff's counsel stated that the defendant in August, purchased for about £5OO cer- tain furniture from the plaintiff as trustee under a deed of assignment, and having since been selling it by retail had added other goods and was now adver- tising that he was selling by action under the deed of , assignment, that he was empowered by the plaintiff to ' sell, and that the stock was worth £s,ooo.—Mr. Grant urged that the defendant was committing no legal wrong in advertising the sale as he had done.—The Vice• Chancellor said if the plaintiff's statements were correct an impudent fraud was being comraitted, and he should have no hesitation in stepping in.— Eventually the defendant undertook to discontinue the advertisements complained of and not to issue any frrther advertisements referring to the plaintiff or this deed of assignment. Upon this understanding the motion stood to the trial. XMAS PRESENTS.—Try J. S. GARLAND'S 51 to 55, Bridge-street, Warrington. Splendid selection.— Advt. The Walton Drowning Fatality.

Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest at Warrington on Tuesday on the body of Frederick Buchanan, (19), at Lower Walton, which was recovered from the river near tWalton Arches on. Friday of last week. On November ith Buchanan was working on the bar ge Dorothy near Walton Arches, when he slipped and fell into the river. All attempts at rescue failed and attempts to recover the body by means of grappling also failed. A.particularly distressing feature of the fatality was that Buchanan was the third member of the family drowned within recent years in the same locality, and under similar circumstances. At the inquest, Robert Buchanan, brother of the deceased, said one member of the family was drowned in February last year, and was employed by Mr. Griffiths on the barge James at the inquest which was held. The jury then recommended that ropes and stanchions should be fixed on the barges, so that if anyone slipped they would have something to cling to. Mr. T.ongton said work could not be carried on at all if ropes and stanchions were fixed. The manager for Mr. Griffiths also said it would be impossible to have ropes and stanchions on the barge, as the work could . not be carried out. A watermari named Appleton, gave- evidence as to the recovery of the body. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and added that more lifebuoys and ropes should be placed on the barges. Mr. Longton said his client would be only tO pleased to carry out the suggestion of the jury in order to save life. Mr. Steel appeared for the relatives of the deceased and Mr Long,ton for Mr. Griffiths by whom the deceased was , employed.

div.head: LIBERAL LABOUR ALLIANCE.
div.p: LIBERAL LABOUR ALLIANCE.
INAUGURAL PUBLIC MEETING OF THE PROGRESSIVE LABOUR LEAGUE.

The Warrington Progressive Labour League is giving great promise that ere long it will take a most import- ant and influential part in local political affairs. Launched only a few weeks ago it met with almost instant success. Supplying a long felt want in forming a party intermediate between and yet representative of both Liberalism and Labour its membership has in- creased by leaps and bounds. Evidence of its vitality was given at the inaugural public meeting which was held in the Co-aperative Hall, Sa.nkey-street, on Monday evening. The attendance at this meeting was large and considerable enthusiasm was displayed. Mr. Morton presided and was supported by Mr. Howes, (president of the League), Mr. Osborne,(and'Mr. Barnes. In a brief introductory speech the CHAIRMAN said he thought an excellent sign of Lhe times was that labour organizations were taking such a practical interest in political matters, and that there was an increasing tendency on the part of labour to influence the policy of the ,great political parties. The labour move- ment was one which should be particularly welcome to the Liberal party whose claim was that it was the party of the masses, advocating as it did government of the people by the people and for the people. (Hear, hear.) In the labour movement it must see a powerful aid in securing opportunities for which it had long waited for bringing about those refoms which were in the interests of the working classes. To give effect to the desire which existed for labour to organize for political purposes the Progressive Labour League had been formed. Along with the endeavour to push labour matters there was in some quarters a tendency—a regrettable tendency—to alienate Liberalism and Labour, and to make what would, with unity be

div.head: A. _SOLID, IItII.E3ISTABLE FORCE
div.p: A. _SOLID, IItII.E3ISTABLE FORCE

Iweak and ineffective. That tendency was altogether out of harmony withpolitical methods,and must always jeopardise the cause of progress. (Hear, hear.) To secure the full .effectiveness of all progressive forces • there must be a unity of such forces in opposition to Conservatism and rebrogression. (Applause). In face of the crisis Wiich had been reached in our political history any division in the ranks of progression was almost sinful. The record of the present Government was sufficient to wipe off the majority of 1,000 gained by Mr. Pierpoint at the last election, and if they only adhered to their principles they would be strong enough to ensure the recording of a majority of a thousand on the other side. (Applause). MI. OSBoRNE moved—" That this meeting, being of opinion that the whole of the legislative tendency of the present. Government is absolutely opposed to the interests of the working classes of the country, recogl- nizes the urgency for combined action on the part of labour and pledges itself to do all in its power to secure the return at the next election of Mr. A. H. Crosfield, the Progressive candidate." In doing so he said he had no desire to say a word against the present borough member other than that he was a representative of the party which was fast becoming a tool of capitalists, money makers and plutocrats generally. They had only to review the actions of the Government to see the truth of that statement. He was sorry to see such letters as had been appearing in the Press lately from writers signing themselves such names as "Loyalist " and " Imperialist," and he regretted the tone of those letters. Englishmen liked fair play and the le ist such writers could do was to come out in the open and sign their names to the abuse they had used. The way they had tried to trample on the personality of Mr. A. H. Crosfield was contemptible and he objected to it. (Hear, hear). As Liberals they did not object to a fair fight and they were fighting for freedom of Empire and freedom of the people, and not the sordid sort of free- dom and imperialism so much talked of. They had one lesson of the present Government in the South African war, where they saw how capitalists could get inden- tured labour, which of course was so much cheaper and would help to swell already big dividends, rather than help the British worker Two blacks did not make a white, but there were certain people who were trying their utmost to make yellow white. (Applause). They had had many figures put , before them with regard to the fiscal question of late, and at a meeting a short time ago Mr. Edwin Wood actually had the amazing ignorance to say that the excesss ' of imports over exports was paid for in bard cash.As work- ing men they had an illustration in the sugar convention of an interference with our trade conditions. Had it helped the worker at all? On, no ; ' but it had taken away from the British working man an important sec- tion of trade. In Birmingham alone 20 per cent. of the working men engaged in the trades which ,relied upon sugar, had been thrown out of emloymeat. It was getting time for the workers of this country to amalga- mate and at any rate they in Warrington should decide to do all they could to secure the return of the Progres- sive candidate. He trusted that when the time came they would see Mr. Crosfield returned at the head of the poll in the interests of the people and of those who had done so much for the cause of progress. (Applause), ' Mr. BARNES seconded. He thought the resolution was one which must have the approval of every fair minded man who had an interest in the welfare of the country. (Hear, hear.) Notwithstanding the number of people who were out of work in Warrington the tax- payers of the town were paving half of the taxation of , the agricultural interest in 'Cheshire. As the result of an act passed by a Conservative Government workmen in towns paid more than their share of taxation and helped to keep 'farmers who only paid half and who were perhaps better off than they were. He would content himself with that one instance to show that the Conservative party were not a party for the working- men. The Conservative party had expressed a desire to bring in a Re-distribution Bill, but he did not think that desire was honest as they so strongly opposed a similar Bill introduced by the Liberal party. He was perfectly willing that there should be a Re-distribution Bill and at the same time he would have a re-distribu- tion of power, and would take away from the House of Lords the power which they had of vetoing any measure. (Applause.) Then the Conservative party talked about bringing in an aliens Bill as they said they were desirous of keeping the alien out of the country, but he did not think that we ought to regard that as an hoaest desire on their part, Then the Conservatives urged that the Liberals had no policy, but they had and always would have a policyand that was a policy of retrench- ment and reform. If there was one reason why they should have another representative it was that Mr. Pierpoint had declared himself a "whole hogger," and i because of that they should leave no stone unturned to wrest thecOnstituency at the next general election from representation by the Tory party. (Applause.) Mr. HOWES in supporting referred to the Radical Labour League as an organization of earnest politicians who meant business, and who would dealTwith questions affecting the empire as well as with questions affecting labour. They were practical politicians who meant to get all that came along and then ask for more. They were raising no impossible standard and saying "We will take nothing until we get this," but were prepared to take half a loaf and wait their chance to get the other half. They were Radicals and were not going to say they were going to have nothing to do with party politics. They were going in for party politics, and were going to see that the man who was returned as the representative of the Borough was pledged to their programme. Speaking recently at a Tory.meeting a local gentleman remarked that the present Government were deserving of the confidence of the people both positively and negatively. Let them see why the Government deserved positive confidence. Did they deserve it for the introduction of

div.head: CHINESE TABOUR
div.p: CHINESE TABOUR

into South Africa? ("No.") That was a big question and .was. becoming bigger every day and would in the end inevitably bring about a great conflict between the yellow and white labour in South Africa. The Chinese on arrival in South Africa were met by the police, their photographs and finger prints were taken for police pur.poses,and thef were then placed in compounds from which they cQuid not escape, or if they did escape, they were pursued, captured, and taken back. Those were marks of liberty and freedom according to the Tory idea. If that was right in South Africa it was right in England, and if it was wrong in England it was wrong in South Africa. We could not have geographical limits to our morality. If the workmen in England thought the Tory idea of Chinese labour was freedom they must vote Conservative at the next Parliamentary election, but if they thought otherwise they must vote against the Conservatives. Several of the labourers in the compounds had been flogged and the question was to be asked in the House of Commons as to what right employers had to flog their workmen. If it was right that workmenshould be flogged in South Africa it was right that they should be flogged in England. When Chinese labour was intro- duced into South Africa we were told that it would lead to a large increase in the number of skilled whitemen employed. That was all right if it was true but how many unskilled workmen had been displaced by the introduction of the Chinese. We would find that UNSKILLED LABOUR HAD BEEN REPLACED by Chinamen and what guarantee had we that skilled labour would not be, in time, similarly replaced? (Applause). How much confidence did the Government deserve for the'increase in the national expenditure? Our expenditure had gone up by nearly £100,000.000 per annum and of this the weekly wage earner paid the greatest proportion. If a man thought it was right that the rich should grow richer and the poor should become poorer he should vote Tory but if he thought it right that the rich man should pay his share of the taxes of the country then he should vote against the Tory. What right had the Tory Government to ask for confid- ence on the question of old age pensions? When they came into power they had a surplus left them by the Liberal Government of £5,000,000, and in addition the splendid income from the death dues. They promised old-age pensions and gave the money to the rich. Surely they did not deserve the confidence of the people for that? (" No.") They also promised to bring abont a wise administration of national finance and had not brought that about. There were numerous
&"JP

other things which they had not done and altogether they could say " We have done those things which we ought not to have done and left nndone those things which we ought to have done and there is no health in us." (Laughter.) The Conservative Government gave up our trading rights in Madagascar and Siam and those markets were now closed to us. According to a member of the Tory party one thing the Government had not done was, they had not harassed " the trade." On the contrary they had plundered the people for the benefit of the trade. The publican was making a great cry that the compensation he would receive would not come from a national tax but from money which he would pay. It would be im- possible to find a more

IMPERTINENT MISREPRESENTATION OF [PACTS. The tax was imposed by the nation and collected by the nation, and was therefore a national trx, and if it was right that the money so paid should be returned to the publican it was only right that taxes should be re- turned to the ordinary taxpayer. Mr. Howes explained that the government of the League would be in the hands of the members and announced that Mr. Fenwick, the miner M.P., would shortly address a meeting of the League. He then proceeded to speak upon the fiscal question, and said that Protection it established would be a curse to the workers. He was prepared to do as the Tories did when they tried to prot e Free Trade was wrong. He would take as an example an isolated indus- try—the glass taade. The glassmaker would go ,to Par- liament and get himself protected. Foreign supplies would stop coming into the country, and all would be well for him. Then the bootman would go to the Government and get similar protection. The glassman would then go to buy a pair of boots, and would have to pay is. more per pair. He would enquire as to the cause of the advance, and would find it was due to the foreign supplies af boots which had been stopped. Then every one else would go in for being protected, and in the end the glassman would go back to Parliament and say "Take back your Protection. It has helped me in my business, but I have to pay twenty times as much for everything I want." Liberals had never urged that we had perfect l free trade but they said we had had a portion of free trade and that portion had enabled us to rise to a position attained by no country under Pro- tection. To got more free trade we would have to take tariffs off and the way to take tariffs off was not by putting additional tariffs on. At the present time trade unions were in a critical condition as their funds were not secure and the Progressive Labour League meant to do all that lay in their power to

GET MR. SHACKLETON'S BILL THROUGH the House of Commons. (Applause.) Then the Com- pensation Acts required alteration. At present if one workmen was killed through the fault of another I workman the relatives of the deceased workman could not claim compensation. In another case case a workman was injured, claimed compensation, and was awarded £B5O in the Court in which the case was tried. He then discovered that his employer was in- mired and that the case had been taken to the Court of appeal by the insurance company. Had the Iman bvl to defend the action the mat- ter would have ended and he would have lost his corn- Ipensation, but the trade union was taking the matter lup and was going to fight the case in the upper court. If that sort of thing was to be allowed then the radical I basis of compensation was gone. (Applause). This served as a fitting example of the tricks which were adopted to swindle the worker out of the compensation which he was supposed to get. They were going to hammer away until they had those things righted aad if they were to be successful is would be necessaay for the workers to weld themselves together and see that at the next general election they returned the man who endorsed their views. Their duty was clear and if they carried out their duty it would be easier for themselves and for their children in the future than they had found it in the past. (Applause).l The resolution was then put to the meeting and un- animously carried. SOME QUESTIONS ASKED. THE VALUE OF ALLIANCE.

Mr. HOWES was send "Considering the position of the workers in regard to the questions of trade union law, unemployed, old age pensions, and the housing pro- blem, is it not advisable and more progressive to estab- lish a labour party independent of the two great political parties ?" In reply he said if they had one party which was willing to take up their entire pro- gramme it was better for them to link themselves with that party, as according to the trade union motto union meant strength and isolation defeat.
O 9 THE POSITION OF IREGAND.

The question was asked fas to what the League pro- posed to do with Ireland. Mr. Howes said the question was fully answered in the programme of the League which included "Justice to Ireland." He was a home ruler and always would be one as it was only right to his mind that the affairs of Ireland should be managed by Irishmen. What the Irishmen must do was to ask the question of candidates for Parliament honours and vote for the man whose answer suited them the best. The question was then asked as to what the League proposed with regard to the recent Edrmation Act. Mr. HOWES said they were against religious education of any description, or if religion was to be taught they held that men desiring a certain class of religious education must pay for that education On that ques- tion they were opposed to the Irisn Catholics who must decide between justice being done to Ireland and the continuance of the present education system. In reply to another question as to whether working- men got a fair share of the product of their labour, Mr. HOWES said they must all remember that all labour was not productive. The workman did not get one-third of , the annual turnover, but it was because he was his own land his greatest enemy. They wanted the workers to realize the dignity of labour and to take a greater interest in things concerning their own welfare instead of selling their votes for a pot of beer. No other questions were asked a nd the meeting close with a vote of thanks to the chairman for his services.

The High School, Warrington. There was a pleasant gathering in the Co-opera tive Hall last evening when the pupils at t High Scho )1, Warrington, which is under th' able management of the Misses Partingtone gave an excellent concert. There was a, large attendance, and the creditable way in which numerous and varied items were submitted showed how admirable is the training received by the children. The proceedings commenced with the distribution of certificates to the more scccessful students by Mrs. Willis, and the recipients were warmly applauded. The programme included selec- tions by the ensemble class, a song by Miss E. Birchall, and two effective action songs. As a fitting close to the entertainment a pretty piece entitled "The Princess and the Pirate " was well performed, the principal characters being : Princess Elia, Miss Annie Kenyon; Countess Bianca (her attendant) Miss Gladys Pierpoint ; Maids of Honour, the Misses Marjorie Bennett and Annie Hignett ; Tessa, Miss Edith Partington ; Dame Gatte, 'Miss Josephine Broome; Nita (her daughter), Miss Nellie Dunn; Prince Guido (the Pirate Prince), Miss Jessie Howard; Justice Malateste, Miss Mary Forshaw; Sergeant Pippo (Son to Dame Gatte), Miss Alice Bennie; Tito (Page to Princess Lilia), Miss Dorothea Bra cecamp.
