div.head: MILK AND WATER.
div.p: MILK AND WATER.

At Tormorden on Thursday at Hebden Bri Igo farmer named Barker satisfied the magistrates that milk which the analyst said was adulterated with eight parts of added water had been sold exactly as it was obtained from the cow, and the charge against him was dis- missed.

div.head: MR. JUSTICE GRANTHAM'S CASE.
div.p: MR. JUSTICE GRANTHAM'S CASE.

The Lewes magistrates on Thursday gave their re- served opinion in the prosecution instituted by the Chailey Rural District Council against Sir William Grantham in connection with the latter's building of cottages. The Chairman carefully explained that it was a" finding," not a "decision." The magistrates found that certain of the Council's building bylaws had not been complied with,but that generally Sir William's plans complied with the by-laws, although defective in somo minor particulars. Sir William's counsel, on that finding, asked for the summons to be dismissed, but this the magistrates refused,though they hoped nothing more would be heard of the case. Council intimated .that the matter must go further, and that Sir William would consider what steps he shonld take.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, December 24, 1904.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 24, 1904.

"This will never do," said Power. "Lady Ock- ham is a kind of cousin of mine, and for the honour of the family we can't let in Eurasian blood. I'll go and call on her, get an invitation, and try and prevail upon her to ask Wallace too. We must do all we can to keep the Englishman in the running." A few days before Christmas the party was assembled at Treherne Court, augmented by two new guests. For Power had been to call on his new-found cousins, Lady Ockham and her beautiful daughter, had struck up a lively friendship with them, and on expressing his great interest in the wonderful Mr. Zigomala, of whom he had heard, at once received an invitation to be present at the approaching seamy. It was rather more difficult to obtain an invitatiot for Wallace, to whom in the meantime- he had been introduced by Harbord, and with whose manliness and sincerity he was charmed; but by asking for it point blank, as a personal favour to iimself, Lady Ocidiam yielded it with a good enough grace. I Pr already had an understanding with his pretty n -Ursula, who knew that in him she had gained a powerful ally. The great stance ,41-as to be held on Christmas Eve, which happened to be the anniversary of the death of the ghostly Lady (Jekham, when it was all the more likely that she would choose to appear. Zigomala proved to he an erratic guest. Him Itabits were extremesy .);Ihe night before the seance, Power r:st up a;osse very late in the library finishing an inters sting novel. It was two in the morning when he ex:inc:susised the lamps, took his bedroom (=die tuisl went quietly up to bed. At a turn •in one of the rambling passages upstairs he was startled to find himself face to face with Zigornala, who wa folk' dressed, and who had been moving noiselessly in Ins pumps. His attitude suggested to Power tha., he had been surprised in turning to go the other way, but had changed his mind and faced round towards the light when he found escape impossible. "There are strange influences in this house," he whispered quickly, his eyes wide open so that the whole circle of the eyeballs was visible. "I could not sleep. I want air—air. There is an atmo- sphere of crime." .

The candle-light :flickered on his ghastly face, casting leaping shadows. Power Inurnittred sympa- thetically, and offered to accompany him on a walk; but Zigomala declined, saying that he would be better alone. He would open the front door, and walk a while; and he glided noiselessly away. From his own room, putting out his candle and peering through a chink in the curtains, Power watched him walking up and down the snow- clad lawn in 'front of the house. At last he dis- appeared, and a creaking board in the corridor &noted that he was returning to his bedroom. Though it must have been after three when Zigomala went to bed, an early housemaid, who was up at half-past six, was startled to meet him coming out of the drawing-room at that hour. The morning was spent in exploring the ancient house-and lounging in the picture gallery, where the portrait of the .reappearing Lady Ockham was studied with interest. Before luncheon there came a telegram for,De Vanderwell, urgently calling him to London to the sick-bed of his sister. Somehow, the news that De Vanderwell had a sister living in London came as a surprise. He had never mentioned her, being reserved about his own affairs. A dog-cart was got ready to drive him to the station, and he left hurriedly, : warmly expressing the hope that his sister might improve so that he could return in time for the sectoice. Zigomala, when he had gone, expressed relief; declaring that he feared De Vanderwell would have been a hostile influence at the seance, and recalling to Lady Ockham his first dislike of the man when they had made each other's acquaintance on board the Swallow.

Lady Ockham had decided that the sitting should be held at. midnight,. after the servants had all gone to bed; and the room chosen was a large ante-room on the ground-floor, between the drawing- room and the library. Legend said that this had been the room of the ghostly Lady Ockham, and here her wraith had appeared to other Ockhams in days gone by. Before dinner on Christmas Eve, while the medium rested in his bedroom, and Wallace and Ursula Egerton had seized the opportunity to go off together to the garden, Lady Ockham shelved the seance room to Power and Harbord. It was a large, square apartment, with long windows opening on to the lawn, and two doors, one into the adjoining corridor and one into the drawing-room. Antique tapestry covered the walls, and raising a piece of this in one corner of the room, Lady Ockham shewed an iron door.

"Here was once," she explained, "the entrance to a secret staircase that led underground to an old priory. Long ago we had it bricked up, and in the thickness of the wall here my husband had a strong-room built to hold the famous gold plate of the Ockhams, and my jewels, when I am at home. When I art away, I need scarcely say that all the things gilt° the bank. Now everything is here." "A convenient place for burglars, said Power.

"They would have all their time to get this door open," answered Lady Ockhain. "Yet solid as it is, one little key will open it, ; but there are only two such keys. One I always keep; the other is in charge of Dixon, the butler, whom I would trust as if he were myself." A footman came with a telegram for Lady Ockham. "Mr. De Vanderwell hopes to be down in time for the séance," she announced; _"his sister is better." And the party separated to dress. As Power was tying his neck-tie, there was a tap at his bedroom door, and Harbord came in, followed in a few moments by Charlie Wallace. For ten minutes the.three men talked eagerly in low. voices; then Wallace went. away, Harbord leaving a few minutes later, and Power strolling down alone. They did not want Zigoinala to know that, they had held a consultation. At dinner everyone was in a state of suppressed excitement., and about ten o'clock De Vanderwell arrived, calm, and self-contained as usual. His sister, he explained, had had an alarming attack of heart failure, from which she had now recovered. Knowing that he should be late for dinner, he had dined at Waterloo before leaving, and had driven out to Treherne Court in a fly from the station. Watching his opportunity, De Vanderwell plucked Power by the sleeve and motioned him to a corner of the drawing-room out of earshot of the others. "May I speak frankly to you?" he asked. "Will you promise not to repeat what I say? "

Power nixided. De Vanderwell wAs a ;pan who seemed to know much, and say little. Power could not place him exactly in the social scale ; his reserve gave him a certain air of mystery. "Then I will go straight to the point," De Vanderwell began. "Do you trust Zigomala ? " His eyes were fixed on Power's with a keenness of scrutiny which the other had not noticed before. D 3 Vanderwell had seemed a rather languid man. Now he was startlingly awake. "Do you believe he is a genuine spirit-medium, or a trickster who intends to cheat us if he can ?"

"Really," said Power, "it is too early for me to form an opinion. What is your own view?" "I am bewildered," replied the 'other, "by his personality. Sometimes I believe; sometimes I doubt. But one thing is clear: he must be carefully watched at the seance." . His manner was curiously eager. "I suppose we shall all keep our eyes and ears open," said Power. "That's not enough. I think we ought to have some concerted plan . to strike a light in the midst of the proceedings, to seize any moving thing we ma 7 see--" . "No, no," interrupted Pcwer, emphatically, alarmed, and fearing for a speedy break-up of the seance. "That Ival never do. We must give the medium a fair chance, you know." "As you will ; but I shall keep my liberty of action."
"In using it, take care," rejoined Power, "that you do not infringe ours. We want to see all we - - ca.n many mar,:f.clati9ns RS possi-alt.'

seemed long beton mictnint came aria -me impatient sitters were assemblsd in tne seance room. The four men examined the fastenings of the Windows, and locked the two doors, taking out the keys. De Vanderwell went round again by himself to give a final glance, and see that all was secure. Before the lights were extinguished, the medium announced that the séance must be held in strict darkness, as only in such conditions could the spirits manifest themselves. Everyone was to rest his little fingers on those of his neighbours, and the circuit was on no account to be broken. Then Power blew out the last candle, and the room Alas in total darkness.

"Do not fix your attention ton closely on what is to happen," said 4igomala. "The best results are those that are unexpected. Perhaps the first sign of power may be a cold current of air upon on hands."

The sitters began a constrained conversation, everyone keenly on the watch for the expected manifestations. suddenly a chilly blast seemed to travel round the circle of hands. Ursula felt it first; then Lady Ockharu cried out: "They are coming; my hands are like ice; T feel a current of cold air upon them." Immediately after there was, a rap upon the table. "Has anyone broken the circle ? " asked Power. Everybody answered "No." . "It is the Others," answered Zigomala, in an awed voice. Power felt De Vanderwell trembling. "I will question them. Tell us" (everyone was very still) "is our circle properly arranged ?" One smart rap resounded on the table& "His fingers are trained to be suppl 7" thought Power to himself, "and he is snapping one of them upon the table without moving the rest of his hand." Zigomala questioned again, and in obedience to repeated raps upon the table, one for "no," three for "yes," the sitters were rearranged. Lady Ockham moved to the left of the medium; De Vanderwell was on his right. Then came Lord Power, Miss Egerton, Harbord, and Wallace next to Lady Ockham.

"There is much power," announced the medium; "some of it, lam sorry to say, malignant. I feel inauences almost intolerably evil. Earth-bound spirits are present, and the manifestations may be violent. But let no one be afraid; and, above all, touch nothing that you may see moving. If the circle be broken, I cannot answer for the result. if Igo into a trance, do not mind. The spirits must take force from me if there are to be materialisations ; and when they are over, I Ethan wake ikaturallv." Miss Egerton spoke suddenly. "Something is stroking my hair," she cried. "My ear has been pinched," said Wallace; "something soft was drawn across my face," called Harbord. "Oh l" exclaimed Lady Ockham, "a warm, tiny hand, like a baby's, has patted my cheek." At the same instant Power felt his trousers suddenly twitched undor the table, down by his ankle.
"Perhaps," said Z.igCtuala, "there will be some materialisations. Pray carry on a natural conver- sation." .

Everyone tried to talk, but broke off nervonsly at the sound of stirrings and rustlings that came from different quarters of the room. The medium seemed to have fallen into a trance; be was quite still, a heavy, regular breathing alone marking his place in the circle. In the nervous tension which now affected all the sitters, it was more than ever difficult to talk connectedly, and conversation dwindled to an occasional remark. Half-an-hour had passed with no manifestations save the rustlings and stealthy movements, when a light was seen in the further corner of the ronm. It looked like a shadowed, transparent globe, glowing with an inner phosphoresence. It grew brighter and travelled upwards. It shone on something, and, growing brighter still, everyone could see that the greenish light revealed a human face—the face of a handsome woman in an Elizabethan ruff, the face of the dead ancestress of the Ockhams whose painted lineaments looked down from the canvas in the picture gallery. Save for a sharp indrawing of the breath by Ursula, everyone was still; every head was turned to stare at the spectre. From the face, the globular light travelled slowly down to the feet and up again, revealing the complete costume of an Elizabethan lady, but diaphanous, like the filmy clothing of a ghost. The spectre waved an arm, pointed a finger at Ursula, then motioned towards the medium. Next she took an imaginary ring, and went through the Pantomime of slipping it on to her wedding finger. The suggestion was clear: the ancestress of tht.P=Ockhatns was giving her blessing to that union of the daughter of the house with the medium from the East, which, according to him, had already been commanded by the spirit of the late Lord Ockliam.

Ursula gave a little cry; there was a sharp, short whistle, aid on the • sound the room was flooded instantly with brilliant light.. Dazzled and dismayed, Lady Ockluun saw Harbord fling himself upon the ghost, and clasp in. his arms a screaming, fighting figure, which writhed and scratched and bit and panted in a vain effort to force its way towards the door. Power leaped to the corner where was the strong-room, and tore aside the tapestry to shew that the heavy iron door stood open. Zigomala's chair was empty. He was • not in the room.

"Too late, by Jove !" cried Charlie Wallace, rushing to the window, when a wild sound of jangling bells broke the stillness of the night. Wallace flung wide the window and leaped out. De Vanderwell had risen, and, very pale, moved slowly after Wallace.

"Mr. De Vanderwell," rang out Lord Power's warning voice, "I will trouble you to stand where you are." He turned swiftly to see that a gleaming revolver barrel was pointed at his bead, and stopped undecided,his hands clutched nervously-at the air. "What in the name of wonder does it all mean?" gasped Lady Ockham. Her startled eyes travelled round the room, and fell at last upon the table. Under her hand, which she had not moved since the séance began, lay a little wax finger, on which rested her own. Though he had his eyes on De Vanderwell, Power could not keep back a smile when he caught on his cousin's face the expression that shewed she realised how the medium had tricked her—substituting a finger of wax for his own of flesh and blood, With which she would have been ready to swear hers had been in contact all the evening. The false Lady Ockham had ceased to struggle now in Harbord's grasp, and was shaken by short, dry sobs. Her ruff had been disarranged, her hair shaken down ; she stood revealed as a rather pretty young woman, despite the artificial pallor of her face, the product of grease—paint and powder. There was a sound of trampling feet by the window; Wallace arpeared, propelling Zigomala in front of him by the ignominious means adopted by policemen when making a capture. The medium was handcuffed; -both men were breathless, and bore traces of a fierce struggle. Wallace gave .his prisoner a final push that sent him staggering into the middle of the room, shut the window, and stood guard over it, Harbord and Power moving to the two doors. There was a silence, broken only by the sobbing of the spectre, the panting breaths of the two men who had been fighting.' "My dear cousin, we owe you," said Power, "an apology for this distuibance ; you owe us your thanks .for saving your jewels." "My jewels'!"- screamed Lady Ockham. She ran to the strong-room, opened drawer after drawer. "All gone," she Vflieti. ; "my pearls, my diamonds, my tiara, my necklaces!" ! "Not gone," said Power, "though they would have been in a few moments more. That Elizabethan dress of the spectral Lady Ockham has many con- veniences for concealment. You see; the game is up," he went on, turning to the girl ; "the less trouble you give us the more lightly you will be dealt with."
Sullenly, with a face scarlet under its paint, the young woman Mosened some straps round her waist, and took from under her vohunii“,,29 irt

Tour large canvas table. Lady Ockliani fell on them like a hawk, tore them open, emptied out a glittering stream of jewels, rings, necklaces, bracelets, and began feverishly to count them over. "All here," she said, "not one misFing. Oh, you wicked man!" she cried, with a look of venom at. the medium. "After the confidence I placed in you-" "Without fools there'd be fewer rogues," retorted Zigomala, with a shrug of the shoulders.

It was five o'clock on Christmas morning before Lady Ockham and Ursula at last went up to bed, and, the three men sat up till the servants were about, talking over the events of the night. Lady Ockham had refused to give the medium and his accomplices into custody, for she would not face the public scandal. So they had allowed the girl —she confessed that she was De Vanderwell's wife and pleaded hard that. her husband should be spared—to change again into her own clothes, which she had left in the drawing-room, near the window by which she had entered; then they escorted the three baffled criminals down the avenue to the lodge gates, and turned them out into the empty country road, at two in the morning, with a five-mile walk through the snow to the nearest railway station. Their luggage Power considerately promised to send after them to Waterloo Station; then the gates were shut upon them, and as the three Englishmen turned to walk back to the house, the last they saw of them, when Wallace had slipped off the handcuffs, was Zigomala dancing and cursing on the road, and shaking his fists at the retreating figures of his enemies. It was an ingenious plot that Power and his friends had thwarted: De Vanderwell, of course, had been in it from the first—he had known Zigomala on the Swallow, where they had pre- tended to be strangers; he had talked to Power to try and discover whether he had any plan to interrupt the séance; he went up to London with a wax mould of the key of the safe, which Zigomala had taken by stealing into old Dixon's bedroom in the night. It was De Vanderwell, too, who had bought the Elizabethan 'costume, having studied it in the picture gallery; and sitting next to the medium, he had released the latter's hand, and imitated his heavy breathing, leaving him at liberty (being already free from Lady Ockham) to walk about the room. Zigomala had rifled the strong-room in the darkness, and passed the jewels to De Vanderwell's wife, who had hidden in the shrubbery, and came into the drawing-room, where she dressed in her ghostly clothes, entering the seance room by mean: of a well-oiled skeleton key which Zigomala had Wallaee was due the idea of a wire aeruss toe iai u. with a bell; for he argued that when the row came, Zigomala would bolt for the window, and try to get away in the darkness, which is exactly what he did do. But for the stretched wire, which brought him to the ground, he might have escaped. As it was, Wallace had a severe struggle to capture the man, who fought for liberty as a wild cat fights, and left on the young sailor's face and hands for many a day marks both of teeth and nails. The "spirit touches" were easily explained, • seeing that the medium had his hands free, and the "spirit light "that shed its ghostly illumination on the face and figure of the spectral Lady Ockham was nothing more than a plaster of Paris globe, liberally speared with luminous paint. Its shattered fragments were found upon the scene of Ilarbord's struggle with the "ghost." The lights that bad flooded the room at Wallace's signal were electric lamps, with which each of the three Englishmen had provided themselves, worked by small batteries in their pockets. Power and Harbord impressed upon Lady Ockham next day that it was due mainly to Charlie Wallace that the medium had been trapped just in time; and, in gratitude to the man who had saved her jewels, she gave her consent to an engagement between the handsome young sailor and her daughter Ursula. And so all were happy on Christmay Day. Si [THE END.]

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Mersey Street Mission.

The third of a series of revival services was held in the above mission on Sunday, the preacher being Mr. George Barratt, of Leigh, who in the morning spoke on "The claim of God on mankind." At the evening service a large congregation assembled, when the preacher took for his text ".What wilt thou say when He shall punish thee?' Dnring the evening a solo was rendered by Miss Houghton.

div.head: Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church.
div.p: Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church.

Selections from the" Messiah "were given in the above place of worship on Sunday evening, the church being crowded. The overture was well rendered on the organ by Master Clatworthv. Miss Jowett of Halifax. sang" There were shepherds,"" Rejoice greatly," and "I know that my Redeemer liveth". Miss Alice Wood- land," Come unto Him " ; Miss Fairhurst, "0 thou, that tellest " and" He was despised" • Miss Snelling "He shall feed his flock." Mr. Ram dassall " Comfort ye " and " Every valley." "He was cut off," and "But thou did'st not leave," Mr. E. H. Pearce, A.L.C.M., .‘ Thus saith the Lord," " But who may abide," and the solo" Why do the nations," all the singers acquitting themselves in a most admirable manner. The choir under the conductorship of M. A. Spruce, were heard to advantage in "And the glory,' "0 Thou that tellest." For unto us"" Glory to God," "Behold the Lamb of God," "All we like sheep," "Worthy is the Lamb," and "Hallelujah." Mr. Fred Podmoro was at the orgari. The Rev. C. L. Stowe gave an address.

div.head: Choral Service at Wycliffe.
div.p: Choral Service at Wycliffe.

The annual Christmas Choral Service in connection with W-ycliffe Church, was held on Sunday evening, when, as in former years, selections were given from the" Messiah," There was a crowded congregation to listen to the efforts of an augmented choir, the members of which without exception acquitted themselves ably in the better known choruses from Handel's sacred masterpiece. The instrumental accompaniments were supplied by a specially appointed and well-balanced orchestra, consisting of :—First violins, Mr. R. H. Pear- son and Mr. W. Brown; second violins, Mr. A. Knowles and Mr. T. F. Wallington; 'cello, Mr. H. Bond; viola, Mr. G. Johnson; bass, Mr. R. Whitfield; organ, Mr. F. Hickman. The soloists were Mr. A. Griffiths, Mr. E. Pownall, Mrs. R. H. Pearson, and Mrs. A. E. Longshaw, all of whom sang well. Mrs. Pearson and Mr. Pownall were especially successful in their solos which like the other vocalists, they treated in a sympathetic manner. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., acted as conductor. The address, a brief one, was given by the Rev. John Yonge.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was again on Sunday a very good meeting of this society. Mr. William Mills presided, and spoke of the good he had personally received by attending the meetings, and the very hearty welcome he received when first he came amongst them. The unity and com- bination of son, speech and prayer at these meetings filled one with interest and abiding inspiration. Mr. A. Ketley, of Manchester, was the speaker, and spoke upon " The child grew, and waxed strong inspirit, filled 1 with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him." He drew some beautiful lessons from Christ's life and work and urged all to follow His example. Although he suffered much, He endured and finished the great work God had given him to do.—Miss Miller very sweetly sang" The Lord is my Shepherd" and "Entreat me not to leave Thee."—The Secretary said this was Peace Sunday, and referred to the great and deadly conflict now going on between Russia and Japan, The loss of life and treasure was great, homes were made desolate, trade stagnated, and werebrought down on every hand. He trusted everyone present would pray that God in His good time would bring war to an end, and that speedily the nations would learn a better way of bring- ing these national differences to an end. He also welcomed three new members; 570 were now enrolled, and during the last 3 months on an average 6 have joined each Sunday. Mr. Bannister took part in the meeting, and Mr. Payton presided at the organ. A very enjoy- able enthering was closed by singing "Peace, perfect I peace."

NEW CHIEF CONSTABLE OF ST. HELENS. The St. H3lens Watch .Committee on Wednesday appointed Mr. A. R. Ellertngton, the Chief Constable ,of Margate, to be Chief Constable of St. Helens. Mr. Ellerington is thirty-two years of age, and has been Chief Constable of Margate since November, 1902. He joined the East Riding Constabulary in 1891, and has Ihad a large experience in all departments of police work, as detective inspector, B:c.,at Barnsley and Wake- field. The salary is £3OO per annum and house.

PA WNBROK}R'SPROMPTITLD. Mary Elizabeth Cann, 70, Howard-street, was charged at the Warrington Police Court on 'Saturday, with stealing ifrom Messrs. Jackson's pawnshop, Winwick- street,a lady's gold ring of the value of 7s.6d.—Supe into the Monaghan stated that the prisoner went the shop and asked to see some rings. She selected a wedding ring and a keeper ring and having paid is. on them left the shop secreting another ring in her hand. Nothing more was beard of her until Friday morning, when she went to Mr.Domville's pawnshop in Priestley- street and pledged the ring for 4s. Mr. E:Evans,the manager, afterwards noticed that it had Messrs. Jack- son's private mark upon it and reported the matter to them. Or examining their stock, they found that the Ting was missing. Subsequently the police were informed and the woman was arrested by Detective Meacock.— She admitted the offence and was fined 20s.

ALLEGED THEFT AT EARLESTONVN. At the Warrington Occasional Court, on Monday, before Mr. T. Halton, George Cosgrove and George Thomas Dean were charged with stealing, on December 10th, a handbag, containing 61b. of bacon, a pay of men's drawers, a pair of men's socks, value 55., the property of Peter Keen. Burtonwood, and also a pair of mcn's socks, value 2s. 6d., the property of Philip Banks, Burtonwood. The evidence showed 'that prosecutors went into the Ram's Head Hotel, Earlestown, and laid the bag contoin- ing the articles on a form and went to the counter to have a drink. Cosgrove and Dean were sitting near the bag and Dean said" Who wants a bag ?" He was told to put it down but he gave it to Cosgrove, who then left the house. Dean followed him immediately after, and information was given to the police. Prisoners were committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. '

Minor Cases.

R. T. Fairclough and A. 3..J011ey. WIFE 31 AINTENANCE.—Frederick Davies,lB, Victoria- street, was summoned for arrears of maintenance being due to his wife amounting to £ll 4s.—He was ordered to pay the money or go to gaol for two months.

MONDAY—Before the Mayor (presiding). Aldermen Francomb and Smethurst, Councillor Tinnion,Messrs. Hayward. Wright, Thornton, Burgess, Pilling, Wilkin- son and W. Roberts. ASSAT:LT ON THE POLICE.—Bridget O'Brien,B, Dakins- yard, was charged with using obscene language in Horsemarket-street on Sunday night, and also with assaulting P.C. Woolacott.—P.C. Woolacott said he heard the prisoner using obscenelanguage. Herennested her to co away several times, but she refused. On the way to the Police Station, she tried to bite his band and leg and she was so violent that he had to obtain the assistance of two men and also get a cab.—Sergeant Willi amson said he was at the Police Station, when the prisoner was brought in. She was very violent and struck one of the men in the face.—O'Brien, who made her 17th appearance, was sent to gaol for a month. AN OLD OFFENDER.—Henry Cafiney, of Friar's Green lodging-house, was charged with stealing from the shop of Elizabeth Allen, Mersey-street. a 21b glass bottle 9f chlorodyne lozenges, value 4s.:—Superinten- dent Monaghan said that in company with Sergeant Conliffe he was making a round of the lodging-houses on Saturday night, when he came across the prisoner eat- ing cough lozenges from a bottle. They Tonnd he had only just brought them in, and when questioned the prisoner said be might as well admit that he had stolen the lozenges from Mrs. Allen's shop. Prisoner did nothing else but steal and had been convicted fifteen times for that kind of offence,—Caffney was sent to gaol for two months with hard labour.

_ SCENE IN THE MARKET-PLACE,—Mary Broderick, 8, Dallam-lane. was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in the Market-place on Saturday night, and James Caldwell, 54, Priestley-street was charged with threatening the police and with attempting to rescue her from custody.—P.C. Gilchrist stated that the woman was in the market creating a disturbance and using very obscence language. She was several times requested to go away, but declined to do so and said all the policemen in Warrington could not lock her up. He was obliged to take her into custody, and the prisoner Caldwell told him to let the woman go and used violent language.—Broderick, an old offender, was sent to gaol for a month and Caldwell was fined 10s. and costs.

div.head: CHRISTMAS SEANCE
div.p: A CHRISTMAS SEANCE
By MRS. C. N. WILLIAMSON, Author of "The Barn Stortners," "A Woman in Grey," "The Noose by the Lock," "A Bid for a Coronet," "Lady Mary of the Dark Rouse,
"Come and dine at the club," said Lord Power to his friend Dennis Harbord, "and let us have a long talk about your adventures on this cruise which seems to have been quite out of the ordinary run."

"There was one set of people on board," said Dennis, when they were settled in a corner-of the smoking-room, "who interested me greatly. I could see a romance—perhaps a tragedy—being played out before my eyes. I will give you the dramatis persona. Lady Ockham—grande dame, widow, rich, clever, but gullible; the Honourable Ursula Egerton, Lady Ockham's only child—pretty, sweet- tempered, •but desperately, overawed by her commanding mother; Charlie Wallace, first officer of the pleasure-yacht Swallow—handsome, brown, simple-hearted, brave, poor, a typical English sailor, madly in love with Ursula Egerton; St. John Zig.omala. Eurasian—clever, unscrupulous, spirit- medium."

"Spirit-medium ?" echoed Power. "Was he employed by the owners to amuse the trippers ?" "Nothing of the kind. He had paid his fare like any other. How it came out that 'be was a medium I can't say. it ran round the ship when we were a few days out. But • when one of the entertainment committee went up to him on deck and asked him to give an exhibition, he was mortally offended, said he wasn't a conjuror, and walked away in a temper. That made him all the more mysterious. He was the kind of fellow some women like, and all men long to kick. He had an olive skin, large almond eyes that drooped at the outer corners, a long, thin nose, and a soft, caressing voice. He was overbearing and brutal to those he could safely bully; coolly insolent to the fellow-passengers- from whom he thought he had nothing to gain; insinuating with women, and crineeing to everyone with a title, of whom, by the way, Lady Ockham was one of the few on board. To her, and to her daughter, the fellow paid con- stant court. He lingered about till they came on deck in the mornings, arranged their chairs for them, and talked all day in his curious lilting voice, that somehow reminded me oat the music snake-charmers play to soothe their pets." "Curiously enough," said Power, 'Lady Ockham is one of the new relatives I can claim since I came -into my title. I have heard she is an eccentric person. How did she cotton to the medium?" "My dear fellow, he had her under his thumb from the second day. The chap was diabolically clever. There were few things he didn't know; few experiences, according to him, that he hadn't tried. I cultivated this set for two reasops First, because queer people interest me, and I like to get at their natures and understand them; and, secondly, because 1 was implored by Charles Wallace to keep a watch over Miss Egerton. The poor beggar endured tortures to see Zigomala always with the girl he loved; and as his duties gave him very little time for spooning, he wanted me to act as watch-dog. As often as I could get away from my little surgery, I sought out the trio on the deck. Ziggie (that's what the men called him) would have been rude if he had dared; but you know a doctor on board ship is a power, and Lady Ockham liked me. "With these kind of cattle, if you want to study them, you musn't take up a hostile line; you must gee into sympathy with them. This I did so successfully that in a little time I found myself as much interested in mysticism, theosophy, the double- life, the astral-body, and so on, as Zigomala and ! Lady Ockham herself. Ziggie ' certainly had a wonderfully persuasive way. With my scientific training naturally I couldn't swallow lots of things the said; but when I asked for explanations, he gave them so cleverly, with such a vast vocabulary drawn from Buddhist terms, and such a show of pseudo-science, that I was bewildered and almost compelled to admit that there might be something in it.' Lady Ockhain drank in every word. She even proposed to him that they should start a new religion together in London! "Well, one glorious starlight night on deck some very odd things happened. We were a little group of six—Lady "Ockham and her daughter, Charlie Wallace, Zigoinala, myself, and a man called De . Vanderwell, an inoffensive, quiet fellow who seemed to know no one on board, but had gradually ; attached himself to this set. Zigomala had been : rude to him at first; but the man would not take a snub, and being very well dressed, apparently rich (for he happened to mention once that he had a ' palazzo in Venice, and it. came out that he kept an apartment in Paris as well as a fiat in London), and of agreeable manners, Lady Ockham rather took him up, especially as he became deeply I interested in all the spiritualistic business. Well, this night everyone pressed Zigomala for some proof of his mediumi%tie power. It is impossible,' said Lady Ockham, that you can know so much of these mysteries without possessing some abnormal powers yourself. Pray let us have evidence of them. We are a group of friends—l think I may say all believers,' she went on, look- ing round; but catching sight of Poor Wallace, the detrimental, who never professed t 9 take stock in the spiritualism, she added, rather viciously, or nearly all. t owe, dear Mr. Zigomala.' "The Eurasian pretended to hesitate, then grace- fully gave way. He said he would give us one of the simplest proofs of his command of unknown laws of nature. He stretched out his brown fore- finger, and I confess I felt a little Creepy down the spine when suddenly from his finger-tip there rang the clear note of a bell." -
"Bosh! Had it concealed in his pocket, and strnck it with the other hand," broke in Power.
"He said that it was done by the clashing of two currents of electricity which he had power to set in motion."

Power laughed. "What else?" he asked.. "Well, then we mule a pile with our hands, resting them on the tSp of each others'. Wallace managed to get his on the top of Miss Egerton's, but Zigomala calmly told him he must take them away, as he wasn't mediumistic,' and put his own in their place. Then each one of us distinctly felt a knock, which passed right down and recorded itself. with a concussion, on the side of the deck-chair on which our hanes rested."

"Either pure imagination," scoffed Power, "or else the fellow snapped a tendon in one of his fingers, and tapped his boot on the deck at the same moment to deceive you. Nothing's more difficult to :judge than the direction of sound."

"Your reiref;hing scepticism," said Harbord, "is like a douche of' cold water on a fevered head. Well, let me tell you the end of the story.- One day I found pretty Ursula Egerton all alone staring over the stern into the foam of the propeller. She had been crying, and in a burst Of confidence told me she was miserably unhappy because her mother insisted that she Must marry Zigomala, whom she detested, while she was secretly engaged to Charlie Wallace. Zigoluala had told Lady Ockham, it appeared, that spirit voices, especially that of the girl's dead father, had decreed the match ; and she is so infatuated with the fellow that she thinks it an honour to have him in her family. When, we came back to the Thames, Lady Ockham invited our little group down to Treherne Court, her old place in Sussex, at Christmas, to bold a seance in the house, so that Ziconiala :might summon the spirit of a dead Lady Ockham, who flourished in the time of Queen Bess, and who, it appears, is a well- established family ghost. The party is to consist of the two ladies, the medium, De Vanderwell, and - la walluee. who anoled desueiatelv for
an invitation, was ignore°.

SOCIETY NOT YET SELF-SUPPORTING,

Although the Warrington and District Agricultural Society is not yet in the happy position of being self- supporting, its work continues to be attended with a good measure of success. There was gratifyingly large attendance at the annual meeting held in the Masonic Rooms, 80ld-street, on Monday afternoon under the presidency of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart, and the report of the year's work was an interesting one. Amongst those present were :—Messrs. John White, C. Mclver, H. F. Greenouzh (chairman of the Council), H. Beresford Melville (secretary), and A. Broome (bon' tr asurer).

div.head: FINANCES,
div.p: THE FINANCES,

The balance sheet was submitted. and showed receipts totalling £633 15s. 4d. Subscriptions, special prizes, &c., accounted for £326 us. 6d., while £l5l 35., was received from entry fees for exhibits, £143 lls. 6d., for admissions at the gate, and £32 Is., for admissions at the grand stand. The payments amounted to £855 Ss. 7d. leaving a deficit on the year's working of £l7l 13s. 3d. On the general account a special donation of £l5O from Sir Gilbert Greenall enabled the society to show a credit balance of L'l3 Ss. 7d.

In moving the adoption of the balance sheet, Mr. J. HEPHERD suggested that in future balance sheets the figures relating to the previous year's show should be given for comparative purposes. Mr. H. F. GREENOUGH seconded the proposition whicl was agreed to.
THE REPORT. LIST OF SUBSCRIBERS GROWING.

_ Mr. H. BERESFORD MELVILLE, the 'non. secretary, presented the report as follows :—This society held its 15th annual show on Thursday, 11th August, 1904, in Walton Park, near Warrington, which was again lent for the occasion by Sir Gilbert Greenall, the president of the society. It is almost needless now to remind the members as to the deep obligation they are under to Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall for the great assistance they give to the support of the society, It is most gratifying to an agriculcural society to have a president, not in name only, hut in one who personally takes the greatest interest in its organization and clerical work. From close observation of the accounts, it will be noticed that the actual receipts hardly meet the expenditure without the valuable financial assistance given each year by Sir Gilbert Greenall. The Vice-President, for the year was Colonel Hall Walker, M.P., who had been a supporter of the society since its formation. The list of subscribers is gradually growing, and it is hoped thot in course of time there will be no necessity to Increase the classes by the addition of such as will chance the character of this particular society's show into merely a sightseeing entertainment, thereby effac- ing the original intention of the first promoters in form- ing a society for the promotion of good stock breeding in the district and the general support of the agricultural industry of the neighbourhood. Some slight alterations were made in the classes. In 1903 prizes were offered for polo ponies, but there was considerable difficulty in obtaining entries and the Council decided to withdraw these prizes this year. An additional pony class for two or three years old gelding or filly was fairly well filled, and it is thought that there will be a large entry when the class becomes better known. The prizes for cheese were considerably increased by the generosity of Lady Greenall with the result that a better entry was made, but it is a matter of regret that if there are more cheese makers in the district, they do not take the opportunity of showing their products at little expense considering the benefits derived thereby It is, however, suggested that the confines of the dis- trict do not embrace the particular localities where most of the Cheshire cheese is made. It must, however, 1 be understood that the district does embrace as much lof Lancashire as of Cheshire; but presumably the ILancashire cheese-makers do not care to enter the "lists" against their Cheshire neighbours, The butter entries do not gain much in numbers, and it might be beneficial if some slight alteration be made in the offer of prizes, inasmuch as there is a general feelin,, that where Jersey cattle are kept there is not mach chance competing with butter made from the milk of other breeds. The hunter and hackney entries were good, both as to numbers and quality, and it is hardly necessary to say that these particular classes are a great feature of the show, hardly surpassed by any other show in the country. The Shire classes were well filled, and undoubtedly the exhibits were up to their usual high standard. There was a better show of cattle throughout, especially in the dairy cox and heifer classes. The Secretary expresed the thanks of the society to the prize donors and stewardswithout whose able assistance the success of the show could not be assured. (Applause). The report was adopted on the motion of Mr. GEORGE MARSH, seconded by Mr. ALFRED BROOME.

div.head: SIR GILBERT GREENALL RE-ELECTED PRESIDENT.
div.p: SIR GILBERT GREENALL RE-ELECTED PRESIDENT.

Mr. GREENOUGH proposed the re-election of Sir Gilbert Greenall as president of the Society. Sir Gilbert had, he said. held the office of president since the inauguration of the society and under his guidance rapid strides had been made. The society was not yet self-supporting, but he hoped the day was not far dis- tant when it would be. During the last few days the Altrincham Society had added another £2OO to its reserve, fund. It was not very long since the Alt rincham show had a run of bad luck, but now the society had a balance in hand of £2OO or £3OO. He hoped that before long the Warrington Society would be in the same pleasant position. (Hear, hear.) Mr. R. B. NEILSON geconded and the motion was heartily agreed to. Sir GILBERT GREENALL said it was with the greatest pleasure in the world that he again accepted the presi- dency. Anything he could do for the benefit of the society would, as in the past, be willingly done, and he would use his utmost endeavour to make their show the best in this part of the world. (Hear, hear.) They had never been very lucky in the matter of weather sinoe they began to hold the show lon the new ground, but he hoped that next year they would have a fine dayand far better attendance, He thanked all those who had been concerned in the working of the society for the great kindness they had always shown to him, and for the willingness with which they had done everything in their power for the success of the show. (Applause.)

div.head: VICE-PRESIDENT.
div.p: THE VICE-PRESIDENT.

The PRESIDENT said it had been arranged that each year the vice-president should be representative of Lancashire and Cheshire alternately. This year it was Cheshire's turn and he had the greatest pleasure in pro- posing that Mr. T. H. Lyon be elected to the office. Mr. S.DAVIES seconded and the motion was unani- mously approved. The meeting expressed agreement with the President's suggestion that the names of the vice-presidents of the society from its commencement should in future appear in the show catalogue. The President remarked that his father, the late Sir Gilbert Greenall, was the first vice-president in 1890,and since then the office had been held by Mr. Stapleton Bretherton' the Mayor of War- rington (two years), Mr. Frederick Mbnks, Mr.Sylvanus Reynolds, Captain Withiugton, Mr- W. H. Jones Mr. Littleton Dewhurst, the Mayor of Warrington, Colonel Cornwall Legb, Colonel Ireland Blackburne, Mr. J. St. Vigor Fox, and Colonel Hall Walker, M.P. !THE COUNCIL. The following were elected members of the Council: —Messrs. N. Massey, Martinscroft; W. Monks, War- rington; R. B. Neilson, Halewood; T. Smith, Bold; P. Davies, Warburton; R. Clarke, inn-, Heatley; H. Mawdslev, Halton; Frank Tinsley, Daresbury. ' Sir Gilbert Greenall was thanked for presiding, on the proposition of Mr. GREENOUGH, seconded by Mr. H. G. ROBERTS. In responding, he expressed the hope that the society would in future be more prosperous in every way. It was announced that next year's show will be held i on Thursday, August 17th.

"Ivories" (London).—As promised last week, I now give you a list of the plincipal breaks made by Stevenson last season. The list only comprises breaks over 300, as his breaks of over 200 were too numerous to detail :

301 (ivories) 357 (crystalates) 303 (crystalates) 381 (ivories) 305 (ivories) 384 (ivories) 311 (crystalates) 385 (crystalates) 319 (ivories) 427 (ivories) 384 (ivories) 451 (crystalates) 330 (ivories) 463 (Ivories) 343 (ivories) 523 (ivories) 346 (ivories) 539 (ivories) 346 (ivories) 703 (crystalates) 349 (crystalates) 788 (Ivories) be average of the breaks made with ivory balls works out at 40779 and with crystalates at 408.4. This may be *ken as a fair proof that crystalate balls are at least as good as the very best ivory bills, forprofessionals when playing with ivory balls use only the very best that can be procured. My argument was not, however, that crystalato balls were better than good, true ivory balls, but that they were infinitely superior to the average ivory balls to be found in the ordinary billiard rooms of clubs and hotels. As a rule the best 'ivory bills soon lose their trueness, and were Stevenson to play his matches with the kind of ivory balls to be found in nine out of every ten billiard'rooms„he would experience a difficulty in making a hundred break, and breaks of 300 would be quite an impossibility. Crystalate balls, being a mechanical mixture •and not an animal growth, are of exactly the same density and specific gravity throughout and what is more they do not gradually shrink and warp like an ivory ball does. I have played regularly with a set of crystalate balls for the last three years, and they are absolutely as true to-day as the first day I played with them. Previously I had to get a new ' set of ivory balls about every 12 months.

Played at Runcorn in good welther. After some kicking exchanges had taken place, in which Houghton and Dixonishowed to advantage, Swinton were penalised for off-side, but nothing came of the kick. The visi- tors' forwards gained possession, and some lively work between Molyneux and Kewin took play to the Runcorn quarter. Butterworth found touch at centre, but the Swinton forwards rushed to Houghton, who replied well. From the centre Flynn broke away with a splen- did run, and passing to Lewis the latter got past Hough- ton and scored a try. Evans missed the goal. Half- time :—Swinton, 1 try (3 points), Runcolm nil. On re-starting Swinton had to face the wind, but by short kicking they worked their way to the Runcorn line. Butterworth put Runcorn on the attack by a big punt, but the effOrts of the home team to score were not very bright. Swinton maintained a long series of attack- ing_ movements without being dangerous, andlile game ended in a win for Swinton by 1 try (3 points) to Run- corn nil. •

div.head: LEIGH v. WIDNES.
div.p: LEIGH v. WIDNES.

At Leigh, before 2,000 spectators. Leigh started, and after Widnes had thrice tried unsuccessfully. at goal from penalties, the Leigh backs started passing, and Neville ran round the full back and scored near the corner, Dunbavin landing a goal from a difficult angle. Then Johnson got hold, and kicked and followed up so fast that he tackled the full back near the Widnes line, and from the next scrummage Dunbavin threw to John- son, who got over at the corner, no goal resulting. Leigh kept up the attack, Widnes only occasionally reaching the Leigh half. The third try for LBigh was scored by O'Neill, the place kick failing. At the interval Leigh led by a goal and three tries (11 points) to nil. The wind favoured Leigh in the second half, and early on Alf Taylor, the Widnes half retired hurt. Neverthe- less Widnes attacked, but were forced back, and Messer intercepting a pass ran a long way, and then threw to Johnson, who gave to Burgess, the latter scoring at the corner. The place kick failed. The rest of the play was even. About five minutes from the finish I. Taylor of Widnes, and Burgess, of Leigh, were ordered off for alleged roughness. Result :—Leigh 1 goal 4 tries (14 points), Widnes nil.

div.head: BRADFORD v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.
div.p: BRADFORD v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.

At Park Avenue, be fore about 5,000 spectators. Neither side was fully representative. At length Phipps kicked down and Gunn misjudged the swerving ball, which, however, he got to touch with a short punt. On the ensuing scrummage the home defence was caught napping the Kingston forwards dribbling over in a knot, and West scoring a try, upon which Carmichael was unable to improve. Half-time :—Hull Kingston Rovers 1 try (3 poirts), Bradford nil. With the wind in their favour Bradford did not at first shape well. Then after a 'good forward burst frsm the pack by the Bradford forwards, Kingston were penalised. Marsden with a long kick landed the goal, reducing the visitors' lead to one point. A brilliant try ensued. The ball came across the line of backs to Dechan, who drew Carmichael on to him, and then passed to Heseltine, who had a clear run in. Eagers' kick at goal was a failure, but just before the close he kicked a goal from a penalty. Result :-.--Bradford 2 goals 1 try (7 points), Hull Kingston Rovers 1 try (3 points).

div.head: OLDHAM V. WIGAN.
div.p: OLDHAM V. WIGAN.

Played at Oldham, before 5,000 jspectatom Oldham had the advantage of a strong wihg in the first half. Early in the game neat combined play by Carey and Harris led to the last-named scoring Wigan's first and only try, Leytham failed at goal. Oldham had rather the best of the play, helped by the wind, and the attack was at length rewarded by Ferguson being enabled to kick a spendid goal, Wigan having been penalised. At the interval Wigan led by one try to one goal. Two minutes after the restart Ferguson kicked a second goal Great dissatisfaction was caused among th,e crowd by Mr. Smith ruling Cash back when, from a pass by Lees he had crossed the line. The issue was placed beyond clZflikt shortly afterwards by Dixon passing to Cash, who scored a try Ferguson failing at goal. Arthur Lees taking the ball behind the scrummage, scored b. second try, also unconverted, ani the game ended with the score :—Oldham 2 goals and 2 tries (10 points). Wigan 1 try (3 points),

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBI NATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBI NATION.
WARRIN. GTO'N 'A' v. BROUGHTON A.'

Played at Warrington on Saturday. Broughton started, and Warrington immediately excelled in clever work, Short being brought down witthin a few yards of the Ii ne. The visitors started to pre'ss, and were dan- gerous when Jordan stepped in and made a fine save. Bate broke away from a scrummage, but his final pass to Kenyon was dropped. Warrington were penned within their own quarters, but a free kick gave the de- sired relief. Although Warrington had the advantage of the wind, Broughton did most of the attacking. A good passing movement by the home backs left Berry in posse as ion, but he failed to pass to Short when the latter had a c apital opening. Kenyon, however,handed into Ouch, and from the ensuing scrummage Bate scored. Knight failed at gaol. Half-time: Warring- ton, three points; Broughton, nothing. Restarting, Warrington pressed, and Harmer made a fine forward dribble. The Rangers pressed, but their stay was only brief, Knight finding touch splendidly. Berry inter- cepted a pass intended for Houghton, and racing away, kicked across the field and Short got over. Knight adding a goal. Result: Warrington, one goal two tries (eight points) ; Broughton, nil. *Salford (A), 1 try; Rochdale Hornets (A), 1 try. *Swinton (A), 5 goals 4 tries; Runcorn (A), nil. *Widnes (A), 1 goal 2 tries; Leigh (A), 1 try. *Wigan (A), 1 goal 2 tries; Oldham (A), nil. *St. Helens (A), 2 goals 2 tries; Chadderton, nil.
FRIENDLY MATCH.
LITCHFORD RANGERS V. FAIRFIELD ETORNETS.

Played on Saturday on the ground of the former. The Rangers won the toss and played with the wind, but made no headway until about ten minutes from half-time, when Heesom scored a well-earned try. Half- time: Rangers, three points, Fairfield, nil. In the , second half the Rangers made great headway, the visitors I were penalised and Green kicked the ball over the line. I Mason scored, and Green failed at goal. The visitors were again penalised and Heesom scored a penalty goal. 1 Skelhorn scored the last try and Heesom failed at goal. ! Final : Latchford, 11 points; Fairfield, nil.

Diagram 39 shows a run-through in-off into a baulk pocket. In such a stroke the cue-ball has to run right against the nap, and therefore if the stroke be played at all slowly, the combined effect of side and nap becomes very marked indeed. Many good players often un- accountably (to themselves) miss simple-looking run-throughs against the nap, such as the one shown on the Diagram. They play them at medium or slow pace (in order to bring the object ball only a little way out of baulk) and strike the cue-ball with plenty of pocket-side (this would be left-hand side in the Diagram). The effect of pocket side in such a. stroke is to pull the cue-ball right away from the pocket, and often the pocket may be missed by several inches, even though the object-ball has been dkvided correctly enough. If the stroke be played with check side (right-hand side in the Diagram) this side will pull th 6 ball to the pocket. Such a stroke as the one under discussion, simple-looking as it is to any good player, requires to be played very 'accurately, for whereas in playing the same kind of stroke into a tap pocket with pocket-side, there is always a fair amount of latitude for inaccuracy of hitting owing to the pocket-side on the ens-ball enlarging the pocket, in playing the stroke into a baulk pocket the side that has to be used is the reverse of \pocket-side, and the tendency of the side is to stop the bail from falling into the pocket should it strike the opposing angle (the angle of the baulk cushion). Nevertheless, it is far safer to play the stroke shown on the diagram with left- hand side than with right on any table that has a cloth with plenty of nap. Should the stroke be played at fast speed the nap would affect the cue-ball very little, but it could seldom be the game to play such a stroke at fast speed. When the cue-ball is comparatively near the object-ball it is often as well to play the run-titrough with little or no side, relying upon running through the object ball straight to the pocket. Should the object ball be much nearer the pocket than shown on the diagram, then the stroke could and often should be played with pocket-side, as owing to the cue-ball having such a short distance to travel to the pocket there is no time for the nap t4S pull it much out of its path. Also when the two balls are very near the side cushion and one behind the other, pocket aide should be used owing to the pocket being a blind one. Such a stroke should, however, be played pretty fast in order that the nap may affect the path of the one ball as little as possible.
A ran-through cannon from the D

• Diagram 40 shows position for a run-through cannon from baulk. Many ordinary players are under the impression that such a stroke must be played with check side (left hand side in the diagram), as check side is used' whed playing a run-through in-off from the D with an object ball dead against the side cushion in the position of either of the balls shown in the diagram. The principal use of check side when p!aying the in-off is to take the cue ball into the pocket off the opposing angle (the top cnshion angle). When the run-through is a can- non and not an in-off, the chief virtue therefore of the check side disappears. It is true that check side on the cue ball will tend to keep it on the cushion should the stroke be played slowly, but poor players, and many fairly good players too for the matter of that, experience a difficulty in playing long distance run-throughs with side, the use of side generally preventing them from hitting the object ball as intended. The cannon can, however, be made easily enough without any side whatever. All that is necessary is a pretty fast stroke quite full on to the object ball. The cue ball should be struck above the centre, but there is no neces- sity to hit it very high up. Played in this way a very moderate player indeed should get the cannon easily enough. Of course a really good player would play the cannon it medium" pace and not by a strong stroke, . Diagram 41 shows two run-through strokes sometimes played at the beginning of a game. In position A a player has given a miss in baulk, his opponent has answered with a. miss under the right side cushion and has placed hie ball in such a position that no jenny is on into either the centre or the top pocket. There are two or three strokes that are often played from such a position and one is the run-through can- non shown on the diagram. This cannon requires playing with a fair amount of pace and is always a very uncertain stroke owing to the difficulty of judging the amount of side neces- sary for the stroke. There are, however, two chances of getting the cannon, for the cue ball may either cannon off the top cushion as shown on the diagram or directly off the side cushion. This cannon used to be played a great deal some years ago by professional players, but of late it has been discarded to a/great extent. The worst of playing such a stroke is that ,)then the cannon is missed the balls are more often than not left very well placed for the other player, fot the object white gets doubled across the table to the vicinity of the red, and the cue ball in

UTTERS TO THE EDITOR.
Christmas.

Sir,—Very eautiful is the thonght that as the stars ,ttre most brilliant when the sky is darkest so Christmas comes to us tc-ith a message of a new and endless life at the season when nature surrounds us with torpor and gloom, and we feel more than usually sensible of decay. And cheering and comforting is the knowledge that the wondrous love of God which breathed through that message finds a response in many hearts and draws them out in love to their fellow men. For under the influence we feel that we are all creatures of the same God, made of t'.e same ftesh and blood, subject to the •same infirmities,and moved by the:same joys and sorrows. And this beautiful feeling manifests itself, not only in kindly greetings and good wishes, but also in actions which wilt assuredly bring a reward. For find- ing employment for the unemployed, putting a fire in the empty grate of poverty, feeding and clothing the hungry and the naked, comfortinc, the sorrowing, and gladdening the child's heart by a 'toy are practical re- flections of the love of Him who first love tt us, and are infinitely more precious and acceptable to Him that the elaborate and animate performances in churches and Chapels, And when we think of this we are persuaded that all that is needed to ameliorate the unhappy lot of the poor and the suffering, and promote peace and goodwill among men is a widening and deepening of the loving andself denyingq)irit of Christ- mas.—Yonrs truly, lONA.
21st December, 1901.

div.head: CHRISTMAS. How it Will be Observed Locally.
div.p: CHRISTMAS. How it Will be Observed Locally.

it is, of course, a natural conclusion that Christmas Day falling on a Sunday will be more quietly observed than is usually the case. Not that there will be any lack of the customary festivities as on every hand there Is abundant evidence that ample preparations are being made, though for the greater part the more unrestrained rejoicings will be witnessed on Saturday or Monday. As usual shopkeepers have risen to the demands of the occasion, and thanks to a plentiful supply, the dis- play of Christmas fare will compare most favourably with similar displays in former years. Moreover especial pains have been taken to make the shop win- dows additionally attractite, and the judicious and artistic introduction of evergreens has contributed largely to the success which has been achieved in this direction. Butchers have aline display of fat stock and dealers in poultry have an extensive show of turkeys and other seasonable Wads with which to meet the requirements of those whose principal item in the Christmas menu is poultry or game. So much has been done for pate?familias and there is also much to appeal to childish enthusiasm in the shape of an extensive variety of toys which cater for to the juvenile taste. Nor have those condemned through stress of circumstances to spend their lives in the Werkhouse been forgotten. By them the coming of Christmas is an event which is joyously anticipated, as on this day they fare as well as most people and perhaps even better than many who do not look to charity to supply their wants. Some idea of what has been done to minister to their needs can be gathered from the following figures with regard to eatables purchased for the Workhouse: Cielbs. of beef, 701bs. suet, 1601b5. currants, 1001bs. raisins, 1001bs. sultanas, 881bs. candied peel, four cases of oranges and a similar number of barrels of apples. For the men five nine gallon casks of beer have been purchased, while for teetotalers there is a plentiful supply of mineral waters. Four ' hundred ounces of tobacco will disappear in , smoke and $2 ounces of snuff will tickle the , olfactory nerves of many of the old inmates. The dining hall especially and the interior ef the build- ing generally has been profusely decorated with ever- greens given by Mrs. Rylands, Mr. F. Monks, Mrs. Avery, Miss Broadbent, lir. J. C. Parr, Mr. T. H. Lyon, Mrs. Frost and Affr. M-ather. An exceptionally pleasant spectacle is provided, the genera,larrangement reflecting the greatest credit upon the staff under the direction of whom the work has been ;done. The festivities at the Workhouse will be carried out to-day, while Christmas day will be observed much as an ordinary Sunday, except that the religious services, as will be the case in every church in the town, will 'have a special significance. At the Padgate Industrial 'schools the celebrations will also take place to-day arid for them special arrangements have been made. A more than usually attractive fare will be partaken of in a wally-decorated hallafter which the customary Christmas games will be indulged in. The children at-the Blue Coat School will be equally well treated and their programme for Monday—the day, set apart for the rejoicings— will be practically the same. The usual Ceristmas hot-pot and mince pies Will be distributed from the Drill Hall to-morrow to the 'deserving poor, Mr. Powys having made ample provision for the wants of those who will attend. Persons to whom Christmas means increased labour are postmen, and a visit to the Post Mee will afford convincing proof that the practice of- sending seasonable greetings in the shape of Christmas cards, is extending Locally the Gymnasium and Conservative Club Assembly Rooms have been hired and an extra staff engaged to deal with the heavy`traffic experienced. The difficulty of dealing -with the pressure this year has been accentuated by reason of the mail service having. been disorganized through' the fog. Townspeople will therefore know the reason-of and excuse any delay in the delivering of Christmas missives.

div.head: CARTONS, LIMITED. _ Dinner at the Lion Hotel,
div.p: CARTONS, LIMITED. _ Dinner at the Lion Hotel,

Messrs. Gartons, Limited, held their annual dinnerat till Lion Hotel last Friday, when about fifty of the staff and fliends sat down to an excellent repast. A glance at the menu and programme was sufficient to show that no pains had been spared to satisfy the desire of all present, and with Mr. Thomas R. Garton in the chair a most enjoyable evearing was,,c...pent. The vice-chair was occupied by Mr. Thomas Baxter (chairman to the com- pany, with Mr. H. Pearson (secretary) and Mr. Jennings presiding at the other tables. Among the friends were Messrs. W. B. Roberts, Arthur Browne, r. Garton Stone, J. Pearson, lowe (Shrewsbury). The menu Included such tempting dishes as :—Hare soup, "a la Freshfleld " ; fish, ala Sankey Brook " ; roast beef, "A la Acton Grange " ; roast gosling, "a la Eaton " ; Garton pudding with "motor sauce"; cheese "a la Walking Day" coT‘duding with" salary." After full justice had been done to the dinner the chairman (who was received with applause) announced the first Toasts "Their Majesties, the King and Queen and Royal Family," which was heartily drunk. In proposing Gartons Limited" Mr. ARTHUR BROWNE said that when, a few years ago, Gartons came into the town an unknown quantity, they made the 45th trade which Warrington could boast of. The business was entirely different from any other in the country— the germinating of seeds, The firm began in a small way at Newton-le-Willows. They soon commenced to grow and were growing still—(hear, hear)—in fact, they had spread all over the kingdom and were known in every agricultural part of the country. They hoped the firm was still in its infancy, and that it would groat up into youth and be one of the leadine, firms of seed merchants in the kingdom. (Applause.) The CRAIRMAN, in responding, spoke of the simple way in which the firm was started 25 years ago as a result of the hobby of Mr. John Garton in probing into - nature. In the near future it would be absolutely necessary for the firm to open branch in every part of the world where agriculture was cars ried on. (Ap plause.) Other toasts honoured were" Agriculture " proposed by Mr. W. B. Roberts, responded to by Mr. Thomas Garton and Mr. Alfred Barber • "The Artistes" by Mr. C. Garton Stone, responded to by Mr. Gibbon (Lvmm.) the artistes who had promised their services were, Messrs. F. J. Dell, H. Gibbon, A. Grounds, F. Field- house, Victor Roberts and Moseley, but the latter gentleman was unfortunately absent through unforseen circumstances. The various items rendered were fully appreciated, repeated calls of " encore " being made but having in many instances to be refused owing; to I the lengthy programme. Although the name of Mr. I Slow did not appear on the programme he yielded to the request of the Chairman and his contributions to the evening's enjoyment delighted the assembly.

Children's Leagne of Pity Meeting. A meeting was held at the Town Hall on Saturday mnder the auspices of the Warrington Branch of the Children's League of Pity—a League which works in conjunction with the .N.g.P.C.C. to brighten the lives of slum children. There was a good attendance. Miss Broadbent, the hon. secretary, said she was very pleased to welcome those present, and to encourage them to go on with their efforts for the society, which. had done suck a great deal of good. —Mr. Henry Taylor, P.C.M., said he and Inspector Cox, of the N.S.P.C.C., had recently visited several homes in Warrington, and the sights were so bad that he could scarcely find words to describe them. It was sad that such a state of things could exist in a Christian country, and people ought to help the poor children and make their lives a little happier. It had been stated that the present condition of things was the fault of the people In some cases it was, but they ought to think of the poor children. It was for their sake that the work was being carried on, and he (the speaker) hoped that those who sympathized with the movement would be even more earnest in the 1 future.—On the motion of Miss Broadbent, seconded by Inspector Cox' a hearty vote of Wanks was accorded to Mr. Taylor for his address.

WIN
SECONDARY SCHOOL BAZAAR,
EFFORTS ON BEHALF OF THE ATHLETIC CLUB.

Bright and pleasing was the scene which presented itself to the visitors at the Warring ton Technical In- stitute on Wednesday and Thursday. The rooms in the basement of the building had been neatly and effectively decorated with flags, streamers and plants, while from the ceiling were suspended numerous Qhinese lanterns. The occasion of this unaccustomed transformation was a bazaar promoted by the scholars and staff of the Secondary School to further the efforts of the Athletic Club to acquire and lay out an athletic ground and erect a pavilion. The sum it was hoped to raise was at least £2OO, and the object was particularly commendable as it is becoming increasingly important that the necessity for physical as well as mental development should not be overlooke.d. Scholars and teachers alike had entered into the project with great enthu- siasm, and an executive committee with Mr. E. S. A. Robson, M.Sc. (Principal) as chairman, Mr. R. 11. klbery, M.Sc., and Miss L. IL Warburton as secre- taries, and Mr. P. Fisher. B.Sc. as treasurer, did use- ful work. Praise is also due to the parents of the students for their willing co-operation, for we under. stand it was mainly from them that over £6O had been raised before the bazaar. Evidence of the useful char- acter of the education imparted at the school was afforded by the fact that many of the articles which commanded a ready sale were the work of the children. The completeness of the arrangements and variety of attractions provided reflected infinite credit upon all concerned. Each stall was draped with material of a distinctive colour, and the dresses of the attendants were of a corresponding tint. The following is a list of the stall-holders : STALL A. (Pupil Teachers and Form Vii.) :—Staff. Miss L. M. Warburton, Mr. R. H. Albery, M.Sc., Mr. E, Hanna, 8.A.; Schalarship A, Edith Harrison, May Clarke Elsie Gandy, Osborne Sinclair; Scholarship B, Bessie Wadsworth, Jessie Werd,Ethel Dunue ; First Year P.T.'s Gertrude Farrall, Isabel Price, Edith Crosby, William E. R. Collins; Form VII., Annie Edgar, Annie Harter, Ethel Hindley, Roy Rice. STALL B. (Forms V. and Vt.) :—Staff, Miss E. Frost, Int, 8.A., Lend., Miss M. B. Morton, L.L.A., Mr. H. 0. Armstrong, F.8.1.C.C., Mr. P. Fisher, B.Sc.; Form VI.. Gertrude Ath,- Dorothy Dean, Flora Norton, Fred Jolley; Po ~ Annie Dallow, Kate Davenport, Lucy Fawcett, Gertrude Miller, William Hudson, Gilbert Harding. STALL C (Forms TEL and IT.) :—Staff, Miss E Wilkinson, L.L.A., Mr. W. Donaghy, M.Sc.; Form IV. Gladys Turton, Winifred Brock, Marion Collin, Charles M. Price; Form 111., Margaret Ashton, Elsie Mason, Cissie Ball, William Miller. STALL D. (Forms I. and IL) :—Staff, Miss M. L. Mitchell, Mr. J. A. Buckley, M.A. ; Form 11., Ruby Witts, Alice Taylor (B), Fred Isherwood, William F. Eccles; Form 1., Lena Duckworth, Gertrude Leigh, Thomas Welch, Percy Crampton. FRUIT AND FLOWER STALL :—Scholarship Pupil Teachers, Edward Bloor, Alfred Cragg, William Hough- ton, Ernest Cannel', John Groake, William MinarcLs, Harry Smith. REFRESHMENT STALL :—Staff, Mrs. Cann, Miss Cann, Miss Watkins; Scholarship Pupil Teachers, Lilian Atkinson, Winifred Cann, Louie Daintith, Gladys Hankinson, Elizabeth Hill, Frances Jolley, Marion Oldfleld, Gertrude singleton, Lucy Taylor.

div.head: OPENING CEREMONY.
div.p: THE OPENING CEREMONY.

There was a large attendance at the opening ceremony which took place in a large room which had•been suit- ably arranged for concerts. Mr. F'. Monks, J.P., chair- man of the Education Committee, presided, and the bazaar was opened by the Mayoress (Mrs. W. Bolton). Among those present on the platform were: Alderman and Mrs. Smethurst, the Revs. John Yonge and Father Wilson, Councillor Craik, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, E. Plinston, W. Bibby, J. Upson, J. Fairhurst, J. Moore 34urray (director of education), E. S. A. Robson (principal), and members of the staff. A beautiful bouquet was presented to the Mayoress by Miss Gladys Turton.

The CHAIRM.4N said he was very glad to be present to help the scholars, as far as he could, to provide appliances for outdoor recreation. Those who had had to do a great deal of work in the world knew that healthy outdoor recreation was just as necessary as any other, and they hoped that success would attend the efforts of the Secondary school athlete club, and that as a result of the bazaar sufficient funds would be ob- tainedto provide all that they required. Although bazaars were perhaps tiresome in that they entailed a great deal of work, it was nevertheless a pleasure to all who assisted to reap the reward of their exertions. The Chairman concluded with the injunction to the young ladies to " get as much money out of the gentle- men as they could." The MAYORESS very briefly declared the bazaar open andhoped it would be a complete success. (Applause) Councillor CRAIK proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayoress for her kindness in opening the bazaar. They regretted very much that his Worship could not accompany Mrs. Bolton, as he was indisposed. The Rev, JOHN YONGR seconded. A great many of them, he said, had taken a great deal of interest in that little endeavour on the part of the staff and scholars of the Secondary School to provide for themselves the means of recreation in the open air was desirable as any other form of recreation. He (Mr. Yonge) was disposed to go a little further and say that it was more desirable. Recreation which sometimes people sought after in crowded rooms and hot atmospheres was hardly conducive to health in the same way, at any rate, as the recreation which the students of that school hoped to find on the recreation ground they .were seek- ing to obtain. He hoped the people of Warrington,who were known to be generous when they had the means, would show themselves generous in that movement so that the sum of £2OO could be easily reached before the bazaar came to an end.

~The motion was heartily agreed to. Alderman S3IIi:THUFtST responded on behalf of the Mayoress. He was sure Mrs. Bolton was very desirous that the bazaar should be a thorough success. They were extremely sorry that illness was the cause of his Worship's absence, and under those circumstances they were specially indebted to Mrs. Bolton for attending. (Applause). Mr. J. UPON proposed a vote of thanks to the Chair man. He need hardly say how much education owed to Mr. Monks. In the Borough of Warrington, one could hardly think of the subject of Education Without coupling with it the name of Mr. Monks. He (Mr. Upson) thought he was right in saying that if it were not for Mr. Monks they would not have had a secondary school in Warrington to day. If it had not been for the intense interest he had shown in the establishment of a secondary school, public opinion would never have been in so advanced a state that thay would have been able to establish the school. Not only was Mr. Monks chairman of the Education Com- mittee but he took a great deal of interest in the work and he showed that by his attendances not only at the full committee, but he (Mr. Upson,believcd his record of attendances at the sub-committees would equal that of any other member of the education authority in Warrington. The work he had done would long after he had passed away, be held in honourable estimation of the people of his b3ro ugh and of succeed- ing generations. The Rev. Father WILSON seconded. The appearance of Mr. Monks in the chair, he said, went a long way to assure them that the bazaar would be a very great success. That it might be so was his earnest hope, and he would call the attention of his hearers to one great claim which he thought the young people who were chiefly interested in the bazaar had upon the liberality of those who patronized it. They certainly had been up and doing, to some purpose, for he under- stood they had already raised no inconsiderable sum towards the object of the bazaar. In addition, many of the articles which they were going to press upon the attention of the visitors were the work of their own heads and hands combined. They were, in, fact,tangible , proofs of the education that was being given at the I school—not merely book education, but education of the hand also and general instrustion fitting them not only to know, but to do. He was sure all present would be happy to do what they could for the success of the bazaar, se that the scholars might be able to secure what he considered an absolute necessity as an adjunct to the school—a proper recreation ground for the girls and boys. (Applause.) The proposing was carried with acclammation. In returning thanks the Chairman said it was quite ' true he had taken a great deal of interest in education because he had felt the advantage of it in his own life not only ass matter of business, but as a source of pleasure in his leisure. He would ask the boys and girls to remember that the object of all education was to make them think, and another thing which should be borne in mind—and he was afraid many people did not recognize the fact,—was that it took some time to think. The business of the day was then entered upon. The sales on Wednesday amounted to £72 nilkin; • total, including donations, of £137. THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

There was again a large attendance at the opening on Thursday. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY presided and expressed regret at the absence of Mr. R. Pierpoint, M.P., who should have opened the bazaar. Mr. Pierpoint had written to say that on account of the illness of his wife he had been detained in London. He enclosed a cheque to be added to the list of donations to the bazaar.

Alderman BENNETT, who discharged the office originally alloted to Mr. Pierpoint, said he was particu- larly pleased when he knew that the Borough member had been asked to open the bazaar as he had taken some part in the passing of the recent Education Act which had made that secondary school possible. What- ever could be said either for or against that Act it had
