div.head: Examiner, Saturday, December 24, 1904.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 24, 1904.

made it possible for us to systematise and co-ordinate our educational arrangements, and in Warrington he could say the results had been extremely satis- factory. The secondary school was one of the results of the Act an by future developments they hoped it would be made possible for the humblest boy or girl possessing the necessary capacity to pass from the elementary school to the university. With regard to the bazaar itself he must congratulate them upon the excel- lent results which had attended their efforts. He sympathised greatly with the object of the bazaar. While it was desirable that those who spent their time ini sport should take an interest in education, it was also desirable that those who showed a desire to improve the mind should not neglect the body, but that the mind and body should be developed in harmonious unity. (Applause.) He had much pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. (Applause.) Councillor FULTON SMITH proposed a vote of thanks to Alderman Bennett for his services. He thought the Education Act of 1902 was fulfilling its mission as was proved by the splendid results from the Secondary schools. (Applause.) Councillor ELLlsosseconded and the vote was heartily accorded, Alderman Bennett briefly returning thanks. The Chairman was thanked for his services on the motion of Mr. PLINSTON seconded by Alderman SMETHURST, and Mr. Jolley's reply brought the open- ceremony to a close. THE ENTERTAINMENTS.

In addition to the attractions usually found at bazaars other aids to enjoyment were afforded in the shape of side shows, cempetitions' &c. Entertainments were also given at intervals by the scholars, and orchestral selections were submitted each evening under the iconductorship of Mr. G. S. Pendlebury, in the main hall of the building. For the enter- tainments the children were largely in char- acter costume and all acquitted themselves admirably and in away which denoted careful training. The school orchestra were also in attendance and showed by their playing that the musical side of their educa- tion is not being neglected. One of the principal features of the entertainments was a Christmas extra- vaganza Our Toys "given by a number of the scholars, and which afforded considerable pleasure to large au- diences. The leading characters were :—Fairy Chora, G. Turton; Lady Doll—Lady Angelina de Montmorency B. Evans; Red Riding Hood. G. Gaudy; 80-Peep a piece of Dresden China, H. Gee; Wooden Soldier, J. Cartwright; Noah, A. Hainsworth ; Gentleman Doll— Lord Tennings, A. Shearer.

PEOPLE'S COLLEGE CONCERT. Another Great Success. To say that Thursday's annual concert in connection with People's College more than realized all expecta- tions is to bestow the highest measure of praise upon the efforts of teachers and scholars alike. It is, more- over, no empty compliment, for high as has been the standard aspired to and attained in previous years, there was a unanimity of opinion that this latest demonstra- tion of the abilities of the children as entertainers, sur- pasied prior achievements. Probably no concert of the reason is more fully appreciated than that to which the scholars of People's College devote their time and talents, and that its popularity increases as years go on was evident from the crowded audience at the Parr Hall on Thursday. Every seat was occupied, and so anxious were the public to witness the entertainment that a great deal of the accommodation had been booked in advance. As usual the children, than whom no one takes a greater pride in or more thoroughly enjoys the event, were massed on the platform galleries. The scene was a bright and animated one, particularly towards the close of the programme, when the charac- ter performers in fancy costumes of striking colours mingled with the assembly. If there was one outstanding feature to which must be attributed the signal successes of the evening, it was the charming variety of the items. From beginning to end the interest of the audience never flagged, and there could be no more convincing evidence of their enthusiasticappro- bation than the fact that almost every item called forth an encore. It is indeed a pleasure to congratulate the staff and pupils upon this happy consummation of many weeks of careful preparation, because .it was, in the 'truest sense, deserved. That stirring Welsh chorus "Men of Harlech " was a fitting prelude to the entertainment, and it was sung with fine spirit. Barely had the applause subsided when the youthful voices joined in singing the praises of old England in the beautiful composition Land of Hope and glory " set to Sir Edward Elgar's music. All the choruses were intelligently interpreted and those which introduced too humorous element met with the readiest acceptance. The late Mel. B. Spurr's rollick- ins. song "How we laugh" kept auditors and children Mile in a state of boisterous mirth which was infec- tious. Almost equally amusing was the description of the Irish Walking contest—the funniest part being that "nobody walked at all." The choice of soloists was a happy one for, without exception, they possessed good voices and did justice to the songs entrusted to them. One could not help noticing the confidence, begotten of sound training, which even the youngest vocalist displayed, and not one failed to obtain a hearty encore. Florence Bennett rendered the pretty song "Three green bonnets" very sweetly and expressively. In the guise of the diminutive black housewife wearied with Callin' up de coons "one would hardly have recognized an active schoolboy, so effective was the make-up. Harold Harcourt,who was responsible for this diversion, was by voice and demeanour admir- ably fitted for the part. Another coon song which gave considerable pleasure was "Dinah' by Stanley Jones,who, possessing a voice of good range, treated a somewhat , difficult number very pleasingly. Fred Kershaw, clad in sombre monastic garb, sang with gusto of the jovial monk who has cast care aside with the resolve to "take life easily." Robert Ormsby, with well-simulated infirmity, told of the days "When I was a boy at school," and his song was certainly one of the best features of the programme. It is not too much to say that the novel character songs by groups of buys and girls came as a surprise,and the delight of the audiencelwas strongly manifest. A number of girls costumed as Italian pedlars brought all their persuasiveness to bear to induce passers-by to "Buy, buy, buy" a bewildering assort- ment of wares. There was such a medley of voices that, the would be purchaser must indeed have been embar- rassed. A song entitled "As in days of long ago " had a special interest as it had been written by Miss E. Brown, a member of the staff, and set to music by Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac. It proved immensely popular for it was quite unique in character. The performers were dressed in the picturesque early English garb of The squires and dames of old" and executed a pretty dance in a courtly and grace- ful way. One of the most gratifying successe. was "Soldiers three" by T. Smith, R. Atkinson, W Swaine, and R. Tanner. The clumsy manceuvres of these valiant warriors who "didn't -like to hear the bullets rattle" created uproarious laughter, and it is doubtful whether a funnier item has been seen at a local concert. As a striking contrast the assembly was next treated to the pomp and ceremony attendant upon a visit of that mighty Eastern potentate "The Rajah of Bhong " who was accompanied by his "beautiful future bride." As the lead- ing characters, Maggie Wilkinson and Williams Barlow earned high encomiums, for although the song was lengthy it was splendidly given. A contingent of girls in typical harvesting dress, submitted a pleasing representation of the work of "The Gleaners." Still another feature deserving of special praise was "The coon drum-major" by selected boys whose striking "make-up "was in itself sufficient to arouse interest to a high pitch. The air went with a grand swing, and in the role of the pompous drum-major Thomas Smith could hardly have been excelled. As an interlude in the musical programme. the sketch from ' Handy Andy" was an acceptable departure and met with suc- cess. The youthful actors conducted themselves with marked self -possession, and their utterances could be distinctly heard throughout the hall. The characters were taken by the following :—Squire Egan, Percy Ashcroft; Mrs. Egan, Ethel Cooper; Tom Durphy Esq., Maurice Aukland ; Mr. O'Gara, Arthur Pember- ton; Andy, servant to the Squire, Arthur Warburton. The many blunders of Andy, whose zeal in the squire's interests ended almost disastrously were the source of ' continual merriment. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., discharged the duties ' of organist and accompanist with taste and skill. To him it is in a great measure due that the children have been brought to such a high state of musical proficiency Before the close of the concert, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, (school correspondent) cordially thanked the audience for their patronage. The crowded state of the hall showed that the concert had been looked for- ward to with as much pleasure as ever. (Hear, hear.) Judging from the applause their expectations hlcl not in any way been disappointed.(Applause.)He also wished to thank the parents without whose valuable help the concert would be shorn of a great deal of its glory. Mr. Payton was to be congratulated upon the very careful I training he had given to the children to bring them to the state of perfection which had been evidenced that ' night. (Applause.) Then the thanks of all were due to I the teachers for their co-operation, and especially to Miss Brown and Mr. Bowen who had rendered great assistance in preparing the scholars for the character song. Alluding to the attendance at school, Mr. Holmes i pointed out that in 1900 there were only 16 children who had never missed an opportunity of being present. This year the number was 250. (Applause.) If there were more centres of education in the town which could ' boast of such a record, it would be of very material advantage to Warrington. Some of those present might not know—he himself was surprised when he heard it —that every day there was something like 4,000 vacancies in the schools of Warrington caused by absentee chil- dren who were registered on the books. That was a great financial loss to the town, for it represented a sum &Biel to about 3d.in the <£ on the rates. His remarks would be incomplete if he dld not refer to the work of their ever popular and highly respected headmaster, Mr. Wallington. (Applause.)- In Mr. Wallington they had in every sense a most worthy successor of the late Mr. Twiss—(applause)—and the other masters who preceded him. They felt that no masters who had had charge of People's College had given more attention to the work and taken more interest in the school than Mr. Walling- ton. No doubt before very long the Education Act would be amended; perhaps a new Bill would be intro- duced. None of those present were able to fore- cast what that measure would be, but he was sure every person in the hall would agree with him that whatever form the Bill took they trusted it would not in any way hamper the efficiency of People's College. In conclusion he would say" Long live the People's College (Applause). The concluding chorus "The Light of the World" was particularly appropriate to the Christmas season and its interpretat ion was most effective.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY. " The Messiah."
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY. " The Messiah."

Tuesday's performance of " The,Messiah " in Parr Hall must be reckoned as one of the best of the Musical Society's achievements. Though the building was by no means full, a fairly numerous audience gathered to enjoy the familiar themes of the oratorio and doubtless also to participate in the pleasant associations which, at this time of the year, they often recall. As a musical work "The Messiah" presents little difficulty to the rank and file of the society's present vocal and orchestral members. Thanks to the stringent regime of these later years and to the tremendous energy and thoroughness of Mr. Crossley the society's present cenductor, a standard of choral singing has been kept in view which greatly simplifies matters in dealing with staightforward works such as the Handelian oratorios. Not that there are no points of importance to be made in so homely a work as "The Messiah." On the contrary, Tuesday's performance showed not only how numerous these are and how carefully all the well-known technical obstacles had been noted and overcome, but it showed also that it is yet possible for new readings to be successfully attempted, as may be instanced in the pianissimo ending of "Surely He bath borne "and the rugged and greatly increased tempo adopted in He trusted in God" with its concluding phrase of unrelaxed energy,—new depar- tures which we think will commend themselves to all intelligent students of these details; Above all else the adequate presentment of the" Messiah" choruses calls for precision and firmness and the realisation of a certain solidity in effect in choral sinning, which may well be regarded as a gauge of members' capabilities in other directions. And it is just in this way that the ensemble singing of Tuesday excelled. There was never any doubt as to the taking up of disjointed parts, never any relinquishing of a grip once made, nor any weakening of a splendid tone volume in the massive terminal harmonies which are so conspicuous a feature of many of the choruses. Nor did the play of light and shade in expression escape attention for, along with a finely ' balanced effect in the united voices, there was often an equally well-graded observance of the p's and Is,of which Behold the Lamb of God" and "For unto us" may be cited as examples. But where so much of the choral work was, as in this instance, beyond reproach, it is needless to particularise further. To say that members fully sustained their reputation is no small compliment when recent attainments are borne in mind, and what- ever the measure of public support accorded them, there can at least be no doubt as to the high educational value to members themselves of such efforts as are involved in the getting up of these concerts. In Miss Lillie Wormald, Miss Edna Thornton, Mr. Gervase Elwes, and Mr. H. Lane Wilson, the society had a quartet of principals in every way worthy of the occasion, each and all of whom scored successes in course of the evening. Indeed some of the more tender solos especially were so touchingly sung that encores would probably have been insisted upon had time permitted. The string portion of the orchestra, led by Mr. It. H. Pearson, dealt with their onerous parts with due restraint and taste in accompanying the solo voices, and, in the tatti, the fine array of violins were heard with good effect, while the woodwind, the horns, and the trumpet contributed their quota with musicianly skill and judgment. In the numerous recitatives and in the many choruses Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Ba.c. rendered excellent service at the organ.

div.head: UNPROTECTED FIRES.
div.p: UNPROTECTED FIRES.
Coroner Brighouse's Strictures on the County Authorities.

Mr. S. Brighouse -yesterday passed some severe strictures upon the lethangy of County Councils in declining to take action to enforce the provision of fireguards in order to prevent many of the regrettably large number of cases in which children of tender years are fatally burned. His remarks were occasioned by the facts disclosed at inquests which he held at Warrington on the bodies of Plina Roughley (2) and Catherine Mullighan (6) who during the week have received injuries from burns which have terminated fatally. In the case of Roughley, the mother of the deceased, who lives at 16, Howard street, stated that at 5.20 on Wednesday night she left her daughter alone in the kitchen. She was absent only a few minutes and upon her return found the child's clothing on fire. She put out the flames and took the girl to the Infirmary where she died the same night. In the other case the facts showed that the little girl IMulligan who lived with her parents at 10, Erwood street, went with two other little girls to the house of a neighbour, Ann Mannion,ls3, Back Dallam Lane. There they were left alone in the kitchen and a Mrs. Stafford, 56, Back Dallam-lane, hearing screams went into Mannion's house and found Mullighan's clothes in -flames. The flames were extinguished and the child taken to the Infirmary where she died on Thursday morning. In both cases the evidence showed that the fires wore without guards of any description. Sergeant Barlow said that with regard to the case of Mullighan, he visited the house of Mrs. Mannion at about 9 o'clock on Thursday night. He found two little children in the kitchen. The fire was altogether un- protected and the children were placing pieces of wood upon it. Mr. Brighouse, to Mrs. Mannion : If I had my way you, would not allow your children to be burned fu this way. I would first touch your pocket and if that was not sufficient I would touch the liberty of the person. If they were pigs, or rabbits you would take greater care of them, but they are only children. . _ _ „
I In each ca;e the 3ury retUrned a verdict of" acci- dental death."

NIT.. Brighouse then addressed the jury. Since the 10th October of this year,in the South West Lancashire t coroner's district—which was only one of 99 coroners districts in Lancashire—he had held 14 inquests on children who had been burned to death, and in not one of the cases were fire guards provided. What he .canted to know was when Was the legislature going to step in I and prevent that sort of thing. It occurred amongst a ; class of people who brought children into the world and were absolutely indifferent as to their education ' and physical culture and welfare generally ! They were people with whom it was impos- sible to argue and upon whom no moral suasion , had any effect. Therefore it was necessary that the , legislature should step in and compel them to do that what they ought to do not only the individual stand- point but from the standpoint of the community. He had brought the matter before the Finance Committee of the Lancashire County Council who were unanimously of opinion that it should be a recommendation to the County Councils' Association that people should be corn pelted to protect their fires so that children should no be burned to death. The chairman of the County Council when the matter was brought before him laughed it out of count and talked about its being grandmotherly legislation. If a lad set off fireworks in the street he was taken before the magistrates and yet 800 children were burned to death every year and no one took any notice. He knew Parliament moved slowly and that pressure had to be brought to bear upon them before any reform could be obtained. Every time he held an inquest in which the circumstances were similar to wha they were in the cases they had had before them, he would ask the juries of the South West Lancashire District to support him in his efforts to bring legisla- ture into play. He would ask them to do so by. attach- ing to their verdicts a recommendation that in their opinion in order to prevent the lamentable loss of life legislature shonld step in. Sooner or later Parliament would have to move in the matter and such recom- mendations from juries would assist them in coming to a decision.
Tha jury unanimously agreed to add to their verdicts a rider endorsing the coronor's suggestion,

div.head: SOCIAL SERMONETTES FOR WORKING MEN.
div.p: SOCIAL SERMONETTES FOR WORKING MEN.
BY JOHN TAYLOR Atalbor of " Scarelb Lights on Lvt.t, LLOottr
Sciai Problems."
SHALL WE TAX LAND OR FOOD ?

" The Liverpool City Council ha 3 by a majority of sixty-five to thirty-two votes resolved to ask the Liverpool members to take Parliamentary action for the ratiug of land values. Mr. Austin Taylor, M.P., has promised that he will never vote again for a duty on sugar."

." Liverpool Post and Mercury." Wben I read these two items of news in the daily ' papers I rubbed my eyes in amazement, and asked my- self what unlikely thing would happen next? Liver- pool has always been hopelessly Tory, and the influence of great landowners like Lord Derby. and the Earl of Sefton, has always been a power to reckon with. I remember what lively times I had about ten years ago, when I held open-air meetings in every village and town, between Preston and Liverpool, one summer. I got crowds of people to hear me, and converted thousands of men to the taxation of land values and land law reform. Bat I incurred the wrath of the landowners, and they refused to let their rooms for election meetings. They threatened me with writs for trespassing on their land by holding meetings in the open air, and they chivied me, and hunted me, and persecuted me in every possible way. Liverpool was bitterly opposed to new ideas, and many of its citizens regared me as a fool or a madman. But nine years of Tory rule has opened their eyes andiemptied their peckets and mlny of them now are sadder and wiser men. They are asking for the rating of land values, and they are pledging their members to the principles of Free Trade. And these political and financial conversions are not confined to Liverpool, for they are going on everywhere. I.—THE TAXPAYERS ARE GETTING TIRED OF

div.head: TORY EXTRAVAGANCE.
div.p: TORY EXTRAVAGANCE.

The burden of taxation is greater than they can bear, and every new addition provokes angry protests, and threats of vengeance, when the day of reckoning comes. Nine years ago we were paying our way as a nation, and saving money, on an expenditure of less than £86,000,000 a year. When the Tories came into power they found a surplus of about five millions in the treasury that had been gathered in by Sir William Harcourt's Death Daties Bill.

This year we are spending one hundred and fifty-two millions and we may expect a deficit of between five and six millions. So that in nine years we have increased our national expenditure by sixty-one millions a year, or more than one million and a quarter every week. The increased expenditure, if it were equally divided among us all, would amount to more than twenty-five shillings each yearly for every man, woman, and child in the country. While our expenditure has been going up at this alarming rate, we have been plunging heavily into debt. The war in South Africa increased our national debt by £168,000,000 and we have a floating debt that is not funded, amounting so between seventy and eighty millions. So the Chancellor of the Exchequer evvill have a nice Budget to present to us next March. If he is to make ends meet and pay his way he must impose some new taxes or he must increase the old ones. It has been suggested that he should funk it, and ride for a fall on the Aliens Bill, and go to the country on the patriotic cry: "England for the English and the devil take the foreigner." If the Liberals win they will have all the discredit and unpopularity of imposing new taxes to pay off Tory debts. • You can take it from me that those debts have got to be paid and the next election will settle where the money is to come from, and who has got to bear the heaviest burden.

div.head: 11.-TriE LIBERALS WANT TO TAX LAND VALUES.
div.p: 11.-TriE LIBERALS WANT TO TAX LAND VALUES.

In Liverpool there are plots of land that are worth a thousand times as much now as they were fifty years ago. And this increased value has been created by the labour and money of the Corporation and enterprising citizens, and yet the owners of the land contribute nothing to rates or taxes if the land is held up for a rise. They have only got to let their land lie idle, and they will have nothing to pay. So they create a great land hunger, and they drive our workers into slums, and burden us with heavy rates for their benefit, without contributing a cent to the rates themselves. If they let their land for buildinr, purposes they make the occupier pay all the rates and taxes, and they do not pay a penny out of their rents beyond their contribution to the income-tax. If they occupy their own land for agricultural purposes, they only pay half the rates that are levied on houses or shops. If you want their land for public purposes they ask you an outrageous price for it, and they put you to great expense in arbitration and valuation costs before you can get it. A Parliament of landowners can always be trusted to look after them- selves and lighten their own burdens by putting them on the backs of their poorer neighbours. The time has come when some of those crooked things will have to be put straight, and some of these great wrongs must be righted. The Liberal party is abso- lutely united on the taxation of land values, and I have met thousands of Tories who are in favour of such a. measure. Why should a London shopkeeper or coster- monger pay eight or nine shillings in the 2 for his rates while his landowner, the Duke of Westminster. does not pay a cent? And why should a great land- owner be allowed to enjoy unearned increment and wealth created by the public rates and taxes, without contributing his share to these rates and taxes? These are some of the questions that will have to be answered at the next election, and if I rightly read the signs of the times the landowners will have to contribute more than they have done to pay public debts and to carry out public improvements. IIL—THE TORIES WANT INDIRECT !TAXATION,

_ They are very fond of this mode of raising money because it enables them to plunder the consumer with- out letting him know that he is being plundered. Dur- ing the nine years they have been in office they have raised the duty on tea from fourpence to eightpence per lb., and the shopkeeper has either raised the price or lowered the quality to the purchaser. It is not likely they will want to increase the duties on beer or spirits, or tobocco, or tea under the next Budget. They have got into such a row about the cost of sugar that they will gladly let it alone' so they are on the look-out for some other articles that will help them to " widen the basis of taxation-" What will they tax next? What is there that they can tax without inflict- ing needless suffering and loss on some portion of the ' community ? If a tax is " for revenue purposes only," it is easiest to levy it in the form of import duties on things that come from abroad and are not produced in this country. Tobacco is grown abroad, and we impose a duty on it equal to seven times its original cost. Tea comes from abroad and will not grow here, and we put a duty on it equal to the first cost or more. Sugar is another foreign product that pays a duty of a halfpenny a pound, or fifty per cent of its value before we signed the infamous convention. Cotton does not grow in this country, so it is a very suitable article to tax" for revenue purposes only," but all the King's horses and 11 the King's men could not get the Chancellor of the Exchequer to impose a duty of a penny per lb. on raw cotton. All Lancashire would be up in arms, and there would be such a shindy that he would drop his pro- posals Ince a hot•coal, and never mention the unlucky subject again. Well, what is there that he can tax that will raise a big revenue withoutcausing endless friction and loss to the consumer? Rumour says that an effort will be made to introduce Protection under the name of " a tax for revenue purposes only," and that is sure to happen if he taxes any article coming from abroad, and does not put a corresponding tax on all similar products raised in this country. If he puts an import duty on all foreign corn he ought also to put a tax on all corn raised in this country of a like amount, or he is swindling the consumer and rob- bing his own exchequer, and giving Protection to our English corn growers. I am inclined to think he wil try his hand at some kind of protective tax in his next] Budget, and if he does there ;will be some very lively times in store for him. The country has been greatly stirred by the rise in sugar, and the burdens of taxation, and it is in no humour to stand much more of it.

Now I have put the broad issues clearly before you. We are over head and ears in debt, and we are crushed beneath the burden of taxation, till the average tax- payer has about got to the length of human endurance. Our debts have got to be paid, and our burdens have got to be made lighter, for we cannot play these fool's games for ever. _ _

The Liberals are pledged to the taxation of land values, and a drastic reduction in our national expendi- ture. They know that whenever they come into power they ss ill have to economise, and save, and raise money to pay off the debts incurred by the Tories, and it will be poetic justice if a good share of the new taxes are raised from the Tory landowners. The Tories have committed themselves to a policy of indirect taxation, and Protection, and Retaliation, that will seriously increase the cost of living, and that will put money into a few rich men's pockets, while it makes millions of men into paupers. I have no doubt what the verdict will be at the next election. The Tories have been sowing the wind, and they will reap the whirlwind, and whatever disaster overtakes them they have richly deserved it.

div.head: UNJ US T SCALES-
div.p: UNJ US T SCALES-

At the Warrington police court yesterday, Thomas Ellison, Ship-yard, was discharged with having in his possession on the Ist December a pair of unjust scales. Mr. Stanley Wilson said the defendant was seen by the Inspector of weights and measures with a hawkers barrow. The Inspector examined the scales which were on the barrow and found they were to the prejudice of the purchaser to the extent of three quarters of an ounce. through an ircn ring having been placed on the arm.—Defendant was in extremely poor circumstances andhe (Ur. Wilson) thought the infliction of a small penalty would meet the case.—Defendant, who pleaded ignorance of the presence of the ring, was fined ss.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
(By " Ovalist.",

The Warrington team are now as near the middle of the League table as they can get, with nine clubs below them and eight above. They may possibly consider their ambition realised, for it has always seemed as if they preferred the middle to the top. Only three weeks ago they were third, and seemed in imminent danger of going to the top, but by grace- fully losing at Salford and Broughton they have sunk to the level which appears to suit them best. In all probability, however, they will be compelled to start winning again to-day, and the New Year may find them once more rising like a bubble in a glass—with the same result ultimately. When the bubble gets to the top it bursts, and if Warrington reach such giddy altitudes they may be relied upon to do something

• The supporters of the team will probably not blame them very sincerely for failing to win at Broughton. In any case the feat is difficult to perform, but when Warrington made the journey minus both the regular centres there was not much hope of their emerging victorious, seeing also that the Rangers have been playing in tip-top form of late. There was no funk- ing on the part of the Warrington men however, and the fifteen who did duty gave a good account of themselves. A. try was scored by each side,and only superior goalkicking turned the scale in the home team's favour. It is a long time since Warrington were oble to boast of two such good goal-kicker § as Fish and Preston, and yet they are not getting the goals they should do. On Saturday each man had about three shots, most of them fairly easy, but not a single one found the mark. It appears to me as if the Warrington goal-placing lacks system. Preston and Fish take turns, apparently with the result that both lack confidence. Would it not be as well if, say for three matches, Preston took all the goal-kicks? Fish's abilities have been well proved in the past, but Preston has never yet had the chance he requires to keep up his reputation in this direction. •

In contrast with the game at Salfird, the one at Broughton on Saturday was full of good football Both sides adopted open tactics, and though the combination was hardly up to the quality expected still there was much interesting play. The Rangers, were rather more finished in their efforts, though only one wls productive. Warrington, with the back division disorganised, could hardly be expected to display any startling brilliance, but for all that they gave a display which was ahead of some recent performances. Hockenhall played a rar e good game in the centre and was a constant worry to the Rangers. Many a.promising movement lot Wilson and Co., was nipped in the bud by the black- haired County half,who tackled like a pocket Hercules. Brooks did well except when combination was required and it was in his hands that the Warrington passing usually ended. The half back duel was fairly even, though of the four men engaged. S. James gave the most effective display. There is . a method about the famous Welshman's work which is usually productive, and he it was who really engineered the home team's solitary try. Horton was nippy and got the ball away with creditable smartness. On the Warrington side J. Davies was not his best, and forward transfers more than once spoiled a:favourable opening.Duckworth was the same steady trier as of yore, and little fault could be found in his play, except a tendency to kick rather too frequently. Warrington are not badly off for com- petent halves, and one pair does as well as another. The unfortunate thing is that out of half-a-dozen not one shows any marked superiority over the rest.

Fish gave a much improved display, and hard luck alone twice prevented him from scoring. He was always more than a match for Hogg, who, like Wilson, is not the dangerous foe he used to be. Frank Harry. struck me as being the smartest of the home three- quarters, and he has certainly developed a lot since his full back days. The two full backs both gave an excellent account of themselves, Poole being the better and more powerful kicker. Warrington's greatest advantage was in the scrummage where the home eight played second fiddle throughout. The Warringt6n men seemed to possess the necessary " devil " for once in a way and made their weight felt.

Bradford and Oldham still run a very level race for the leadership, while Leeds and Broughton Rangers possess more than an outside chance. The struggle is still keener at the other end of the table, only a poin t dividing Batley, St. Helens and Runcorn—all likely candidates for the wooden spoon. Batley seem almost certain to spend a season in the second division, while Runcorn are going very unsteadily at present. They have indeed fallen on very hard times, and had more than their share of ill fortune. Houghton and Butter- worth still stick to the ship and they may yet pull the c)aft clear of the whirlpool.

Warrington are at home again. to-day, and should have no great difficulty in preserving their unbeaten record at Wilderspool. Wakefield Trinity are old opponents and will be heartily welcomed. The last time Warrington and the Trinity met was in the first round of the Northern Union cup five or six years ago, when the Trinity just gained the ver- dict at Belle Vue. " Surefoot " Boscow made a mull on the line which gave the home side the winning five points, though Warrington had all along been the better team. This is Wakefield's first season in the senior league, and they are having rather a rough passage. Warrington will find them in rather a des- perate mood, and there will have to be no trifling.

The team has undergone further changes, and may be considered stronger than last week. Isherwood and Dickenson both return to the centre and I hope the rest will have done them good. At half-back, Duck- worth will partner Hockenhall, two likely candidates in R. Bate and J.Davies being ineligible. The former broke a finger last Saturday, and Davies has been neglecting work. Thus the fifteen is Hallam, back; Fish, Isherwood, Dickinson and Harris, threequarters; Hockenhall and Duckworth, half-backs; Boardman, Preston, Shugars, Belton, Thomas, Cook, Naylor, and W. Swift, forwards.

The " A " team did splendidly against the Rangers "A " and won by 8 points to nil. R. Bate, Berry, and Short all played fine football throughout a well contested game. To-day the Juniors will be thoroughly extended at Chadderton, but the team which is selected should give a good account of itself. The 12 are: Knight; Kenyon, Berry, Brooks, and Short ; D. Davies and Jordan ; Morrison, Lunt, Harmer, Ashton and Coleman.

centre-half, who had been playing a sterling game, was injured, und was practically a passenger during the rest of the game. To this misfortune, must the defeat of Stockton Heath be chiefly attributed.

In the second half, the Sale forwards played a fine long passing game, thus taking full advantage of the weakened half back line. Before the end came Sale notched 3 goals, thereby winninz with comfort.

The Sale forwards and halves were the body of the, team, P. Robson showing up favourably, but the full backs were weak. For the home side E. Pierpoint at back played a sound game, while L. Fairclough and J. Richardson at half also showed good form.

The 2nd team journeyed to Sale, with only 10 men, and were defeated 4-1. Seeing that after half-time Stockton Heath were playing with only 8 men; two men being injured, this really speaks well for a team playing away from home. For Stockton Heath the goal was scored by W. Longdin.

div.head: IRON TRADE. Birmingham Market
div.p: THE IRON TRADE. Birmingham Market

Not much interest attaches to the meetings of the trade on the Birmingham Iron Exchange round the great public holidays, and the attendance on Thursday was quite as small as usual at such times. The great differ- ence from last year, however, is that the tone is dis- tinctly healthy, while prices are very firm, and nearly all manufacturers are full of work.

div.head: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
WEEK ENDING DECE.IIBER 17th, 1904. During the week, the following births and deaths were registered :—Warrington Registration District births, 49, deaths, 23. The excess of births over deaths was 26.

The birth-rate was ‘qual to 37.3. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 17.5 per 1,000 against 16.3 the average of the previous 4 weeks and against 224 the corresponding period of last year. The death rate from the seven chief zymo tic diseases was equal to nil per 1,000, against 1.6 the average rate of the. previous 4 weeks and against 46 the corresponding period of 1903. The ages of mortality were :- 0-1. 1-5 5-15 15-25 25-65 65—up. Tota I 8 1 2 1 8 3 23

The deaths included-1 from influenza, 1 from phthisis, 2 from other tubercular diseases, 21rom lung diseases, 1 fromheart disease, 16 from all other causes. The following cases of infectious disease have been reported during Vie week :—Scarlet fever, 17 cases ; puerperal fever, 1 case; erysipelas, 3 cases. Total number of patients in hospital, week ending 17th December, 75. METEOROLOGY.—The mean temperature was 41 Fah. and therefore 2 degrees higher than the preceding week The maximum temperature 56 F., was recorded on the 16th inst., and the minimum temperature 32 F., on the inst.
The rainfall measured 1•34 inch. The general direc- tion was S.W.
J. GUEST GOWNALL, Medical aMcer of Health,.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

PAOPLE'S EvENlNG.—Another of the pleasant evenings engineered by the Vicar, the Rev. J. R. Jones INl.A.,took place on Friday night last, at the Mission r oom. The programme consisted of (1) illustrated and well-known Christmas hymns sacred songs and (2) scenes in the life of our Lord. The lantern slides were very beauti- ful, and the audience joined heartily in singing some of the hymns thrown on the screen. Miss A. Davies sang • twice, pictures illustrating the songs appearing during their progress. The Vicar was responsible for the letter press, and Mr. J. Woodward ably manipulated the lantern. The collection taken realized a nice sum, and was given to the support of the Warrington Nursing Association. There was a large audience. OUTWARD BOUND.-0a Monday last two of our local men boarded the "Somerset" en route for Australia, these being Messrs. Joseph Foden jun., and J. Plumpton. Mr. Foden has for some years held a responsibie post with the Penketh Tanning Co., and has been a prominent Wesleyan. The hearty good wishes of all who know the voyagers go with them to their new home.

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.—At the Wesleyan School on Wednesday night, the usual weekly meeting was held, the president, Mr. A. Birch presiding. "Five minute papers," were the subjects, taken by the members. Messrs. Birch, Ambler, and J. G. Withinshaw, gave graphic and interestinc, accounts of their travels in great Britain, Switzerland, and Ireland, respectively, and their descriptions of persons and places met with in their travels were attentively listened to. The Doxology concluded a pleasant meeting.

div.head: SCALDED BY BEER.
div.p: SCALDED BY BEER.

At the Lion Brewery, Blackburn, on Thursday after noon a huge brewing pan boiled over, and some of the. liquid found its way through the floor into a lower room where a quantity of malt was stored. Two work- men named William Brown and James Henry Bradley were trying to save the malt from damage, whena fresh, stream of boiling liquid came through and scalded them. so severely that they were taken to the infirmary.

PADGATE JUNIORS, v. ORFORD TANNERY. The above fixture was played at Orford last Saturday in fine weather before a good attendance, Padgate lost the toss and played against the wind. Hughes kicked off and play settled in the home 25. Several scrummages were formed in the same 25 and the Orford backs getting possession nearly resulted in a score but Astley coining in at a critical moment kicked the ball into touch. The Padgate forwards now got possession and a good dribble by Ashton resulted in Deeley scoring. Furness failed at goal. After the drop out Orford got going and fine passing by the backs ending in them scoring and kicking a goal. Padgate played better after this and a good movement by Hughes nearly ended in a score. He ran half the length of the field and cross-kicked and Deeley meeting the ball dribbled over near the posts. The point was however disallowed. Then came the best score of the match. Furness getting the ball well in his own 25, ran half the length of the field and scored under the posts. Chamberlain kicked the goal. Half- time :—Padgate 8 points, Orford 5. Padgate had the the best of the game in the second half mainly through the fine play of the forwards. Wallace scored a good try and Furness failed to convert. Chamberlain also dropped a beautiful goal and Padgate ran out well de- served winners by 13 points to 5. Final :—Padgate 13 points, Orford 5.

-- BROUGEHON RANGERS V. WARRINGTON. Warrington were sadly handicapped for the above match on Saturday, the two centres, Isherwood and Dickinson, both bele,' absentees. The former suffered from rheumatism and the latter from an injured knee. Hockenhall and Brooks consequently went centre, Duck- worth and Harris coming in at the eleventh hour. The home side was at full strength. A strong wind blowing diagonally across the:ground interfered somewhat with the play, but a goed open game was witnessed by 9,000 people. Teams and officials : Broughton Rangers.—Poole, back; Hogg, Wilson (captain), Elarry, and Harris, three-qaarter backs; S. James and Horton, half hacks; Trotter, Smith, Scott, Orem, Winskill, Templeton, Ruddick, and Whitehead, forwards. Warrington.—Hallam (captain), back; Fish, Hocken- hall, ' Brooks and Harris, three-quarter backs; Jack Davies and Duckworth, half backs; Shugars, Naylor, Preston, Belton, Cook, Thomas, Boardman, and Swift, forwards. Referee.—Mr. D. Noble (Barrow). Touch judges, Messrs. R. H. Moore (Oldham),and W. Lancaster (Roch- dale). Warrington won the toss, and Trotter started against the wind with la long kick which was misflelded by E. Harris near the corner. From the ensuing 'scrummage Warrington were penalised and %V. Harris kicked a goal from an acute angle. This reverse was unfortunate for Warrington, bat they roused themselves to wipe it out. They, were soon on the attack, and Fish had an opportunity of equalising but failed at an average shot. J. Davies got away from the scrum, but a forward pass in the direction nf Fish spoiled the effort. Dackworth cleverly punted for touch near thellline, and the ball was sent out again by the halves, but the passing broke down at Brooks when a score ought to have ensued. A breakaway by Sam James enabled the Rangers to cross the half-way line, and the smart collaring of J. Davies gained farther ground for the home side. Fish a moment later sent the leather into touch at the Rangers quarter-flag, and try as they ,would' the home side could make but little headway against their opponents. A neat effort on the part of James came to grief at Hockenhall, and then Hallam very cleverly es:tricated himself from a difficult position amidst cheers. Hockenhall so far had played s•plenclidl7 for his side, and again proved troublesome to the Rangers with a grand dodgy run. A penalty to Warrington was taken by, Preston, but the kicks: was at: fault Play continued in the home quarter -anal by a line effort on the part of Sam James the centre line was reached. The little Welshman however, was tackled, but Harry took the transfer splendidly, and raced away past E. Harris and Brooks. Hallam bailed the way, but,the Ranger screw-kicked across the goal mouth for Hogg to gather and score beneath the posts. It was a very fine try, and when W. Harris added the extra two points the cheering was renewed. Following this roverse War- rington attacked strongly. Fish again missing a penalty shot which was anything but difficult. A moment later he ran down touch and finding his eoerse barred, he screwed the ball across and in the scramble E. Harris got hold and scored near the posts. Fish took the easiest of place-kicks and again failed. Evidently he was out of luck. The interval arrived soon after with the Rangers leading by 7 points to 3. Preston restarted and Warrington 'were in difficulties right away, and only the activity and speed of Fish saved the situation. Cross punting on the part of the Rangers did not benefit the side much, but Poole put in a fine punt which found touch well in the Warrington quarters. The visitors' forwards worked hard, and gave Duckworth and J. Davies plentp of opportunities of shining, but the latter could not get their three-quarter line going. The game] in this half was decidedly in favour of the home side, and Poole made full use of the wind. _Fish was fouled by Poole when he was going strongly, and then a rush or the Warrington forwards corned the game into Rangers' quarters. The Rangers by the aid of Same James again took up an attacking position. only to see the advantage lost a moment later owing to a penalty. Sam James again placedthe leather well for his side, but Hallam retrieved splendidly. The Rangers continued to attack until Elockenhall. inter- cepted a pass and kicked over Poole's head. He and Fish raced for the ball and it looked odds on a score, but an 'awkward bounce lost time and the situation was saved by Hogg. The Warrington front rank at this period carried the packs in great style, and the home scrummagers were having a bad time. By degrees the Broughtonians carried play to the Warrington quarters, where Fish was in evidence, only to see his efforts more than neutralised by Poole. Fine passing amongst the home backs was upset by Hockenhall, who again proved the salvation of his side. Dnckworth then charged down Wilson's kick and amidst excitement raced to the line ; the Rangers' captain only collaring him when nearly over. The Rangers kicked clear and had the satisfac- tion a moment later of having two points added to their score, as Hogg, takinc, a pass from Wilson, cleverly dropped a goal. Towards the close of the game the home side overplayed their opponents, and Hallam was severely tested.—Final : Rangers, 3 goals, 1 try (9 poinis) ; Warrington, 1 try (3 points). HULL v. BATLEY. Hull certainly shone in the nit.tch with Batley on the Boulevard Ground, and showed themselves the superior team from first to last. They had to start in face of a stiff wind, and yet for the most part they kept play in the visitors' quarters, and before the interval had scored 8 points to nil. The first try by Cook was the result of some pretty smart work by Goddard, Burchell, Abbott, and Jenkins. It was unconverted, but Good- fellow added the goal points of the second try by Goddard, for which some credit was due to Jenkins. Cook scored again. Result :—Hnll 2 goals, 3 tries (13 points), Batley nil. SALFORD v. WAKEFIELD TRINITY. There was a capital attendance at Belle Vue,Wakefield to welcome the Reds reappearance. The teams crossed over with a clean sheet. The Salford men more than held their own, and Lomas was soon in evidence. Gaining possession well inside his own half, he ran finely to near the home goal, where a passing bout was indulged in. Richards dropping a goa 1 while surround- ed by the home team. Newbould was the next to show up With a neat run, but failed to part wi th the ball, his efforts coming to nothing. Lomas here again got hold. Running again up the touch line, he passed to Thomas, who got over Lomas failed at goal. The Salford pet again got going, and had a clear field with the excep- tion of the home custodian, who brought him down finely. He however had his turn at last, running

THE REVIVAL IN WALES. DEVOTIONAL MEETINGS IN LONDON. So many of the Free Church Leaders have been brought into contact with the remarkable Revival in Wales that the National Council of the Evangelical Free Churches has been urged to hold Devotional Conferences in London. Meetings will be held on Saturday the last day of the year at Christ church, Westminster Bridge Road and will be presided over by Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., President of the National Council. The afternoon meeting will commence at 2 o'clock for ministers and other and at 3 o'clock a general testimony meeting by eye witnesses of the remarkable scenes in Wales. In the evening a Prayer and Consecration Meeting will be held at 7 o'clock. Among those who have already intimated their inten- tion of being present are :—Rev. Dr. Horton, Rev. Thomas Spurgeon, Rev. G. Campbell Morgan. D.D., Gipsy Smith, Rev. Charles Brown, Rev. J. Elvet Lewis, Rev. C. Silvester Horne. M A., Rev. J. Tolefree Parr, Rev. J. Scott Lidgets, M.A., Rev. Thomas Phillips,B.A. Mr, W. R. Lane, Dr. John Clifford, Rev. J. Monro Gibson, M.A., L.L.D. FAILURES IN ENGLAND AND WALES.—According to "Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of failures in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, December 16th,was IS4, viz.:—New bankruptcy proceedings published in the London Gazette, 92; deeds of arrangement registered, 92. The respective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were: bank- ruptcies, 93 ; deeds of arrangement, 77—total 170 ; being a net increase in bankruptcies of 26S,and ,a net increase in deeds of arrangement in 1904,t0 date, of 455.
